POLITICO https://www.politico.eu European Politics, Policy, Government News Fri, 13 Nov 2026 23:38:48 +0000 en hourly 60 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.11 EU deal on Ukraine talks overshadows AI-focused summit in Dublin https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-deal-on-ukraine-talks-overshadows-ai-focused-summit-in-dublin/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 13 Nov 2026 19:10:16 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9325266 They came to discuss AI, but EU leaders spent most of their time during a summit in Dublin on Friday grappling with questions about Ukraine — namely who should represent them in future peace talks.

Despite plenty of disagreement about whether it should be a single person (and if so, who) or a collection of them, they managed to strike a deal: Future talks would involve national security officials from Germany, France, the U.K., Italy and Poland — the so-called E5 powers — plus representatives from the European Commission and European Council. A classic European compromise.

“It is essential to have a team and to speak with one voice,” European Council President António Costa said after the summit, noting that Donald Trump had also tasked two envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, with conducting negotiations.

Ireland, which holds the EU’s rotating presidency and hosted the informal gathering, had billed the meeting as a rare chance for a high-level discussion on how to develop artificial intelligence in accordance with European values.

But the question of how to secure peace in Ukraine — and who should negotiate on Europe’s behalf — quickly dominated discussions, as leaders sparred over the format of future peace negotiations and warned about the risks of a potential deal brokered between Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Indeed, a meeting next week between the U.S. and Russian leaders has set Europe on edge, prompting warnings about a possible Yalta-type agreement in which superpowers would decide on European security questions over the heads of countries directly concerned, reminiscent of talks toward the end of World War II that divided Europe up between the four allied powers.

“That is why I want to make our message to the U.S. very clear: Please, no surprises!” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said regarding the Trump-Putin meeting, scheduled to take place during an APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 18-19. “Continue to play on Team Europe and on the same team as Ukraine. And let’s work together for genuine peace in Ukraine.”

The question of who should represent Europe in future discussions about Ukraine and the post-conflict security order was added to the summit’s agenda at the last minute, following a request from Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni.

Earlier in the day, Merz had voiced preference for a narrower group made up of officials from Berlin, Paris and London, while Kaja Kallas, the EU’s chief diplomat, argued that she was best placed to lead discussions.

“I know that the Russians don’t want me, but do we have a say on who is representing Russia? No, we don’t,” said Kallas.

“We have a really strong team,” she went on. “I’m ready to do this work with foreign ministers.”

It wasn’t all about Ukraine. Over a lunch of baked salmon fillets and crushed Ballymackenny potatoes, EU leaders grappled with the question of how to make AI more “sovereign” — that is, less dependent on U.S. and Chinese technology providers. 

“Our independence cannot be outsourced, it must be built here at home,” Macron wrote in a post on X in which he also announced that France and the Netherlands would host a meeting of “Tech Creators” on Dec. 2. 

Amid a global outage of Microsoft software (since resolved), Mistral CEO Arthur Mensch urged leaders to direct some €260 billion currently spent on foreign technology toward home-grown tech infrastructure, research and development. While the bloc has solid foundations on which to build AI solutions, Europe needs “speed, financing and a strong coordination between member states,” said Mensch.

Just as leaders including Ukraine’s president were gathering in Dublin, Russian President Vladimir Putin said he was open to Europeans joining the talks, reversing Moscow’s previous opposition. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov quickly followed up with qualifications, however, stating that Europeans must first demonstrate “genuine intention and readiness to contribute to the peace process” before being admitted — a condition that Kallas quickly dismissed as a “trap.”

“If we start to talk about what Russia is asking regarding the security architecture, we actually walk into the traps that Russia is setting us, which is that we divert attention away from that there is no ceasefire,” she told reporters in Dublin.

Other officials said that Russia’s preconditions for allowing Europe to join the talks would mean concessions to Moscow’s war demands, namely a withdrawal of NATO from European states bordering Russia, the lifting of sanctions and a ban on foreign troops in Ukraine.

Giorgio Leali, Pieter Haeck, Sebastian Starcevic, Caroline Hug and Shawn Pogatchnik contributed to this article from Dublin.

]]> en Why Europe failed to find a superhero to take on Putin https://www.politico.eu/article/why-europe-failed-to-find-a-superhero-to-take-on-vladimir-putin/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 13 Nov 2026 18:14:04 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9324267 LONDON — Some European leaders wanted a superhero negotiator to take on Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump, secure a fair peace deal for Ukraine, and safeguard the continent’s own security, as ceasefire talks gather pace. 

They were never going to find one. 

That had already become the view of diplomats and officials close to the discussions, granted anonymity to comment on the sensitive Ukraine peace process that’s dividing opinion in European capitals, even before the EU decided on Friday that it would have to be a team effort. 

The push to identify one representative to speak for Europe was understandable. The appeal of having a single, respected leader taking the reins is largely based on a desire to project European strength and unity — as well as an interest in making negotiations with Russia, the U.S. and Ukraine efficient and effective. 

Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy himself said this week he wanted Europe to identify within days who will take its place in the talks, and suggested he’d prefer it was one person (he even indicated that he had a preference, though would not reveal a name).

He didn’t get his way. Instead, leaders at a summit in Dublin on Friday, decided that the “E5” made up four big EU countries ― Germany, France, Poland and Italy ― and the U.K., plus officials from the European Commission and Council, would take the work forward as a team.

Technical discussions

The search for a top representative to fill Europe’s seat at the negotiating table at the next round of peace talks had become a political obsession in Brussels that missed at least two big points. 

The first is that the leadership level is not currently where the negotiations are at. Talks this week in Abu Dhabi were technical discussions between senior officials. The big political players like Putin and Zelenskyy were not there, never mind Trump. Russia sent a Kremlin aide to lead its team and Ukraine tasked its intelligence chief with making its case. 

If these officials make progress toward a deal, leaders will no doubt want to get involved. Ultimately, it will be leaders who sign any peace agreements that follow — and there’s no limit on the number of EU presidents or prime ministers who could join such a meeting as signatories or guarantors of the final deal. 

The next thing that needs to happen, according to both Ukraine and the U.S. envoys mediating the talks, is for Europe to join the discussion with Russia — at this technical level. 

‘Not a superstate’ 

The second point some member states and Brussels insiders were missing is structural: There are just too many European stakeholders with equally important but very distinct interests and remits, making consolidation of all the different strands under one person impossible. 

The Commission can’t negotiate Europe’s future security architecture — that’s for NATO members and national capitals to decide. But equally NATO, Paris and Berlin cannot negotiate EU sanctions or Ukraine’s accession to the bloc — these are in the Commission’s remit. 

And the idea that the “E3” — Europe’s big economic and military beasts of Germany, France and the U.K. — would let either the Commission, the European Council or NATO do it all on their behalf is not realistic. 

As one EU diplomat put it: “The reason why Europe hasn’t found one person who can represent the whole of Europe is that Europe is not a superstate.” 

In the context of the Ukraine talks, European interests encompass many EU member states but also countries like the U.K., and Norway, as well as Turkey and Moldova, the diplomat said. “Who can promise troops on the ground on behalf of the rest of Europe? Who can offer billions in financing? It’s difficult.” 

The conclusion some officials involved in the Abu Dhabi process reached was that Europe would have to be represented by a team, much as it has been already, albeit at one step removed from the main negotiating room so far. Different members of that team will own different issues. 

What Putin wants

Then there’s the question of content: What will be discussed and what will Team Europe’s collective position be? 

“What we actually say is more important than the exact configuration of the people in the room,” Sweden’s Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said on his way into Friday’s meeting of EU leaders.

The reason why American and Ukrainian officials want Europe’s participation is because they believe beginning a discussion about reshaping the continent’s security structures could unlock a more cooperative approach from Russia. 

Russia’s top negotiator Vladimir Medinsky said Europe’s security framework was the main topic discussed in Abu Dhabi this week: “The conflict in Ukraine showed that the entire security system operating after Yalta and Potsdam is working poorly, and an abscess broke through in Ukraine,” he said. 

Ukraine’s team noted that the hardline Russian approach softened a little when Moscow’s representatives saw the chance to talk about their wider demands on European security.

But Europe itself wasn’t part of that conversation.

Timing is still everything

The first thing to resolve will be on the sequencing of the negotiations — most significantly, when should Europeans allow themselves to discuss Russia’s demand to overhaul regional security? This is a critical and potentially existential question for European countries. And it is already a subject on which top EU officials are weighing their positions with care. 

Those close to the talks believe a clever way can be found to offer Russia a conversation about regional security as part of careful sequencing of the negotiations, without binding the issue completely into the final peace agreement for Ukraine. 

But different EU spokespeople are saying different things on this sequencing point, in what is either a clever strategy, or a sign of continuing disarray.

Kaja Kallas, the EU’s top centrally contracted diplomat, said there must be no discussion of wider European security architecture — such as NATO configurations, troop deployments and working forums for consultations with Russia — until after the peace deal is finalized. 

But in Abu Dhabi, EU officials signaled their readiness to allow parallel tracks in the talks,  so Ukraine’s peace settlement and Europe’s future security structures could be discussed at the same time. 

Officials in national capitals also agree that the “sequencing” of the negotiations on this point is key. Behind the scenes different countries and factions have different views on what the right strategy should be, just as they struggle with the question of whether it’s right to engage directly with Putin at all. 

And of course the question of Europe’s role may yet be moot. The U.S. envoys said on Thursday night that Putin had consented to letting Europe join the talks, but the Kremlin called this into question on Friday. 

After the negotiations in Abu Dhabi concluded this week, Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law and senior envoy, acknowledged the twin problems he faces. “If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiation,” he said.

]]> en Cut off from Europe, Russia will have to rewire its Arctic gas trade https://www.politico.eu/article/cut-off-europe-russia-rewire-arctic-gas-trade-lng-eu-ban/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 13 Nov 2026 17:56:13 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9322200 An EU ban on Russian liquefied natural gas imports starting Jan. 1, 2027 will force Moscow to find new buyers for exports from Yamal, its flagship Arctic project, and new ways to ship the gas.

Yamal’s LNG, gas that is cooled into a liquid so it can travel by ship, goes west through the Kara and Barents seas, around northern Norway and into European waters. Between January and October 2026, 81% of Yamal’s recorded deliveries were destined for Europe as companies scrambled to get ahead of the upcoming ban, according to new analysis by the NGO Urgewald. It estimates Europe’s bill for that period at €8.7 billion, already above its estimate of €7.2 billion for all of 2025.

The ban will end the long-term contracts that still tie Yamal to Europe. Russia will have to redirect the gas, most likely to buyers in Asia, and reorganize the shipping network to reach them. Longer voyages mean higher costs and fewer trips per tanker each year because of the distance.

The LNG trade “is going to look completely different,” said Malte Humpert, senior fellow and founder of the think tank Arctic Institute. The ban gives Moscow “a bigger incentive” to find another route, he said. “It’s not easy. It’s not cheap. It’s very slow,” but Russia will “figure it out.”

From black markets to new ports

An increase in black market LNG trade could be one way out. A classic shadow fleet has not been needed so far, since Yamal is not under sanctions, said Sebastian Rötters, sanctions campaigner at Urgewald.

Nor is a shadow fleet well suited to the job. They typically use old, unregistered oil tankers that can easily disguise their movements. On the other hand, there are fewer LNG carriers globally and they follow a limited number of routes, making them easier to track, said Martin Vladimirov, a senior analyst at the Center for the Study of Democracy, a think tank that follows EU sanctions policy.

One possible workaround is a “virtual swap.” Russia could sell more gas to countries such as Turkey or China, which could then sell more of their own or other countries’ gas to Europe. That would preserve Russia’s income even as its LNG is barred from European ports, Vladimirov said.

But even if Moscow finds buyers, it still has to get the LNG to them. That means Russian ships unable to access Europe will need to rebuild their logistics chains to sail farther or transfer their cargoes to other ships elsewhere before sailing on to alternative markets.

Either way, officials are already gearing up to confront the anticipated increase in black market activity. The matter requires “more attention on the European level,” said Lithuanian Energy Minister Lukas Savickas, whose government will helm the EU’s six-month rotating presidency from January.

That means a holistic approach that steps up monitoring of interconnection points, pipelines and ports across the EU rather than focusing on individual ships or companies, he said.

How far the ships have to go will be determined by who is willing to buy. If China, South Korea or Japan are the only buyers, “they have to go really far,” Humpert said, but if Moscow can sell part of the gas to Turkey, Egypt, Pakistan or Vietnam, they wouldn’t have to.

“Imagine the gas station you’ve been driving to for the last seven years, suddenly the gas station is three or four times as far away,” Humpert said. Yamal sits on Siberia’s Arctic coast. Europe was Yamal’s nearest major market, a voyage of about six to 10 days, compared with Asia, which takes much longer to reach.

East vs. West

Russia has two main ways to get Yamal’s gas to Asian buyers.

One is to sail east through Arctic waters on the Northern Sea Route. But Russia has only 15 specialized tankers capable of navigating the route in winter. They are costly to operate, so most have been used for short trips to Europe, where they can unload and return quickly, Rötters said.

Vladimir Panov, head of the Arctic Directorate at Rosatom, Russia’s state nuclear corporation, said last month it plans to send the gas east year-round, with help from a new nuclear icebreaker expected in early 2027. That will be easier said than done. Only 11 ships have made that eastward winter trip since 2018, and some returned with hull and propeller damage.

Repairs are another problem. Ships damaged in the ice can no longer be fixed in EU yards. Europe is currently the specialist in repairing icebreakers. China’s repair capacity is limited, Rötters said. The tanker Alexey Kosygin, for example, has spent an unusually long time in a Chinese shipyard after being damaged.

The other option is to sail west first. Because Russian ships cannot stop in Europe, they could transfer the gas near Murmansk from the specialized tankers to conventional carriers, which would then take it to Asia. Russia has bought an estimated 20 to 25 second-hand conventional ships for this purpose over the past year or two, Humpert said.

The shorter way to Asia would run through the Mediterranean and the Suez Canal, but Russian LNG carriers have largely avoided it since March, when the Arctic Metagaz, which was carrying gas from Russia’s sanctioned Arctic LNG 2 project, was attacked off Malta. No Russian gas has passed through the Mediterranean since, Rötters said. That leaves a route around Africa, which takes 35 to 40 days one way.

Ripple effects

That’s not to say Moscow is without options, thanks mainly to non-European companies, said Humpert, of the Arctic Institute. Novatek, the company behind Yamal, acquired two medium-ice-class vessels from a Japanese company a month ago. “I would never bet against Novatek,” he said, adding that Moscow could restore most of its Yamal LNG exports within a year or two.

Each winter voyage also gives Russia more experience navigating the frozen Arctic, Humpert said. These winter routes differ sharply from the summer routes Brussels is focused on, and Russia is currently the only country able to sail the former. What Moscow learns about ice, ships and logistics under the ban could benefit it in the future.

All this will unfold in a region the EU’s new Arctic Strategy casts as a vital part of its future trade, economic and security policy.

The effects of the ban extend well beyond Russia. At a time when the Iran war has already tightened supply, Europe will have to buy LNG elsewhere, “and most likely that LNG will be more expensive,” Humpert said. Urgewald says the benchmark price rose to €86.79 per megawatt-hour in October, up from €75.34 in September and €35 in January. Rötters said those higher prices help Moscow cover part of the cost of the longer routes.

European ports like Belgium’s Zeebrugge terminal, the largest EU destination for Yamal gas this year, will also feel the loss of that supply.

“Only 20% of European digital services run on European infrastructure,” Mistral CEO Arthur Mensch said in remarks Friday after he addressed EU national leaders during their first-ever meeting on artificial intelligence in Dublin.

Mensch didn’t specifically address the Microsoft outage, which lasted nearly 24 hours and affected millions of users in 74 countries. French President Emmanuel Macron closed the day with a post on X: “Our independence cannot be outsourced. It must be built here at home, in Europe,” he wrote. “When it comes to artificial intelligence, too, Europe has everything it takes to compete. We have no time to lose.”

An EU diplomat present at the leaders’ talks said that “we need to pick up speed, permitting and investment to compete on the world market, to have sovereignty.”

Tech sovereignty, including control over the cloud, chips and models that power AI, has been a rallying cry of the second mandate of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, and was one of the key agenda items at Friday’s gathering of the leaders of the EU’s 27 member countries.

“We have outsourced too much of our digital infrastructure to actors outside the EU,” Finnish European Parliament lawmaker Aura Salla said in a press release Friday following the outage. She suggested that government contracts specifically “must support European technology.”

Others zoned in on the risk created by relying on digital infrastructure controlled by a couple of large companies.

The Microsoft outage is a “reminder of the systemic risk created by concentrating digital infrastructure with a few global tech giants,” said Sebastian Toffaletti, secretary general of the Digital SME Alliance, in a statement shared with POLITICO.

In the U.K., the Liberal Democrat party’s tech spokesperson Victoria Collins said the outage demonstrated the need for a digital sovereign strategy, saying: “We need urgent action to stop relying on a handful of companies.”

In Germany, lawmaker Johannes Schätzl from the Social Democratic Party said it raised questions about public procurement. “Digital sovereignty must be measured by whether we can remain operational even during outages like this,” he said.

Joe Bambridge and Kilian Hocke contributed reporting.

]]> en EU countries to announce deportation hub deal with Rwanda https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-countries-to-announce-deportation-hub-deal-with-rwanda/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 13 Nov 2026 16:23:33 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9323754 EU countries are set to announce a deal on Monday to send rejected migrants to a deportation hub in Rwanda, three people familiar with the scheme confirmed.

Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands have been meeting regularly to lay the groundwork for a deal with to set up centers outside EU territory to which they can deport migrants without a legal right to stay in the EU. The deal is part of a broader push by the bloc to gain greater control over who enters the EU — and who gets to stay.

The anticipated deal, which is set to be announced in Vienna, would only apply to asylum seekers who have already run through all of their options for securing legal residence in the EU and were rejected.

The countries previously confirmed that they aim to close the first deals to set up the off-shore centers in 2026, with plans to make them operational as of next year.

The deportation hub in Rwanda would function as a pilot project and deals with other countries and involving other EU countries are likely to follow.

A recent reform of EU rules made it possible for EU members to cut deals to set up such deportation hubs with other countries on the condition that they meet international human rights standards.

Specifics of the scheme, including the nationalities of the people that would be moved to the hubs, their living conditions there and oversight of the deal, all depend on the agreement countries cut.

But human rights groups have warned that the hubs risk opening the door to human rights abuses, far removed from EU oversight or recourse.

Plans by the Conservative British government plans to deport asylum seekers to Rwanda were slapped down by the U.K. Supreme Court in 2023, which ruled the scheme unlawful. After coming into power in 2024, the Labour government shelved the plans, with then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer calling the Rwanda plan “dead and buried.”

The U.K. had aimed to move people to Rwanda to process their applications remotely, whereas the incoming deal of the EU countries would target people who have been ordered to leave the bloc’s territory.

Seb Starcevic contributed to this report.

]]> en What Vladimir Putin won in Abu Dhabi Ukraine peace talks https://www.politico.eu/article/what-vladimir-putin-won-in-abu-dhabi-ukraine-peace-talks/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 13 Nov 2026 16:18:55 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9324120 Jamie Dettmer is associate editor and a foreign affairs columnist for POLITICO.

The Russians surely must be stoked with the outcome of the latest round of U.S.-brokered Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi. In the United Arab Emirates, Donald Trump’s envoys endorsed the Kremlin’s long-standing demand for everything to be negotiated in one fell swoop.

And the U.S. president subsequently raised the prospect of a “very big” deal involving all of Europe.

The ambitious aim apparently now agreed between Washington and Moscow is to discuss all the issues together. And then to “find a pathway to settle them all at the same time,” Jared Kushner explained to reporters in a post-talks briefing in the UAE’s capital. Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, was representing the U.S. in the talks, along with Steve Witkoff, a real estate investor who is Trump’s special envoy to the Middle East.

So much for sequencing — generally seen by experienced diplomatic negotiators as crucial to any successful peace talks. And so much, too, for starting with a ceasefire or the tiresome breaking down of complex issues into discrete and manageable tasks to try to move things along while raising confidence and inspiring trust. 

To be sure, Russia and the United States won’t be able to strike a deal on their own. Ukraine will get a say, and European leaders have already pushed back against Trump’s big, beautiful deal, rejecting any attempt by the White House and the Kremlin to reshape the continent’s security architecture.

But it has been a longstanding Kremlin goal to get the U.S. to agree to the “let’s talk about everything” strategy, a process that will succeed in “diverting attention from what really is the critical issue, and that’s the war on Ukraine,” said Eugene Rumer, who served on the U.S. National Intelligence Council under President Barack Obama. 

Rumer told reporters in a briefing that the lack of sequencing speaks volumes and is a hallmark of Russian diplomacy which aims at “muddling any situation.”

It’s difficult to quibble with his pessimism. Russian President Vladimir Putin has a long track record of using peace talks to delay, obfuscate and exhaust opponents as he continues doing whatever he wants — all the while insisting that everything is interconnected and must be solved all at the same time.

Trying to solve everything means solving nothing. But then that’s the point. “It is obvious that Putin is simply stalling for time, trying to destroy or capture Ukraine or win this war of attrition, waiting for aid to stop in Europe and for Europe to be divided,” Ukrainian opposition lawmaker Mykola Kniazhytskyi told POLITICO.

The “let’s negotiate everything together” approach has been a key part of the playbook Putin and his Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov have used time and again when it comes to Ukraine, and earlier in Syria. Ukraine’s former commander-in-chief Valerii Zaluzhnyi, now his country’s ambassador to London, has been warning that it is designed to exhaust and wear down opponents and was also a classic Soviet ploy.

“Putin wants Empire, Ukrainians want freedom,” Kurt Volker, a former U.S. ambassador who served as a Special Representative for Ukraine Negotiations during Trump’s first term, told POLITICO.  “The rest is detail.” Assumptions that Putin wants peace, will negotiate seriously, or will accept a reasonable deal, “are all misguided,” he added.

Negotiations as a weapon of war can be used to distract, stall, allow time to maneuver and to ensnare the well-meaning — something that was highlighted between 2014 and 2017, when Lavrov and then U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry “negotiated” over Syria. The talks helped Moscow save Syria’s Bashar al-Assad from defeat, persuading then-president Obama to take his finger off the trigger and ignore his own red line on Damascus’ use of chemical weapons.

The only other top Kremlin aide as relentless as Lavrov in this technique of exhaustive obfuscation is Putin’s favorite “historian,” Vladimir Medinsky, who served as an arch-patriotic culture minister from 2012 to 2020. An advocate of putting up statues of Joseph Stalin, he has led the Russian delegation in talks with Ukraine stretching back to Istanbul in 2025. There he invoked the Great Northern War of 1700-21 as a warning that Russia is ready to fight Ukraine for as long as it takes to win. Medinsky again led the Russian delegation in Abu Dhabi.

In fact, Moscow’s red lines have not shifted one iota in the years since Putin launched his full-scale invasion. The Russian leader and his top aides have emphatically outlined them for years — conditions that would, in effect, rip the nation of Ukraine to shreds. They want guarantees that Kyiv will never join NATO, that it will remain geopolitically neutral and unable to command its own fate, with severe limitations placed on stockpiles of weapons and the size of its army. Moscow also wants Crimea and the four eastern regions it claims as part of the Russian Federation to be internationally recognized as such.

And until then — as Medinsky has bragged — Russia will continue to wage war.

]]> en Whitehall to increase face-to-face job interviews after surge in AI applications https://www.politico.eu/article/whitehall-increase-in-person-job-interviews-after-ai-applications/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 13 Nov 2026 15:00:00 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9322536 LONDON — The U.K. civil service plans to hold more in-person job interviews and diminish the role of written candidate statements in an attempt to combat a surge in applications created by AI.

Recruiting managers have seen a sharp rise in the number of applications for each role without any change to the overall number of viable candidates across the system, said a U.K. government official with knowledge of the conversations not authorized to speak publicly.

Cabinet Secretary Antonia Romeo believes some applicants are using AI to generate bland personal statements, meaning they can apply for more roles but fail to show their personal skills. 

In the most extreme cases, entire applications — even virtual interviews — appeared to have been generated by bots and not human beings, the official added.

There is at least one case in which civil servants became so suspicious during a virtual video call that the candidate was not a real person that they terminated the interview early.

The official said the civil service plans to move away from personal statements — and for flagship recruitment schemes, leaders are looking at reintroducing compulsory face-to-face interviews.

Fewer personal statements

The changes are likely to form part of a wider review of Whitehall which Romeo is due to deliver to Prime Minister Andy Burnham by summer 2027.

Romeo said in her annual lecture on Tuesday that she planned to “strip back and simplify” Whitehall recruitment to attract the most talented people from all backgrounds, adding she wanted to end “formulaic job ads, generic interviews and slow processes.”

This includes scrapping “success profiles,” a core feature of the civil service’s bureaucratic recruitment process. A new selection framework is due to be launched from April 2027.

However, a rise in face-to-face interviews will also mean some recruitment takes longer — just as civil service budgets are under intense pressure.

It is also an example of the challenge facing ministers and officials who plan to embed more AI into the civil service itself. 

Romeo said on Tuesday that AI would “radically rewrite” the way Whitehall works, including with “frontier teams” in departments with looser recruitment rules and a more AI-focused “Fast Stream” program for university graduates.

Dave Penman, general secretary of the First Division Association union for senior civil servants, said he had also seen an uptick in suspected AI-generated applications to the union. “These legitimate concerns don’t mean that the whole system is broken and everyone applying for jobs is faking it. I suspect what the civil service is facing is similar to many other areas of recruitment.”

]]> en EU institutions survive Microsoft outage unscathed https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-institutions-survive-microsoft-outage-unscathed/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 13 Nov 2026 13:36:35 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9322083 BRUSSELS — The European Union institutions kept calm and carried on regulating on Friday, as many other parts of the world muttered at their computers over a massive digital outage at U.S. tech leader Microsoft.

The European Commission, Council of the EU and European Parliament were able to carry on business as usual, with systems remaining largely unaffected.

Microsoft’s global outage, which disrupted Outlook, Teams and Copilot started on Thursday, with internet traffic monitoring site Downdetector reporting issues in at least 74 countries. The tracker logged nearly 140,000 reports of Outlook problems at its peak.

Microsoft on Friday morning said recovery was still uneven. “At this time, we have no evidence of malicious activity associated with this incident. We will continue to treat this with urgency until full mitigation,” it said.

At the European Commission “the impact … is very limited and does not affect our operations,” spokesperson Thomas Regnier told POLITICO. He said the outage had a “minor impact on a limited number of applications, such as the slowness of SharePoint.” Outlook and Teams were “fully operational,” Regnier said.

The Council of the EU, which gathers representatives of national governments, also carried on work: Outlook and Teams were “working on our side,” a Council official told POLITICO, declining to give more details on the institution’s IT setup.

The Parliament’s press service said in a statement to POLITICO that it was unaffected and was monitoring the situation as a precaution.

The outage is exposing the reliance of companies and governments on Microsoft services — an issue that has also been a longstanding concern in Europe among proponents of keeping more control over IT and digital infrastructure.

In October last year, a similar outage of Amazon Web Services servers prompted immediate calls for Europe to boost its tech sovereignty.

Efforts to move away from American tech providers got a boost in the past two years due to concerns that the U.S. administration of Donald Trump could disrupt digital services in Europe for political gain. Governments across Europe have launched a wide range of initiatives to boost local competitors to U.S. Big Tech and build public services on homegrown platforms.

One example is the government of Germany’s northernmost state of Schleswig-Holstein, which in 2025 moved about 40,000 mailboxes from Microsoft Exchange and Outlook to open-source alternatives to reduce their reliance on U.S. tech.

The state’s digitalization minister, Dirk Schrödter, said in a comment to POLITICO on Friday that disruptions like the Microsoft outage “must be taken very seriously,” whether the state uses open-source software or products from individual providers. “We must be able to intervene ourselves at any time if problems arise,” he said.

Francesca Micheletti contributed to this report.

“Today, the leaders agreed that our European team for the negotiations on peace in Ukraine is the European Union institutions and the E5 of the ‘Coalition of the Willing’,” European Council president António Costa told reporters after the meeting on Friday (13 November).

Under the arrangement, the EU will take the lead on Ukraine’s “European future, its reconstruction, and prosperity”, while security guarantees “must be addressed within the framework of the coalition of the willing, in close coordination with Nato”, Costa said.

“Europe must speak with one clear and united voice in all discussions that shape the future of Ukraine and the security of our continent,” he added.

Read more

Trump vows ‘beautiful’ Russia deal, as EU agonises over which envoy to send to Ukraine peace talks

The decision largely formalises the current arrangement, in which France, Germany and the UK sit at the table alongside Italy and Björn Seibert, chief of staff to European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen.

Earlier on Friday, a senior diplomat called that set-up “not ideal”.

It also leaves open whether foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas will take a seat. EU capitals did support sending her to the talks, the diplomat said, adding that it was “just not possible”.

‘Setting traps’

Kallas, for her part, defended her role as she arrived at the summit, and warned that Russia was “setting traps” by trying to divert attention from its aggression with a debate on Europe’s security architecture and the role of Nato.

    ]]>         ‘Very overdue’ – MEPs welcome proxy voting for pregnant members and new mothers https://euobserver.com/248856/very-overdue-meps-welcome-proxy-voting-for-pregnant-members-and-new-mothers/ Fri, 13 Nov 2026 15:39:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=248856 An overwhelming majority in the European Parliament agreed MEPs can delegate their vote to another member in the months before and after childbirth, retaining their say in key files.]]> An overwhelming majority in the European Parliament has agreed that MEPs can delegate their vote to another member in the months before and after childbirth, retaining their say in key files.

    The statute change, passed with 578 votes for, 25 against, and 4 abstentions on Thursday (12 November) will mean that an MEP will be able to vote for one other colleague for three months before, and six months after, childbirth.

    It is “well overdue” that the rules for voting change, Sigrid Friis, a Renew Europe MEP from Denmark told EUobserver. She herself worked up until her due date, provoking some comments about the need for a midwife in the parliament.

    “No member should lose her right to vote because of becoming a mother,” declared the parliament’s president Roberta Metsola in a statement back in April.

    Read more

    MEPs discuss proxy voting for pregnant women and new mothers

    Delegating one’s vote would only apply for the plenary sessions, with both the absent MEP and the one voting for them would be identified in the minutes for transparency’s sake.

    Maria Ohisalo, a Finnish Green MEP, told EUobserver she is “really happy” about the reform.

    “I voted for hours with our baby in the plenary,” she said, recalling her infant was not eligible for child care during the first Strasbourg plenary after giving birth.

    Another MEP who preferred to stay anonymous recalls some colleagues’ annoyance at taking multiple breaks during trilogue negotiations when she was with her newborn.

    The initiative, started by parliament president Roberta Metsola in 2025, still needs an EU Commission opinion and a go-ahead from the council before a final vote in the parliament.

    Estonian prime minister Kristen Michal has laid out how to build up Europe’s defences. He also urges the use of Russian assets frozen in Belgium, and discusses Baltic expertise in fighting Putin. The liberal leader spoke with Ondřej Kundra in early November.

    Has anything brought you satisfaction recently as a politician?

    Kristen Michal: I recently attended the opening of Estonia’s largest timber building in northern Estonia. It may sound amusing this would bring joy to a prime minister, but in my previous role as environment minister, I launched this project in 2023.

    It is a truly beautiful area, both in nature and culture – I recommend visiting. It has a maritime museum in a former seaplane harbour, as well as Estonia’s only submarine. And beside it stands the largest wooden building of its kind: our new natural history museum, under whose roof we want to bring together institutions focused on ecology and climate.

    It is not merely a wooden structure; it is also probably one of most cost-effective buildings, amounting to about €2,100 to €2,200 per square metre.

    One of our state agencies began its construction, and I was genuinely emotional at the opening ceremony – it is rewarding for a politician to see that something they started was actually completed.

    Estonia is one of the foresighted Baltic member states which has warned for years about the Russian threat. EU Commission president Ursula von der Leyen has recognised that Baltic warnings about Russian expansionism unfortunately came true…

    I would probably have been happier if Baltic states had not been right. We spoke about Russia in the past, warning that Putin had imperial dreams of restoring the Soviet Union, that he was not concerned solely with Ukrainian territory, but also with stripping Ukraine of its sovereignty, or that he had further territorial ambitions. It would of course have been preferable if our warnings had not been proven wrong. But they were proven right.

    Even before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, you warned the West about energy dependence on Russia and about unpreparedness for cyber threats. Now, Europe has learned its lesson. Are you satisfied that EU member states have woken up to reality, or do you think they remain blind to such threats?

    ]]>         The impact of the ICJ’s genocide ruling in Myanmar will go far beyond Asia https://euobserver.com/248744/the-impact-of-the-icjs-genocide-ruling-in-myanmar-will-go-far-beyond-asia/ Fri, 13 Nov 2026 10:21:20 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=248744 On 19 November, the International Court of Justice will deliver its judgement in The Gambia v Myanmar case. The case concerns the Rohingya, but its implications extend well beyond Myanmar. The Court’s interpretation of the Genocide Convention may also matter for the ongoing case brought by South Africa against Israel — and for the credibility of international justice itself.]]> At first sight, a case concerning the Rohingya in Myanmar may seem remote to European readers. But the judgment the International Court of Justice (ICJ) is due to deliver on 19 November addresses questions that go to the heart of international law: when can a state be held responsible for genocide, what evidence is required to establish genocidal intent, and how should the court assess the conduct of state authorities?

    The case was brought by The Gambia, which alleges that Myanmar violated the 1948 Genocide Convention through its treatment of the Rohingya. The court’s answer will matter not only to the victims of the alleged crimes, but also to the interpretation and application of the Convention in other cases.

    One of the most important precedents is the court’s 2007 judgment in Bosnia and Herzegovina v Serbia and Montenegro. Bosnia brought its case in 1993, alleging that Serbia was responsible for genocide committed during the Yugoslav war. In 2007, the court found that genocide had been committed in Srebrenica in July 1995.

    But it did not find that the acts of genocide could be attributed to Serbia. It held that Serbia had nevertheless breached its obligations to prevent genocide and to punish those responsible.

    The distinction is fundamental. The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) dealt with the individual criminal responsibility of those who committed or participated in the crimes.

    The ICJ, by contrast, had to determine whether the conduct could be attributed to a state and whether Serbia had breached its obligations under the Genocide Convention.

    Read more

    After students voted out Vučić, can Serbia’s uprising against ‘evil’ change how the state really works?

    The court also set a demanding standard of proof. It held that allegations involving charges of exceptional gravity, such as genocide, must be established by “fully conclusive” evidence, and that it must be “fully convinced” that the allegations have been clearly established.

    Where genocidal intent is not directly established but inferred from a pattern of conduct, the court added that this intent must be the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the acts in question.

    These requirements attracted criticism. Some considered that the court had effectively approached the question as if it were deciding the criminal guilt of an individual, rather than the international responsibility of a state.

    Others argued that requiring genocidal intent to be the only reasonable inference set an exceptionally high threshold, making it particularly difficult to establish genocide through circumstantial evidence.

    I was an ICTY judge when the ICJ delivered its judgment in 2007. I followed it with particular interest — and some surprise. At the tribunal, we were dealing every day with the individual criminal responsibility of those involved in the crimes committed in Bosnia.

    The evidence concerning Srebrenica and the role of Bosnian Serb political and military leaders was familiar to us. Yet the ICJ was operating within a different legal framework, with a different question to answer.

    Read more

    [Interview] Ex-Bosnia envoy sees no risk of renewed violence, but the fractured country’s EU dream is rotting away

    In its 2015 judgment in Croatia v Serbia, the court largely maintained its approach. It rejected both Croatia’s claim and Serbia’s counterclaim, finding that neither side had established the specific intent required to prove genocide. The demanding standard of proof therefore remains an important feature of the court’s jurisprudence.

    The Gambia v Myanmar proceedings bring these questions back before the court. The judges will have to assess how genocidal intent can be established, including through patterns of conduct and circumstantial evidence, and how the actions of state officials engage the responsibility of the state.

    Myanmar, unsurprisingly, argues for continuity with the court’s established case law. The judgment will show how the court applies that jurisprudence to the evidence before it — and whether it offers further clarification.

    The wider interest in the case is reflected in the participation of eleven states under Article 63 of the court’s Statute: Belgium, Canada, Denmark, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, France, Germany, Ireland, the Maldives, the Netherlands, Slovenia and the United Kingdom. They are not parties to the dispute. They have intervened because they consider that the interpretation of the Genocide Convention is at stake. Under Article 63, the court’s interpretation of the Convention will also be binding on the states that have intervened.

    Belgium’s participation is particularly significant. It is not simply an observer of proceedings taking place far away. By intervening, Belgium has chosen to take a position on the interpretation of a treaty that lies at the centre of the international legal order.

    The judgment will also be closely followed in the case brought by South Africa against Israel. Both proceedings concern the same Genocide Convention, and the ICJ’s reasoning on the interpretation of its provisions, the assessment of evidence and the establishment of genocidal intent may be relevant to the South Africa case.

    The Myanmar judgment will not decide that case, nor should its outcome be prejudged. But the court’s legal reasoning will inevitably attract attention. The two proceedings raise questions that are closely connected, even though their facts and procedural stages are different.

    There is another reason why the composition of the court has attracted attention. Gambia appointed Navi Pillay as its ad hoc judge, while Myanmar appointed the German international law scholar Claus Kreß. Pillay is a distinguished international jurist: she served as President of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, was a judge at the International Criminal Court (ICC) and later served as UN High Commissioner for Human Rights. In October, she was awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote peace and international law.

    German students, Belgian demonstrators, and young Romanians, Spanish or Greeks taking to the streets are all calling for political transformation.

    Europe is getting older

    On 1 January 2025, 22 percent of the European Union’s population was aged 65 or over, compared with 17 percent in 2005. That represents approximately 99 million people. The EU’s median age has also risen from 39.6 to 44.9 years over the same period, according to Eurostat.

    The post-war decades in Europe were built around an ambitious social promise: that education, employment and social protection could offer each generation better prospects than the previous one. The expansion of welfare states, public education and social security helped establish a model in which economic growth was accompanied by expectations of social mobility.

    Today, that expectation is under pressure.

    Rising public debt, budgetary constraints and austerity policies have forced governments to reconsider spending priorities. Education, healthcare and social protection have increasingly become part of difficult budget negotiations. And for younger generations achieving the same degree of financial and social security, as the two previous generations seem suddenly out of reach.

    Different countries, shared frustrations

    Brussels, the EU capital as well as the Belgian one, has been the scene of several demonstrations, just like other European capitals, since October, bringing together thousands of people. With no agreement on a budget, the coalition government is in freefall. Centre-right prime minister Bart de Wever submitted his resignation to the king on 2 October, but it was not accepted.

    But cuts still need to be made. Belgium’s public deficit reached €33.22bn last year, representing 5.2 percent of its GDP.

    In its 2026 conclusions, the National Bank of Belgium points out that “the decline in revenue could not be offset by spending restraint.”

    The reforms targeted pensions, unemployment benefits, healthcare and public spending – the social protection of the state.

    “Those Who Sow Misery Reap Anger,” was the slogan on some protestors’ placards.

    The demonstrations were led by trade unions, but young people have also joined in. Students and secondary-school pupils have expressed concerns about education funding, school conditions, access to higher education and their future employment prospects.

    The German initiative Gen Z Steht Auf [Gen Z Stands Up] took it in a different way. The movement began with youth, as it was the case in France – the biggest youth movement across Europe yet.  

    The Germans called for demonstrations in 21 cities on 31 October across the country. And their demands extended beyond education. Greater investment in social security, health care and affordable housing while opposing military conscription.

    Production: By Europod, in co-production with Sphera Network.

    EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms.

    Find the full transcript below:

    Ukraine’s war effort depends heavily on two American tools: Starlink and Starshield. Both belong to Elon Musk’s SpaceX, and both can be switched off. Europe says it wants to reduce that dependence.

    Is it possible, and why is Europe so far behind? Starlink is SpaceX’s satellite internet service. It’s sold to the general public, to companies and to armies. It relies on a constellation of around 10,000 satellites in low orbit, which makes it possible to get a connection almost anywhere on Earth.

    Starshield is the version designed for governments and militaries. It uses the same technology, but with dedicated satellites and dedicated encryption. In other words, it’s more secure.

    Read more

    Russia faces a strategic crisis and record losses, but thanks to Trump it sees things positively (Ukraine Battlefield update, Day 1,713)

    The problem is that its use completely depends on the goodwill of Elon Musk. But also on the US government. Starshield is a government system, and it’s Washington that actually makes it available to Ukraine.

    This has already led to some awkward situations. A few weeks ago, Ukraine noticed that the speed of its drones had been throttled overnight. The explanation was clear: it was an American move. The issue has since been resolved, but it illustrates a real unease.

    So how did Ukraine end up in this position? At the start of the war, the country’s cable-based internet infrastructure was damaged. On the battlefield, the army now uses SpaceX terminals to receive internet signal, because they’re small and very practical.

    And that is exactly what Europeans don’t offer. Most European satellites are in high orbit. They cover very large areas, but they have two drawbacks in wartime. Because they are further away, the delay in transmission is longer. Second, the equipment needed to receive the signal is much bulkier, so it is not suited to the front line.

    Elon Musk made a very strategic choice: putting tens of thousands of satellites in low orbit.  It’s much cheaper, and much easier to operate. Now could Europeans compete on this market?

    The closest European equivalent, on a smaller scale, is the OneWeb constellation, run by the French company Eutelsat. Eutelsat was originally a European intergovernmental organisation. But it was dismantled and its activity has been taken over by a company.

    The French state is still its largest shareholder, with around a third of the shares. The United Kingdom and an Indian group also hold stakes.

    Through OneWeb, Eutelsat has around 680 satellites, in both low and high orbit. The company says it could replace Starlink in the medium term, meaning sometime in the 2030s.

    It plans to reinforce its fleet with several hundred new satellites. But most of them will actually replace older ones. So it’s not a big increase, compared with Starlink.

    Read more

    Russia’s fake war maps at Abu Dhabi peace talks aren’t fooling anyone (Ukraine Battlefield update, Day 1,721)

    There is also another project designed to secure European connections. It’s called IRIS². This one is a European project, carried out by several companies, including Eutelsat. The EU is its main customer. Unlike OneWeb, it’s not a commercial venture. But both share the same goal: reducing dependence on Starlink.

    The ambition is a constellation of at least 348 satellites by 2030, with deployment starting in 2029. So again, fewer than a thousand. That’s still far from Starlink.

    But here, it’s worth saying that satellites in low orbit are much cheaper to put in place, which also explains the sheer volume SpaceX has been able to launch in recent years.

    With far fewer satellites, but in higher orbit, Europeans can also cover the whole planet. It’s just that the system isn’t as flexible.

    Finally, is money part of the explanation? Yes, of course. The United States spends around six times more on its space programmes, civil and military, than Europeans do.

    There’s also another factor that helps SpaceX deploy thousands of satellites at low cost: it has its own launcher, the Falcon 9.

    Eutelsat, on the other hand, has to buy launches from third parties. So it’s much more expensive, and it doesn’t control the pace at which it can put satellites into orbit.

    Before wrapping up, a quick word about China, another big actor. It’s quite new in the space industry, and it’s not really spending huge amounts of money for the moment. But it’s worth keeping an eye on Beijing on this front too.

    ]]>         War of propaganda: Russia calls Ukraine a ‘burden’ and uses Moldova as a ‘testing ground’ to sabotage EU enlargement https://euobserver.com/247967/war-of-propaganda-russia-calls-ukraine-a-burden-and-uses-moldova-as-a-testing-ground-to-sabotage-eu-enlargement/ Wed, 11 Nov 2026 14:32:04 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247967 From fake celebrity sex scandals to ominous warnings about land seizures and soaring bills, Kremlin-linked campaigns are working to turn ordinary voters against EU accession long before any referendum is held.]]> As the saying goes, the first casualty of war is the truth. But in the case of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, it seems the truth had been under attack for a while. 

    As recently as this summer, claims that Russia had actually made significant battlefield gains were debunked after analysis found that interpretation was based on misuse of a report which actually found Ukraine had made the greater advances.

    It chimes with the continuing battle for control of the narrative over Ukraine, not least when it comes to the prospect of that country, and possibly its neighbour, Moldova, ultimately joining the EU.

    Media organisations in those countries have become acutely aware of what they say is Russian disinformation about EU enlargement, often circulated via the Telegram app and other online platforms such as Facebook.

    They have heard various narratives against EU membership, such as a purported loss of state sovereignty, of the EU wishing to prolong a ‘proxy war’ with Russia through Ukraine, and even of Ukraine being divided up between EU member states.

    As Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine approaches its sixth year, the likelihood of it joining the EU is still being actively debated. Neighbouring Moldova is also driving towards EU membership, even though it is aware that Russia is actively opposed. 

    It means both countries, and others in the region where people have expressed a desire to join the EU, such as Georgia, find themselves the subject of online campaigns which, critics say, are aimed at undermining those efforts.

    Read more

    Moldova seen as ‘best performer’ on EU-accession reforms, despite onslaught of Russian sabotage

    Disinformation is not new

    It is also hard to argue that this is a new phenomenon. Over 10 years ago, the EU set up a task force in order to challenge “Russia’s ongoing disinformation campaigns”. 

    A number of months after the war began in 2022, the OECD think-tank in Paris published a policy paper on ‘Disinformation and Russia’s War of Aggression against Ukraine’, in which it said: “The Russian disinformation narratives are often false, or obscure facts with half-truths and ‘whataboutisms’.” 

    And just last year the delegation of the European Union to Ukraine looked at information manipulation and disinformation that summer targeting Ukraine-EU relations.

    It was a topic of discussion when the deputy prime minister for European integration of Moldova, Cristina Gherasimov, visited Ireland earlier this year. 

    Speaking to The Journal in Dublin last February, Gherasimov said that disinformation “continues constantly”.

    Read more

    How EU hopes to ‘shield’ elections against Moscow’s propaganda

    “This is one of the most powerful tools of Moscow: disinformation, not necessarily about our own country or process in our own country, but a narrative that targets the EU as such. It targets the EU credibility for candidate countries or aspiring countries, for EU membership.

    “Some of the narratives are usually around the future of candidate countries in the EU, saying that we are not ready,” she said.

    This argument, she added, also centred on the idea of the EU as weak and unable to stand up for its own citizens.

    Another line is that new entrant countries would be seen as a ‘poor relation’ and would not be as competitive when it comes to agriculture and other areas once they joined the EU.

    “What we’ve learned from our own elections is that disinformation does not stop after the elections, it continues constantly, and it adapts very quickly in terms of the narratives that it promotes, depending on the vulnerabilities that exist in each society that is targeted,” she added.

    “One very usual narrative targeting the EU is that all the land will be expropriated once Moldova joins the European Union, and that is meant to draw equal lines with how it used to be during the Soviet Union period for us, and that is meant to inflict fear that the EU is not there to support and protect its citizens, but it’s there to actually prey on them,” said Gherasimov.

    Ukrainian accession efforts labelled ‘futile’?

    Moldova knows about disinformation: a report in the New York Times last September said the Stimson Center – a research organisation in Washington – called the country “a testing ground for hybrid warfare operations” that “are likely to shape similar efforts” across Europe. 

    The same New York Times article referred to how, ahead of Moldova’s parliamentary election, social media platforms were flooded with fabricated posts, videos and websites, sometimes created using AI. 

    As outlined in this Euronews report, one post even impersonated the celebrity magazine OK! with a false story declaring “Moldovan president in celebrity sperm scandal!”. The concocted story, which incorrectly claimed that president Maia Sandu was buying sperm from gay celebrity donors to have a child, falsely used the name of a real reporter. 

    This demonstrates how disinformation frequently attempts to erode political reputations and steer voters towards particular political agendas. 

    Read more

    EU accession of Moldova and Ukraine is alternative to Nato, as Russia draws new Iron Curtain in Europe

    As with other forms of political disinformation, this takes many forms when it comes to EU accession, according to Vladyslav Lesyk, a journalist at Ukrainian media outlet Rubryka.

    “For instance, Russian sources have spread fakes asserting that granting candidate status is a merely formal decision that offers no actual benefits.     “Another Russian narrative suggests that joining the EU would mean Ukraine losing its sovereignty. This builds upon a broader Russian narrative, maintained since the start of the Russo-Ukrainian war in 2014, which portrays Ukraine as a state with an illegitimate government controlled by the West, specifically the EU and the US,” said Lesyk.

    Read more

    Wave of Russian sabotage attacks exposes counter-intelligence gaps on Nato’s eastern flank

    Disinformation is not new: EUvsDisinfo documents numerous past examples, including the infamous false story from 2014 of a boy allegedly being crucified by Ukrainian nationals in Slovyansk. This was cited to be part of a Kremlin-orchestrated campaign targeted at inciting hatred against Ukrainians.

    Ukraine has long articulated a desire to join the EU and the process is well underway. Since June 2022, Ukraine has official EU candidate status, with accession negotiations having formally started. Last September Ukraine successfully completed its screening process.

    Billions of euros in financial assistance have already been provided, while the EU has repeatedly affirmed its support for Ukraine’s independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity.

    On the flip side, Lesyk said narratives spread in European countries lean into the idea of Ukraine becoming a “burden” on EU member states. 

    “In this context, Ukraine is presented as a poor and corrupt state whose accession would supposedly drain the European budget. A specific sub-narrative focuses on the negative impact of Ukrainian grain on European farming. Russians have been spreading the narrative of ‘harmful’ Ukrainian grain for several years to sow discord,” he said.

    Yet as this analysis from the European Policy Centre points out, Ukraine joining the EU would have very obvious benefits – including opening up the country’s energy potential to the EU, boosting EU food security, and providing ready trade in critical minerals.

    Lesyk said Telegram is the primary hub for disseminating these Russian narratives in Ukraine, as it allows for the use of anonymous channels and is one of the most popular sources of information in the country. 

    Regarding Moldova, media and fact-checking organisations have tracked a number of lines of attack regarding proposed EU membership, ranging from farms there closing due to Moldovan agricultural products not being in demand, to higher utility bills, and same-sex marriage. 

    These were analysed in depth by the website NewsMaker.md. Romanian fact-checking website Veridica has tracked numerous disinformation campaigns, including that Moldova could become a destination for migrants, could lose its statehood, or even be annexed by Romania.

    Read more

    [Interview] ‘Whenever we take pro-European political decisions, Russia cut or reduced gas supplies’. Moldova energy minister Dorin Junghietu on why Chișinău is betting on diversification

    In Georgia, another country seemingly at a crossroads when it comes to possible EU membership, websites such as OC Media have tracked what they believe are coordinated Russian information operations in recent years.

    Salome Khvedelidze of OC Media said some of this runs on Facebook and other platforms. The International Society for Fair Elections and Democracy detailed material it described as “the dissemination of anti-Western, particularly anti-EU narratives”.

    Since Russia’s war against Ukraine in 2022, Georgia has turned increasingly authoritarian, suspending EU accession talks and deepening its ties with Moscow.

    Recently, the ruling Georgian Dream party sought to ban the five main opposition parties – a move which is currently being fought in court. The European Parliament warned that this puts the country’s path towards EU membership at risk.

    According to Khvedelidze: “What makes Georgia different from Ukraine and Moldova, however, is where the main source of anti-EU propaganda actually comes from.”

    “In Ukraine and Moldova, disinformation about EU membership is driven by Russian proxies, Russia-backed/funded media, and certain political figures, while the governments themselves are pro-European,” she said.

    Arguably, it gives the impression of a message that is always changing but always the same. According to Cristina Gherasimov: “It adapts very quickly in terms of the narratives that it promotes, depending on the vulnerabilities that exist in each society that is targeted,” she added.

    It is not always straightforward to verify which narratives come directly from Russia and which originate elsewhere, but there is little doubt about Russia’s attitude towards the EU, and its history of spreading disinformation abroad.

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/13/microsoft-outage-shakes-up-companies-local-governments</link>
      <description><p>Local officials warn some services remain unavailable even as Outlook starts to resume normal operations after outage</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/live/2026/nov/13/microsoft-outage-down-today-live-update-outlook-teams-365-when-fixed-latest-status-cause-news">Microsoft outage – live updates</a></p></li></ul><p>The Microsoft Outlook outage has shaken up companies and local governments across the US that use its suite of email, calendar, video conferencing and cloud storage systems.</p><p>Even as Outlook started to resume normal operations Friday morning, local leaders from across the country, including in Miami, Maryland and Los Angeles, warned residents that certain staff or services were still unavailable due to the outage that started around 1pm ET on Thursday.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/13/microsoft-outage-shakes-up-companies-local-governments">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Nationwide FAA ground stop: nearly 11,000 flights delayed or canceled at airports across the US</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/13/faa-nationwide-ground-stop-flights</link>
      <description><p>Transportation secretary said stoppage is due to ‘communication issue’ and homeland security says there’s no indication of ‘nefarious attack’</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live/2026/nov/13/us-politics-latest-news-updates-democrats-republicans-donald-trump-van-hollen-chuck-schumer">FAA grounds thousands of flights – live</a></p></li></ul><p>The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a nationwide ground stop for all flights in the US on Friday, delaying or canceling more than 11,000 US flights, according to aviation tracker <a href="https://www.flightaware.com/live/cancelled/">FlightAware</a>, and throwing airports into sudden chaos.</p><p>In a post on X, Sean Duffy, the US transportation secretary, said the stoppage is due to “a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers” and that the FAA’s technicians are looking into the matter.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/13/faa-nationwide-ground-stop-flights">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/12/jensen-huang-affair-timeline</link>
      <description><p>CEO behind the meteoric rise of Nvidia stepped down after it was revealed he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy </p><p>Jensen Huang has stepped down as CEO of <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/nvidia">Nvidia</a>, the company at the center of the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/artificialintelligenceai">AI</a> boom, after leading it for more than 30 years.</p><p>Huang, an electrical engineer by education, stewarded the company from a $1bn firm when it went public in 1999 to a company valued at more than $4tn in 2026. But in a matter of days, after it was revealed he had an extramarital affair with a woman that US officials believe to be a Chinese spy, Huang managed to wipe more than $600bn from the company’s valuation.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/12/jensen-huang-affair-timeline">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Rallies are planned at more than US 40 campuses as workers seeking better pay and conditions decry stalled talks</p><p>Starbucks baristas, students, elected officials and allies are planning rallies at <a href="https://starbucksworkersunited.controlshift.app/events?link_id=2&amp;can_id=debd8d2ad19f005d15f9bbdff314d42a&amp;source=email-nov-12-day-of-action-for-starbucks-baristas&amp;email_referrer=email_3490793&amp;email_subject=nov-12-day-of-action-for-starbucks-baristas&amp;&amp;">over 40 college campuses</a> across the US on Thursday to support the Starbucks Workers United <a href="https://www.boycottstarbucks.net/">boycott campaign</a> as the union nears five years of deadlock with the company over contract negotiations.</p><p>Starbucks Workers United is <a href="https://sbworkersunited.org/what-were-fighting-for-updates-on-contract-bargaining/">seeking</a> better pay and stronger staffing levels, including a $17 an hour minimum wage for baristas and a minimum staffing of three workers per store. It has called on the public to <a href="https://www.boycottstarbucks.net/">boycott</a> Starbucks until its first contract is reached.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/12/starbucks-workers-campus-rally-contract-talks">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Sales of built units fell to 3.75m in October, down by 8.8% from last year, with mortgage rates at nearly three-year high</p><p>US existing home sales hit a 16-year low in October as buyers were driven away by high <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/money/mortgage-rates">mortgage rates</a> and rising inflation, according to new data released on Wednesday.</p><p>Sales of already built units dropped to 3.75m in October, down by 8.8% from last year, the National Association of Realtors (NAR) reported. The median existing-home sales price increased slightly to $416,700.       <title>Democrats’ US election sweep brings the price of their promised social contract into focus</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/11/democrats-election-medicaid-costs</link>
      <description><p>‘The post-election wish list is about to run into harsh fiscal reality: there is no money’</p><p>Is this an opportunity for a new America? As the Reagan revolution four decades ago launched US society down the path to low taxes and meager solidarity, perhaps the Republican bloodbath last week could turn US politics toward building a new social contract anchored on an aspiration to equitable prosperity.</p><p>One can sense the ambition of the bumper new crop of <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/democrats">Democrats</a> ushered to power last week, calling for support for programs for children and their parents; emphatically endorsing the long-held dream of Medicare for All. The project includes rolling back <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/donaldtrump">Donald Trump</a>’s cuts to Medicaid and food stamps, and restoring subsidies for health insurance under the Affordable Care Act that Republicans allowed to expire. And that’s just the start.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/11/democrats-election-medicaid-costs">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <pubDate>Wed, 11 Nov 2026 11:00:46 GMT</pubDate>
      <guid>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/11/democrats-election-medicaid-costs</guid>
      <media:content width="140" url="https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/07a0f439eb97562ba66c202a2de731facf252107/569_0_5465_4372/master/5465.jpg?width=140&quality=85&auto=format&fit=max&s=3dcbcf803b3e2858de7228608b765158">

      <description><p>Trump-appointed judge Jeffrey T Kuntz partially denies British broadcaster’s motion to dismiss over edit</p><p>Federal judge Jeffrey T Kuntz ruled on Tuesday that Donald Trump’s lawsuit against the BBC can proceed, denying in part the British broadcaster’s motion to dismiss the case.       <title>Farewell to Elon Musk’s Cybertruck. Has any car ever been more repellent? | Arwa Mahdawi</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/nov/11/farewell-cybertruck-elon-musk-car-repellent</link>
      <description><p>Safety campaigners have condemned it and owners have complained about it. Goodbye to a steel monstrosity seemingly designed by a five-year-old</p><p>Elon Musk is having a rough go of it, isn’t he? The world’s richest man spent almost half a billion dollars on the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/04/elon-musk-midterm-spending-analysis">midterms</a> in a failed attempt to defend Republican control of government. Now the tech mogul, who moved from California to Texas to escape Democrats and regulations, finds himself in a newly blue state. He also finds himself the subject of an unflattering <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/sep/08/musk-review-epic-study-worlds-richest-most-banal-man-elon-film">documentary</a> and, if the Democrats follow through on threats to investigate him, could potentially be in a spot of legal bother.</p><p>And to top it all off? Musk’s beloved Cybertruck, the steel monstrosity that looks as if it were designed by a five-year-old, is <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/06/tesla-to-wind-down-cybertruck-production-as-elon-musk-focuses-on-robotics-and-ai">winding down production</a>. According to Musk, this isn’t because it’s an abject failure, but because he is channelling his energy into other things. “This is not a case of Cybertruck being unprofitable, as has been misreported by legacy media,” Musk <a href="https://x.com/elonmusk/status/2119691615774146614?a=pN3ISFVZZ-aU4_-TlJw&amp;s=20">tweeted</a> on Monday. “But rather that the opportunity cost of the complexity of Cybertruck is vastly outweighed by the value of incremental Cybercab production.” (The Cybercab is a two-passenger robotaxi.)</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/nov/11/farewell-cybertruck-elon-musk-car-repellent">Continue reading...</a></description>
