<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comSat, 14 Nov 2026 01:34:36 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[‘Greenhushing’ has replaced greenwashing in corporate climate action, says AIB chief]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/environment/climate-crisis/2026/11/13/greenhushing-banks-quieter-on-climate-but-letting-money-talk/https://www.irishtimes.com/environment/climate-crisis/2026/11/13/greenhushing-banks-quieter-on-climate-but-letting-money-talk/Fri, 13 Nov 2026 14:17:39 +0000“Greenhushing” has replaced greenwashing in corporate climate action, the head of the country’s largest banks has said.

Greenhushing refers to companies deliberately downplaying or remaining silent about environmental actions, even when they are genuine

AIB chief executive Colin Hunt said many banks and businesses were talking less about climate because of political changes but were actually doing more.

“Businesses were far louder about this topic before January 2025 [when Donald Trump began his second term as US president],” he said.

“The fact of the matter is that in certain geographies people have stopped talking about transition and talking about the renewable energy opportunity, but the capital has been deployed at a pace that has never happened before.

“So we’ve moved from greenwashing to greenhushing. Nobody’s talking about it, but the critical thing is, don’t mind the talk, don’t mind the chat – is the capital being deployed?

The pioneering Somali tuk-tuk driver seeking support for a revolutionary idea at Cop31

“The answer is yes, it is and it’s being deployed largely silently.”

Hunt, who is attending the Cop31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, was speaking as AIB announced a doubling of its green finance fund for 2030.

The company set a target in 2019 of lending €30 billion to green, energy-efficient and energy transition projects by 2030. It has already loaned €28 billion.

It has now set a target of €60 billion for 2030. The money is lent to a wide range of projects from retrofits under the low-interest home energy upgrade loan scheme and green mortgages to wind and solar projects valued at hundreds of millions of euros.

Hunt said this would be a floor rather than a ceiling and demand could well outstrip the target again.

He also said AIB was still committed to green lending making up 70 per cent of all new loans issued by the bank by 2030.

“In the first three-quarters of this year, 43 per cent of our lending was green or transition in nature. We’ve got a very strong line of visibility now well into the 60 per cent and with a fair wind we will hit a target in 2030 that looked audaciously ambitious when we set it in 2019.”

During the Cop31 meeting, Hunt met former US vice-president Al Gore, who will be guest speaker at the bank’s annual sustainability conference in Dublin next February.

Hunt said Democrat victories in the US midterm elections could mean less need for greenhushing.

Climate crisis: Everything you need to know

“It might change the volume of the conversation, but the transition is happening. It is happening in front of our eyes; it’s just that people aren’t talking about it,” he said.

He said when it came to overseas loans for large renewable energy projects, the US was the fastest-growing market for AIB.

“I get a sense out of this Cop that I think there’s more optimism out there than I’ve detected in the past,” he said.

]]>Adam Vaughan<![CDATA[Irish Independent publisher Mediahuis Ireland reports €3m drop in turnover]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/13/mediahaus-ireland-reports-3m-drop-in-turnover/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/13/mediahaus-ireland-reports-3m-drop-in-turnover/Fri, 13 Nov 2026 17:50:38 +0000Mediahuis, publisher of the Irish Independent and Sunday Independent, saw its turnover fall by €3 million to €92.3 million last year.

Recently filed accounts for Mediahuis Ireland Limited also show the publisher spent €2.56 million acquiring a 25 per cent stake in Irish sports-video streaming service Clubber in 2025.

The deal valued the streaming service, best known for live-streaming lower-tier GAA games, at €10.4 million.

Clubber was set up in 2020 by former Microsoft Ireland executive Jimmy Doyle.

The accounts show Mediahuis Ireland made a profit of €6.5 million last year, up from €6.3 million in 2024.

The company – which also publishes the Sunday World, Belfast Telegraph and several regional titles – is a wholly owned subsidiary of Belgian media group Mediahuis MV.

The turnover recorded for Mediahuis Ireland Limited relates entirely to activities in the Republic, the accounts noted.

During the financial year, the company was approved for funding from Coimisiún na Meán (CnaM) totalling €1 million to support eligible journalism.

“The purpose of the funding was to supplement and enhance coverage of local authorities and District and Circuit Court hearings, and news reporting that is underprovided for or at risk of underprovision,” CnaM said.

The accounts also show Mediahuis Ireland employed 392 staff at the end of 2025, up one on the previous year.

The two directors of Mediahuis Ireland were listed as chief executive Sheena Peirse, who joined the board in October 2025 when former chief executive Peter Vandermeersch exited, and Ian Keogh, who was appointed a director in February 2024.

Earlier this year, the company acquired Image Media, the publisher behind Image magazine and other titles, for an undisclosed sum.

It said the acquisition was aimed at building “a more diversified, digitally led and multi-platform media business”.

Accounts for the parent group, Antwerp-based Mediahuis MV, indicate it made a profit of €156.7 million last year on the back of a €1.23 billion turnover.

The company operates primarily in Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg and Germany and has more than 30 titles in its stable.

]]><![CDATA[AIB doubles 2030 green and transition lending target to €60bn]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/13/aib-doubles-green-and-transition-lending-target-to-60bn/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/13/aib-doubles-green-and-transition-lending-target-to-60bn/Fri, 13 Nov 2026 18:46:27 +0000AIB chief executive Colin Hunt said on Friday that the bank has doubled its 2030 green and transition lending target to €60 billion.

The announcement was made by Hunt at the UN Climate Change Conference (Cop31) taking place in Antalya, Turkey.

AIB has already deployed €28 billion in cumulative green and transition lending since 2019, equivalent to 93 per cent of its existing €30 billion target.

The bank provided €6.3 billion in green and transition lending in 2025, accounting for 43 per cent of all new lending. A further €5.3 billion was deployed in the first nine months of 2026, it said.

“Banks have a critical role in turning climate ambition into practical action. That means financing renewable energy, helping households improve the energy efficiency of their homes and supporting businesses large and small as they make the transition,” said Hunt. “A sustainable economy will be a stronger, more competitive and more resilient economy.”

AIB’s international climate capital business has been the fastest-growing division in recent years, which specialises in large renewable and infrastructure projects across Ireland, Britain, Europe and North America.

On the retail side of the bank, close to 60 per cent of the mortgage business written last year was for green loans – where the property has a building energy rating between A1 and B3.

Cop31 host Turkey is striving to place a proposal to expand global electrification at the centre of an eventual deal emerging from the latest annual conference, saying the plan will lead to emissions cuts by speeding the shift away from fossil fuel-powered cars, boilers and other equipment.

The proposal does not require the increased electricity use to come from renewable sources, although some countries, including last year’s Cop host Brazil, are advocating for progress on a plan to require countries to more clearly map out their transition away from fossil fuels.

Big fossil fuel producers and consumers at the talks are resisting any deal that would specify firm new targets or a shift away from oil, gas and coal, ​observers said as the first week of talks drew to a close. – Additional reporting: Reuters

]]>Bryan O'Brien<![CDATA[Microsoft outage: What happened and what does it say about online services?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/2026/11/13/microsoft-outage-what-happened-and-when-will-it-be-fixed/https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/2026/11/13/microsoft-outage-what-happened-and-when-will-it-be-fixed/Fri, 13 Nov 2026 18:27:12 +0000Millions of people were unable to access their emails, Teams chats or meetings on Thursday night and Friday after a Microsoft 365 outage brought down services across the globe.

The outage was into its second day on Friday, though Microsoft said it was seeing “encouraging recovery progress in Europe”. It affected businesses, government agencies and even Microsoft employees all over the world.

The Health Service Executive said it had been affected by the global Microsoft outage, with emails not being transmitted.

Those also reporting issues have included the US House of Representatives, an Australian spy agency, airlines in India, European government agencies, and police services, ambulances and hospitals in the UK.

Microsoft is still investigating the cause of the outage, which it has said is not a cyberattack but a configuration error.

Experts say that the outage has laid bare the dangerous dependence of countries on a few US tech companies.

What happened and why?

On Thursday, the outage website Down Detector showed an increase in users reporting issues with Microsoft 365, the assembly of cloud software that includes Teams, Word, Excel, PowerPoint and Outlook.

By Friday morning, Microsoft had narrowed down most of the problems to Microsoft Exchange, the email service behind Outlook. Teams meetings and chats had returned to service.

On Friday afternoon, Microsoft said there was “encouraging recovery progress in Europe”, improvements in North America and Asia Pacific, and Japan was “stable”.

What caused the disruption?

Microsoft has said that this was not the result of a cyberattack, though suspicions were high because of several cyberattacks that have hit organisations in Europe in recent weeks. So far, the problem appeared to be a configuration update that resulted in some servers becoming overloaded and taken offline, Microsoft indicated.

When the company attempted to apply a fix, servers that had come back online again became unresponsive when traffic began returning to them.

As some servers went down, traffic was funnelled on to the remaining servers, causing traffic problems for those remaining online.

More details are likely to emerge over the coming weeks. “We don’t know what actually went wrong, and that will take weeks to discover,” said Steven Murdoch, a professor of security engineering at University College London. “The people who are working on it are too busy fixing to understand or report on the cause.”

Why has Microsoft 365 been down for so long?

An outage that runs for so long for a service as critical as Microsoft 365 is unusual. The company has not said why it has lasted this long, but a clue might be in its updates: as servers returned to being unresponsive after being fixed, engineers had to work through alternative solutions, taking longer than expected to get servers back up and running.

What does the incident say about our reliance on online services?

Experts have said that outages such as this underscored the world’s reliance on cloud services provided by a few large US tech companies – Amazon, Google and Microsoft. This reliance has been a growing source of unease through each high-profile outage.

It has grown more pronounced because of the hostility of the Trump administration towards Europe, which has prompted some governments to consider alternatives to US software.

As the name Microsoft 365 implies, the world has quickly become accustomed to online services being available 24/7. Given that software is no longer solely downloaded to individual PCs but is also stored on a server owned by a company, outages such as this will happen. Most of the time they are brief, but sometimes they are not.

Outages in recent years from telecommunications providers, from the PHP incident to the CrowdStrike incident, show just how varied the sources and causes of a large outage can be.

There are many different pieces of the puzzle keeping services online – but the effect of one of those services going down is much greater than it ever has been.

Mark Gregory, an associate professor at Australia’s RMIT University, said it was important for organisations to thoroughly test updates before rolling them out to the live network.

That was in addition to the extra security testing companies must carry out to ensure their services are protected from threat actors armed with AI tools that can find vulnerabilities quicker than ever before.

Should we have backup options when services go down?

Gregory said companies that relied on services such as Microsoft 365 should have backup options such as Google’s Gmail in the event of an outage. Others have suggested the free and open-source Office alternative LibreOffice.

Around the world, it has become increasingly clear that many companies – and government services – do not have good backups, with businesses resorting to faxes and phones. – Guardian

]]>Manan Vatsyayana<![CDATA[Microsoft ‘deeply sorry’ for global outage that left millions without services]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/big-tech/2026/11/13/microsoft-outages-continue-as-tech-giant-works-to-restore-services/https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/big-tech/2026/11/13/microsoft-outages-continue-as-tech-giant-works-to-restore-services/Fri, 13 Nov 2026 12:47:39 +0000Millions of Microsoft customers, including high profile businesses in Ireland, had their services disrupted for much of Friday as a result of a global outage that the tech giant put down to a technical issue that arose from a “recent network change”.

In a statement, Microsoft said it was “deeply sorry” for the disruption and moved to quell early speculation that its system might have been the subject of a cyber attack.

“This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI agents,” it said. “The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions.”

The disruption, which began on Thursday and continued into Friday, left users unable to send or receive emails through Outlook. It also affected Microsoft Teams, its Copilot AI assistant and other Microsoft 365 services.

In a statement, the HSE said that similar to other customers, it was impacted by the outage with email not being transmitted.

Doctors and the Houses of Parliament in the UK were also impacted, with Australian police and the Japanese government reporting problems. The German government said it “anticipates a very big impact” on the economy and that it was in touch with Microsoft.

Richemont, the Swiss luxury group that owns brands including Cartier and Chloé, was forced to delay its half-year results. OpenAI and Anthropic both also reported “errors” affecting Microsoft 365 connectors.

Microsoft, which has its European hub in Dublin and employs about 3,000 people here, said it restored services “gradually, validating stability at each stage”.

“While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration. We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously.”

Microsoft users in Ireland began to see their email services being restored from late on Friday morning.

The company said it would provide a “full post-incident report once our review is complete”. No time frame was put on the release of the review’s findings.

Monitoring website Downdetector first showed a spike in users reporting problems with Microsoft Teams in Europe at about 6.15pm on Thursday.

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice-president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, said on X that there was no indication that the disruption was due to “malicious or cyber activity”.

In an update on Friday, the tech giant said that although it had managed to get servers operating multiple times overnight, those servers had crashed.

Microsoft said it had tried several solutions to mitigate the problems, including isolating parts of its infrastructure and shifting traffic to alternate routes.

HSE services affected as global Microsoft outage hits Ireland

As the disruption spread across the globe, businesses and state agencies which rely on Microsoft’s technology reported that they were unable to carry out day-to-day operations and could not use critical communication tools.

Singapore authorities said the disruption affected some of its state systems, but added that emergency services were “fully operational”. Workers coming back from an extended Diwali holiday break in India also complained on social media about the Microsoft outage.

In Japan, the government and many major companies were affected by the outages. Deputy chief cabinet secretary Masanao Ozaki warned that the shared government IT infrastructure, which relies on Microsoft, was experiencing disruptions.

Several Japanese companies told the FT that their emails could be delayed due to issues with Microsoft Outlook. Logistics group Sagawa Express had to suspend same-day reservations for its luggage storage services at train stations and airports nationwide.

. - Additional reporting by the The Financial Times Limited/PA

]]>Andrew Caballero-Reynolds<![CDATA[Global stocks dragged down by AI insecurity, but oil companies stay on the up]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/13/global-stocks-dragged-down-by-ai-insecurity-but-oil-companies-stay-on-the-up/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/13/global-stocks-dragged-down-by-ai-insecurity-but-oil-companies-stay-on-the-up/Fri, 13 Nov 2026 18:04:49 +0000Global shares were largely dragged down by a drop in trading confidence for artificial intelligence-linked companies, carrying on the fallout of the resignation of Nvidia ex-chief executive Jensen Huang. The energy market, however, saw stronger returns as supply insecurity caused by war in the Gulf drove oil prices higher.

Dublin

The Iseq All-Share index decreased 0.24 per cent on Friday to close at 14,976.07.

Typical Iseq high-flyer Ryanair saw its share price descend 0.39 per cent to close at €25.70 per share, coming back down to earth after continuous day-on-day growth in share price last week after the airline’s chief executive signalled an expansion of the company next year.

Bank of Ireland ended the trading week in the red, too, down 0.69 per cent to €19.39 a share. Retail banking rival AIB fared slightly better, with its share price increasing 0.17 per cent to close at €11.63.

Minerals miner Kenmare Resources was the day’s top gainer, up a clean 3.33 per cent to €3.10 a share, meanwhile nutrition business Kerry Group jumped 0.99 per cent to close at €101.70 as the demand for weight-loss drugs matches the rise in the company’s profile.

London

The London Stock Exchange fared slightly better, albeit with mixed results. The blue-chip FTSE 100 index ended the trading week in the green, up 0.36 per cent higher than Thursday’s closing price. The mid-cap FTSE 250 index, however, was down 0.45 per cent by close of markets.

The British energy sector saw an improvement from declines registered the previous day, with oil and gas giants Shell and BP up 1.51 per cent and 1.39 per cent respectively, as investors bet on the price of oil from the Middle East continuing to rise amid uncertainty over supply.

High street brands, however, ended the week in the red – with bookshop retailing WH Smith down 4.67 per cent and shoe manufacturer Dr Martens falling 3.88 per cent following on from Thursday’s nearly 15 per cent collapse in share price after investors learned of last year’s pretax losses.

Europe

Shares across the Continent largely declined following sliding share prices in companies typically boosting Europe’s leading indices. Blue-chip Stoxx 50 ended the traded week 0.16 per cent down from Thursday’s closing price, while its mid-cap equivalent Stoxx 600 rose marginally, up 0.01 per cent.

Dutch semiconductor company ASML Holdings suffered significant losses, with its share price dropping 2.76 per cent, as the wider AI-linked market fell off in traders’ assessment of the market.

Much of the banking sector saw slightly smaller losses, with France’s BNP Paribas down 0.12 per cent and Germany’s Deutsche Bank dipping 0.57 per cent. Spain’s Santander, however, was up 0.07 per cent.

New York

Early trades on Wall Street were mixed, as downward trends in artificial intelligence-linked stocks weighed heavily on indices that we generally pulled into the green by promising inflation data that eased investors’ macroeconomic concerns.

The fallout of Huang’s headline-marking and market-shaking resignation rippled across indices and impacted other chipmaking companies too. The company, seen to be a global leader in AI development, was down nearly 4 per cent from Thursday’s closing price.

Microsoft’s stock largely recovered from the collapse in investor confidence of the software giant, following a widespread outage of its cloud platform that paralysed potentially millions of users’ online activity for hours. Just before midday New York time, it was up 0.07 per cent from Thursday’s closing price, after it fought to restore its digital services.

New York’s top indices were a mixed bag by midday, too: the S&P 500 was little changed, but the Nasdaq 100 fell some 0.40 per cent and the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose about 0.30 per cent.

]]>Angela Weiss<![CDATA[BMW owners in US told to park outside over risk of cars catching fire]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/13/bmw-owners-in-us-told-to-park-outside-over-risk-of-cars-catching-fire/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/13/bmw-owners-in-us-told-to-park-outside-over-risk-of-cars-catching-fire/Fri, 13 Nov 2026 17:14:07 +0000Drivers of nearly 721,000 BMW vehicles in the United States should park outside due to a defect that could cause a fire, the US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) said on Friday.

BMW last week recalled 14 models from the years 2012 to 2018 over an improperly sealed electrical connector on the water pump that may be exposed to water and short circuit, increasing the risk of a fire while parked and turned off.

The vehicles were previously recalled in 2024 due to a water pump issue and must be repaired again. BMW identified 10 incidents that could be related to the issue in vehicles that had been repaired under the previous callback, NHTSA said. No crashes or injuries have been reported.

“If you have one of these vehicles, you should park your vehicle outside and away from buildings and other vehicles until the vehicle is repaired,” the agency said in consumer alert on Friday.

The company does not yet have a fix available, though one is under development. Notifications are expected to be mailed starting on December 25th, NHTSA said.

BMW iX4 coupe-SUV joins Neue Klasse line-up with claimed range of up to 827km

BMW didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

BMW is seeking to cut costs and overhaul its management ranks to contend with increasing competition from Chinese automakers. The German carmaker last week trimmed its profit outlook and laid out plans to boost production of its next-generation models to shore up profitability in the coming years. – Bloomberg

]]>vesilvio<![CDATA[Dublin Zoo records €625,000 impairment charge after mothballing plans for new restaurant]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/13/dublin-zoo-records-625000-impairment-charge-after-mothballing-plans-for-new-restaurant/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/13/dublin-zoo-records-625000-impairment-charge-after-mothballing-plans-for-new-restaurant/Fri, 13 Nov 2026 16:55:55 +0000The operator of Dublin Zoo has recorded a €625,000 impairment charge after mothballing plans for a new restaurant proposed for the African Plains area of the zoo.

Also, the zoo closed on Friday, September 11th, and Saturday 12th of September, arising from security measures in connection with the visit of US president Donald Trump to Dublin. Trump met President Catherine Connolly and Taoiseach Micheál Martin in separate engagements at the Phoenix Park

A Dublin Zoo spokesman said today, using seasonal averages, “we estimate a potential loss of around 5,000 visitors over the two days of closure”.

The spokesman was unable to provide a financial cost arising from the two-day closure.

The €625,000 impairment charge contributed to the operator of Dublin Zoo and Fota Wildlife Park in Cork, the Zoological Society of Ireland, recording an operating loss of €1.45 million last year.

In the society’s 2025 annual report, the directors said that adverse weather conditions and economic pressures affecting visitor behaviour contributed to lower visitor numbers at the zoo and Fota Wildlife Park in 2025, where gate receipt income declined from €17.7 million to €16.68 million.

On the impairment charge concerning its “deferred catering development project”, the directors state that the society secured planning permission for the restaurant and the board approved the project proceeding to tender stage.

They said that, however, “following a reassessment of trading performance, economic conditions and very substantial construction cost inflation in the intervening period of project planning, the board decided to defer the project indefinitely and instead consider incremental enhancements to existing catering facilities”.

The accounts indicated that the board “may revisit the project at a future date should economic and operating conditions improve”.

The directors noted that the €625,000 provision “has been made in the financial statements for all project costs incurred to date”.

Overall, 2025 was an “operationally complex year for the group”, the accounts said.

Trading performance was affected “by adverse weather conditions, economic pressures affecting visitor behaviour and the temporary closure of Fota Wildlife Park following an outbreak of highly pathogenic avian influenza”.

Numbers attending the zoo, including Wild Lights, reduced by 10 per cent from 1.16 million to 1.04 million, while numbers attending Fota Wildlife Park reduced from 428,745 to 408,453.

Along with gate receipt income declining by 6 per cent to €16.68 million, shop income fell from €3.79 million to €3.36 million and annual-pass income declined from €2.9 million to €2.7 million.

However, overall revenues rose from €25.9 million to €26.3 million as “other operating income” more than doubled to €3.57 million, which included €700,000 in emergency funding from the National Parks and Wildlife Service for Fota Wildlife Park in response to its enforced temporary closure.

]]>Patrick Bolger<![CDATA[Take the time to prepare for retirement ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/13/take-the-time-to-prepare-for-retirement/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/13/take-the-time-to-prepare-for-retirement/Fri, 13 Nov 2026 14:29:54 +0000Getting your finances straight, prioritising your mental and physical health and finding enjoyable ways to spend your time are key to a happy retirement

If you’ve spent years working for the boss from hell, then it’s likely retirement can’t come fast enough. But if your working life has been tolerable or, better still, enjoyable and fulfilling, calling it a day can come with mixed emotions.

We’ve all come across energetic retirees with a bucket list as long as your arm, but not everyone views this pivot in their lives in the same light. Worries about health, having enough money to live on or caring for others can peak around this time.

And there’s always the potential for family friction if adult children assume that their recently retired parent has nothing else to do but look after their grandchildren.

Retirement is a huge change for the retiree but it also triggers upheaval for the whole family, especially for a partner used to having the house to themselves for most of the day. Suddenly having to share 24/7 with someone who mopes around the place or has no interests or hobbies can be a huge strain. It is a possible explanation for a spike in separations among those in their 60s.

In an ideal world, those nearing retirement age would begin planning ahead. A good place to start is by sorting out your immediate finances. (Your pension is a whole different ball game that needs to be dealt with separately.)

Once retired, you may have less money to spend day to day which makes it important to decide what your financial priorities are. Do you want to spend your money on travel, on your home or hobbies or helping out the family?

Incomes typically fall post-retirement so while you are still bringing in a regular wage it is worth dealing with outstanding debts such as loans and credit cards.

If you have multiple loans and/or several credit cards with outstanding balances, try to pay off what you can before you retire and consider consolidation to save on fees and card and interest charges.

Some people like to have two credit cards for emergencies. However, it is best to stick to one as your main card for buying and become vigilant about paying off the balance each month, bearing in mind that there will be no monthly salary to cover the cost if you overspend or let the interest build up.

Check with your bank if they offer any perks to older customers, such as an account with reduced fees and charges. These accounts are usually available for those aged 66 or over.

Some banks also offer financial advice and planning for older customers but, like a lot of things in life, if you want it you have to ask for it.

Retirement can be an opportunity to reinvent yourself and to do the things you’ve always wanted to do. It can also provide more time for grandchildren which can be good or not so good depending on the circumstances.

The sentiment often expressed by grandparents is that while they love their grandchildren, it’s great to be able to hand them back to their parents. That is something that has become a lot trickier with childcare costs and places at a premium.

As a consequence, some adult children expect parents to step up for child-minding duties. Declining to do so or putting conditions in place can go down badly at times. These are potentially troubled waters so it may be worth thinking about how much babysitting you want to do and to be clear in your own mind about the boundaries before the time arrives.

Otherwise what starts out as a casual or stopgap arrangement can morph into a full-time commitment that is hard to get out of.

One solution is not to be permanently available. That’s where getting stuck into new hobbies or activities comes in. Volunteering, a new sport, a hobby, taking up an academic course or joining a choir or sea swimming group are all sociable ways of spending time that help foster good mental health and maintain the interpersonal connections that inevitably diminish when you’re no longer in full-time employment.

One often hears retirees opining that they’d prefer to watch paint drying than going hillwalking or playing bridge. But there are many other options if you dig a little. For example, rug tufting (very satisfactory as you do it with a gun and the pieces take shape fast) or joining a percussion group. Rhythm and beat are very therapeutic, and percussion includes a myriad of styles from African djembe to Japanese style drumming to learning to play the bodhrán.

Making stained glass pieces seems to suit those who like precision and wielding a soldering iron, while fused glass is a wide-open form of expression where creativity can run wild. Add to that activities like stone cutting, willow sculpture, axe throwing and Mahjong, and you are still only scratching the surface of what’s out there.

Health

Having ticked the boxes marked “money” and “filling time”, the third pillar is health and what you should do to mind it.

There is no shortage of health gurus telling us how to eat and how to exercise and it can be easy to get overwhelmed by all the noise. But strip it back and it’s pretty simple.

Move as much as possible, stay hydrated to avoid urinary tract infections, maintain social contacts and eat to preserve muscle strength, bone density and a good gut microbiome. Appetite can reduce with age so it’s important to keep a steady calorie intake to maintain energy levels and feel well.

As we get older, the combination of underlying medical conditions and natural ageing can disrupt the systems that normally keep us upright. Balance problems are one of the main fall risks for older adults.

A bad fall can be life changing which is why it’s worth incorporating exercises to maintain balance into your daily routine. These exercises require no special equipment and even 10 minutes a day has been shown to cut the risk of a fall. One of the simplest is calf raises which can be done at the worktop while you’re waiting for the kettle to boil.

ExWell Medical is a not for profit social enterprise that runs medically supervised exercise classes (and online health information sessions) for older people in the community. It was started by Dr Noel McCaffrey in 2019 and the aim is to keep people moving even if they are living with health issues, debilitating conditions or recovering from serious illnesses such as cardiac events or cancer.

The classes are pitched at different fitness levels and some can be done seated. To join a group, you must be referred by a medical practitioner. Full details of the locations of ExWell’s classes are on the organisation’s website.

For those who feel they would benefit from a more formal introduction to what retirement may bring, the Retirement Planning Council of Ireland runs year-round courses for those coming up to retirement. You can pay up and go as a private individual or your company may be willing to foot the bill so it’s worth checking that with HR.

The courses cover areas such as financial readiness, pensions, legal and lifestyle transitions.

]]><![CDATA[Public sector pay deal: did the Government capitulate or did unions settle for too little?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/11/13/public-sector-pay-deal-did-the-government-capitulate-or-did-unions-settle-for-too-little/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/11/13/public-sector-pay-deal-did-the-government-capitulate-or-did-unions-settle-for-too-little/Fri, 13 Nov 2026 06:00:01 +0000There was always going to be a deal. The question was where both sides would settle. We got the answer in the early hours of Wednesday morning.

A 10.75 per cent pay hike spread out over 33 months (to March 2029) at a cost of €5.2 billion to the exchequer.

The latest round of public sector pay negotiations was unusually fraught by Irish standards but not by European standards, where industrial relations have been souring for months on the back of persistent inflation.

A fierce standoff over cost of living and pension reform has paralysed France.

If you believe one side of the commentariat, the Government capitulated at the last minute to avoid the mayhem of another one-day national strike coinciding with Ireland’s hosting of the EU summit.

But to evaluate the true merits of the deal, you need to go back to the starting point for negotiations.

Government and unions held exploratory talks in early July, but the real discussions didn’t start until October under the auspices of the Workplace Relations Commission.

On the table was the Central Bank’s latest quarterly bulletin, published the previous month, containing the bank’s inflation forecasts for 2026, 2027 and 2028 (3.4 per cent; 3.1 per cent; 2 per cent).

The forecast for 2027 had been upgraded by nearly half a percentage point since the summer, reflecting the deteriorating economic backdrop.

Public sector pay deal: What’s in it for me?

Inflation-proofing wages was the primary objective of unions.

As the negotiations progressed, the Central Bank’s inflation forecasts began to look shaky.

Oil prices were on the march again. Speculation was rife that the US and Israel were about to attack Iran again.

Unions began coming up with their own estimates of future price growth based on the latest readouts. The fear was that they would sign up to pay rises that would later be crushed by inflation.

The Government’s initial offer of a cumulative 7.75 per cent pay hike didn’t even cover the conservative inflation forecasts, hence the deadlock.

The deal eventually struck gives public sector workers in higher-income brackets a pay bump of 4.6 per cent next year (when the backdated element is included), followed by 3.1 per cent in 2028 and 3.2 per cent in 2029. Lower-paid workers, those earning less than €50,000, will get bigger pay increases.

Based on the current inflationary outlook, which has improved since the US midterm elections, this will give public sector workers modest but real wage increases.

Another benchmark for both sides to consider was the expected rise in wages in the private sector.

The Government’s recent economic and fiscal outlook, published alongside last month’s budget, forecasts that wages across the economy – which is mainly private sector – would rise by 4.1 per cent in 2027 and by 3.7 per cent in 2028 and 2029. The public sector deal is roughly comparable.

The deal includes a review clause that can be triggered by either side if economic conditions or inflation rates change “significantly”, reflecting the fact that both unions and Government are unsure about the economic outlook. Not an unreasonable position given the last five years.

Jack Chambers warns public sector pay deal could be reviewed if economy contracts

The Government typically defends pay deals as a means of preventing industrial unrest, ensuring continuity of service and pay predictability.

There is, however, a big unknown for Government.

The Department of Finance’s latest expenditure outlook report says Budget 2027 includes “the costs associated with the recruitment of circa 7,000 additional [public sector] staff”.

But public sector employment has grown by 85,000 since 2019, which equates to an average of 12,000 a year.

There is also nothing in the report or other reports about the additional staff (nurses, teachers, gardaí) needed or expected after 2027.

The Government’s €5.2 billion costing is therefore something of a shot in the dark.

In its back pocket, however, is the promise of more corporation tax, the exchequer’s golden goose. Receipts from the business tax are expected to climb to €45 billion by 2030.

But weaving more day-to-day spending around risky tax receipts is a gamble the Government has been repeatedly advised against.

The Irish Times view on the public pay deal: the Government pays up for peace

The draft deal (it still has to be ratified by unions) will cost the Government an estimated €2 billion next year, which means Budget 2027, which allocates €1.2 billion for the deal, is already out of date. €800 million out of date.

They say the definition of a good deal is when both sides walk away thinking they could have done better. That’s probably not the case here.

Both sides will sell it as a good deal in the context of the economic backdrop. But there are big unknowns to do with inflation and cost.

]]>Chris Maddaloni<![CDATA[Irish reunification will be costly - here are the key decisions which will decide the size of the bill]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/12/the-key-political-choices-that-will-determine-the-cost-of-irish-reunification/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/12/the-key-political-choices-that-will-determine-the-cost-of-irish-reunification/Thu, 12 Nov 2026 14:41:03 +0000The economics of a united Ireland has been a disputed territory for years, with analysis ranging from claims of large gains to significant costs. How do we make sense of this?

A new analysis from Prof Stephen Kinsella of the University of Limerick – The Economics of Reunification – published by Fine Gael as part of its ardfheis initiative on the topic, provides a vital guide through the arguments.

It shows, above all, two things. One is that the costs depend crucially on what model is chosen, how it is implemented and crucial negotiations with the UK on the issue of pensions and debt. And second, that the long-term growth performance of Northern Ireland will be crucial in determining the economics of reunification and whether it can be financed.

There is no one answer to the question of what a united Ireland would cost. It all depends. And this underlines the vital role of planning and preparation.

Kinsella, who is an adviser to Tánaiste Simon Harris, draws on a range of previous work, much of it undertaken post-Brexit. He estimates that the first-year cost of reunification ranges from about €3 billion to €25 billion.

This is obviously a huge range. But this is where the story lies. As the assumptions and political choices change, so do the potential costs.

Kinsella frames the issue of the economics of the reunification debate around two questions. The first is who should pay which parts of the difference between Northern Ireland’s income and its expenditure. The second is what structures can be put in place to improve convergence between income and productivity levels in Northern Ireland and the Republic.

Disposable income per household is 13 per cent higher south of the Border, and the FDI model has boosted the Republic’s economy and its public finances. In contrast, the North has a net fiscal deficit of €17 billion, funded by the UK exchequer. This does not transfer automatically to the costs of reunification, but it is important nonetheless.

In a best-case scenario, if the UK agreed to take on the historic cost of the North’s pensions bill and the debt interest on the part of the UK’s national debt which would be attributed to Northern Ireland, then much of the €17 billion deficit would fall away.

Kinsella assumes some additional costs would accrue to the Republic from investment and running a separate administration if a federal model was chosen. This is one of a range of integration models in the paper, which also includes what he calls a “managed integration” plan – involving phased harmonisation in areas such as pay and welfare rates over 15 years – and a costly scenario that harmonises everything at once.

This variety of political decisions on what form unification would take and who picks up various bills leaves a potential matrix of costs not only, of course, in year one but for many years into the future. Bringing public pay and welfare rates in the North up to the Republic’s level, for example, would be a hugely expensive exercise.

The most important decisions are:

The pensions and debt issue

What happens to the accrued pension liabilities of Northern Ireland public servants and those who qualify for a state pension has been a key difference over the years between those taking an optimistic and pessimistic view of the economic benefits of reunification. Added to this is the interest on the part of the UK national debt, allocated to Northern Ireland in relation to its size within the UK.

Together these sum to close to €10 billion of the €17 billion annual UK estimate of the Northern Ireland deficit.

Pay convergence

Partly relying on what model of unification is chosen, it is clear that, as Kinsella puts it, “a nurse, teacher or civil servant in Belfast would expect the same pay as one in Dublin and a pensioner or jobseeker in Derry would expect the same weekly payment as one in Cork.” This would cost between €2.3 billion and €12.4 billion on day one, depending on how the gaps are measured, according to the report.

Northern envy at Republic pay rates

Huge decisions would lie ahead in this area and on the wider issue of how – or whether – public services would be integrated. Savings might be expected here from unified structures, but this would mean job losses, and Kinsella warns that the gains might be modest enough.

The model chosen

Choosing between the different possible models for reunification also has an impact on the economics.

A key message is that trying to unite the two economies in an unplanned rush is potentially very expensive and would require strong growth in Northern Ireland to make the finances add up in any fashion.

So-called managed integration over 15 years would still carry a high cost, on his calculations. Extra investment needed to increase productivity in the North would also need to be factored in.

As Kinsella says in his conclusions, a key message is that political choices will drive the cost of reunification – “the price depends far more on decisions made by policymakers than on any fixed bill”. The pensions and debt issues are vital in the short term, while over time closing the pay and welfare gap is crucial.

In any scenario, the financing is complicated, requiring significant borrowing even if there is financial assistance from the UK or even the European Union (where other member states might look askance at the idea given the public-finance constraints they face).

For the financing to work, growth becomes vital. Northern Ireland has averaged 1.3 per cent a year GDP growth since the early 2000s. Under a managed transition scenario, this would need to rise – depending on the assumptions – to between 3 per cent and 4.7 per cent on average each year to underpin a funding model.

Kinsella concludes that “this is a high bar, but it is possible”. Other assumptions might lower the growth targets a bit – again showing the importance of the key decisions.

A key conclusion from reading the report is that the potential financial implications for the Republic and its citizens are significant. Kinsella points to a range of potential costs per head in the Republic, which runs from €650 in year one to more than €2,600, with ongoing significant costs in future years.

Cross-Border tax rules putting off employers and workers, says report

Ireland’s public finances give it leeway to fund reunification, but this still carries costs. “However the costs are shared,” Kinsella writes, “someone has to pay them year by year.”

Like previous work by economists John FitzGerald and Edgar Morgenroth, the report points to the investment needs of Northern Ireland in areas such as education and skills, infrastructure and other measures to boost productivity.

There are potential gains from unification, too, as – for example – corporate taxes are cut in the North, encouraging inward investment, and new trade opportunities open up as the Irish Border disappears and Northern Ireland becomes a full part of the EU.

The extent of the resulting dynamic is hugely difficult to model with any confidence, but the North’s lacklustre economic performance compared with the Republic does point to some potential gains.

As the report concludes, whether reunification happens is a political and constitutional question. But the economics will be vital, and the report again underlines the complexity of the task and the huge preparations which would be required.

]]><![CDATA[Winter in a seaside town]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/opinion/letters/2026/11/12/winter-in-a-seaside-town/https://www.irishtimes.com/opinion/letters/2026/11/12/winter-in-a-seaside-town/Thu, 12 Nov 2026 06:00:01 +0000Sir, – Your article (‘Economically it probably would make sense to close’: Clifden businesses prepare for barren winter, October 24th) highlighted genuine challenges facing seasonal tourism destinations. However, the bleak headline and imagery were at odds with the resilience and enterprise expressed by local businesses.

Seasonality is normal worldwide. While some businesses close or reduce hours, many remain open year-round.

Businesses are investing considerable effort and expense in attracting visitors, supported by Tourism Ireland, Fáilte Ireland and regional tourism networks.

The timing was particularly unfortunate. Published over the October Bank Holiday weekend, when Clifden was bustling despite stormy weather, it risked discouraging visitors planning their next getaway.

At Connemara Chamber, we recognise the challenges of seasonality and sustaining employment.

The real story is not that Clifden is closing for the winter, but that its businesses and community work extraordinarily hard to ensure it doesn’t. That is a story worthy of a headline too. -Yours, etc,

Simon Ashe,

President,

Connemara Chamber,

Galway

]]><![CDATA[We must find ways to restore homes above businesses that still thrive]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/opinion/letters/2026/11/12/we-must-find-ways-to-restore-homes-above-businesses-that-still-thrive/https://www.irishtimes.com/opinion/letters/2026/11/12/we-must-find-ways-to-restore-homes-above-businesses-that-still-thrive/Thu, 12 Nov 2026 06:00:01 +0000Sir, – David McWilliams is right (“Ireland’s towns offer part of the solution to the housing crisis. We should seize it now,” November 7th). Empty floors above shops could house people again, and redundant ground-floor shops should be allowed to become homes. But allowing conversions is one thing; making them possible is another.

I run a pub in Baltimore, west Cork. Everywhere I travel, I see vacant rooms above businesses, while my staff struggle to find somewhere to live. I spent years renovating derelict properties in California, so I know old buildings are complicated.

My wife and I live above our pub in a building that has housed people for generations. I want to make our home safer and create accommodation for staff. A fire consultant advised us that the required fire lobbies and relocated stairways would fundamentally disrupt the pub’s layout, eliminate access to essential facilities and storage, and render the business unworkable.

That was his opinion, not a ruling by the fire authority, but it shows why owners like me hesitate.

The buildings have not changed. Our definition of what is safe has. And rightly so. But if an old building cannot accommodate modern fire-safety arrangements, must it simply be written off as housing?

Surely we should first ask what is the safest workable alternative. Otherwise, rooms that housed families for generations will remain empty.

Building regulations already allow alternatives, and the Government offers grants. But what good are either if owners cannot find a workable solution without spending thousands – or opening a costly can of worms that could put their entire business at risk?

McWilliams is right about redundant shops. But we must also find ways to restore homes above businesses that still thrive.

Best may be the ideal. But better must surely be worth pursuing. – Yours, etc,

William Hillyard,

Baltimore,

West Cork.

Sir, – David McWilliams makes some interesting points on “market towns” which he says are withering away in the face of “massive global shifts” (Ireland’s towns offer part of the solution to the housing crisis. We should seize it now).

Growing up in the ’80s, Listowel in Co Kerry, with an urban population of 5,000, was always classed as a “market” town. And it lived up to that term literally and figuratively, with a busy livestock mart bang in the middle. Together with 48 pubs, numerous grocery stores and newsagents, it was a bustling place for commerce and socialising.

Today, Listowel is classed as a “heritage” town. It still has a population of 5,000, but the mart is long gone, and the buildings and land where they stood remain empty save for Birds Amusements once a year during Listowel Race Week. Approximately 11 pubs are holding on, and all the newsagents and small groceries stores are gone, save one.

For the last decade Listowel has had a 20 per cent or more rate of commercial vacancies, despite Kerry as a whole having one of the lowest in the country, at 12.3 per cent. It hasn’t helped that the Fine Gael-Labour government got rid of our town council and moved the busy post office from the high street into a supermarket.

In last week’s edition of the local newspaper, Kerry’s Eye, the front page spread said “We Want Your Money” – 5,000 businesses face rates hike of 7 per cent to fill €20 million hole in Kerry County Council’s budget.

Not all of the issues facing market towns in Ireland are solely the result of global shifts in the way people shop. Many of the problems are a direct result of both government policy and inaction.

Thankfully there are some green shoots in Listowel town centre at the moment. It remains to be seen if these shoots will grow and prosper or if government policy will kill them again before they get a chance to flourish. – Yours, etc,

Tom McElligott,

Listowel

]]><![CDATA[Former DCC healthcare unit to buy Portlaoise-based Beechfield Healthcare]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/12/former-dcc-healthcare-unit-to-buy-portlaoise-based-beechfield-healthcare/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/12/former-dcc-healthcare-unit-to-buy-portlaoise-based-beechfield-healthcare/Thu, 12 Nov 2026 06:00:00 +0000Vital Healthcare, formerly part of London-listed DCC, has agreed to buy Portlaoise-based wheelchairs-to-stairlifts supplier Beechfield Healthcare for an undisclosed sum.

Industry sources estimated that the deal was valued at more than €20 million.

Beechfield, which was founded 30 years ago and is majority owned by managing director Trevor Flanagan, reported a €2.3 million pretax profit last year, according to its latest set of accounts, filed last week with the Companies Registration Office.

The business will be combined with Vital’s medical supplies company Fannin, broadening the group’s offering across hospital, community and home-care settings, Vital Ireland said in a statement. The deal remains subject to clearance from the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission.

DCC, which is in the process of being acquired by US private equity firms KKR and Energy Capital Partners, sold its healthcare division – comprising Vital and DCC Health & Beauty Solutions – last year to UK-based Investindustrial for an enterprise value of £1.05 billion (€1.26 billion).

DCC was recently renamed DCC Energy after abandoning its conglomerate roots to focus on the energy sector.

“As more care is delivered outside of hospitals in line with the HSE Sláintecare strategy, healthcare providers need trusted partners who can deliver the products, services and support that patients rely on every day,” said Mark Coffey, chief executive of Vital Ireland.

“This proposed acquisition reflects our ambition to become the partner of choice for healthcare providers supporting patients in their homes and communities.”

Flanagan, along with Beechfield commercial director and fellow shareholder James Gargan, will remain on board following the deal. The business – whose activities include community care equipment, acute care and decontamination, sleep medicine, CPAP machines for people with breathing problems when sleeping, and stairlifts – employs more than 40 people.

Alvarez & Marsal acted as lead corporate finance adviser to Beechfield and its shareholders; William Fry acted as legal adviser. Arthur Cox acted as legal adviser to Vital Ireland.

Flanagan previously led a management buyout of the company in 2008.

Vital Ireland is a group of healthcare businesses providing products, services and expertise across medical devices, pharmaceuticals, scientific services and community care. Its companies include Fannin, Iskus and Medisource.

]]>Bill_Vorasate<![CDATA[Ireland was once a world leader in natural fibres – and could be again ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/science/2026/11/12/ireland-was-once-a-world-leader-in-natural-fibres-and-could-be-again/https://www.irishtimes.com/science/2026/11/12/ireland-was-once-a-world-leader-in-natural-fibres-and-could-be-again/Thu, 12 Nov 2026 06:00:00 +0000Last month saw a flurry of activity as Dublin hosted several international conferences as part of Ireland’s presidency of the Council of the EU. The International AI Summit drew a lot of attention, but I was at least as interested in the Global Bioeconomy Summit, which was organised around the publication of the Global Bioeconomy Vision 2040 and Dublin Goals.

As someone who works in economic development but is also pretty passionate about the environment, the bioeconomy is one of those areas where several of my interests tend to collide in exciting ways. At its core, the bioeconomy is about using biological resources and process to produce food, building materials, energy and chemicals.

Many of the most pressing challenges we face are a result of dependence on finite resources, not least fossil fuels. With the bioeconomy, we have an opportunity to solve those problems in collaboration with nature. Lest this sound like hippy-dippy wishful thinking, it’s something that innovative Irish companies are already doing.

Cork-based HaPPE Earth, for instance, makes compostable personal protective equipment for hospital use. Almost half of all the plastic we use is designed for single use, much of which is unnecessary but some of which, like PPE, is entirely understandable. I don’t think I’m alone in being unenthusiastic about the idea of being examined or operated on by someone wearing second-hand PPE, no matter my enthusiasm for the environment. But instead of worrying about the number of uses, HaPPE instead changed the material to one that could be disposed of without the environmental impact of plastic.

There is similar potential in other sectors. Anaerobic digestion can convert agricultural waste into fuel, while pyrolysis can turn digestate and agricultural waste into biochar, which can dramatically reduce the amount of carbon emissions from concrete production.

Bioeconomy has many meanings and plenty of potential in all its forms

Potential does not necessarily lead to economic opportunity, however. There can be quite some distance between a good idea and a commercially viable one, and for much of the bioeconomy there are areas such as manufacturing capacity, available investment and market demand that would benefit from further support.

The Dublin summit did give some cause for hope, though. The Taoiseach, alongside Ministers Martin Heydon and Darragh O’Brien, launched Ireland’s first National Bioeconomy Strategy, while European Commissioner Jessika Roswall launched the Biobased Europe Alliance, which hopes to secure €10 billion worth of commitments to buy products from the bioeconomy by 2030. The Global Bioeconomy Vision 2040 and the Dublin Global Bioeconomy Goals, meanwhile, set a range of ambitious (although not binding) goals based on growth, climate and nature, and fairness and inclusion.

Both Vision 2040 and the National Bioeconomy Strategy highlight textiles and construction as key areas to grow, which is good news for Irish firms which, like HaPPE, have already begun to develop innovative bioeconomy products. Research from projects such as BioDirect, led by Stephen Barry-Hannon at Munster Technological University, have unearthed a plethora of imaginative pilots, but identified barriers that frequently prevent these from being scaled up to commercialisation. These include weak demand, lack of finance, fragmented standards and regulations, and a lack of shared processing facilities.

Of course, growers need predictable demand, processors need an adequate supply of material and manufacturers need consistent quality to produce a product customers want at a competitive price. These issues aren’t unique to the bioeconomy. But unlike many other manufacturing processes, we have the potential to produce many of the raw materials for these on the island.

Ministers announce move to scale up all-island bioeconomy with €9m in seed funding

Indeed, Ireland was once a world-leading producer of natural fibres. Flax was a significant crop along the Lagan and upper Bann rivers and a big factor in Belfast’s industrial growth. Even today its city hall is on the site of a former linen exchange, and one of its six quarters is the Linen Quarter, formerly home to factories, weavers and warehouses to support the industry.

No less significant, although not as well known, was hemp. Sadly, Hemp Street off the Newtownards Road is all that remains of the vast ropeworks, the world’s largest. It employed more than 3,500 people at Connswater, making rope from plant fibre that supplied the adjacent shipyards as well as international markets, and was a key target for German bombers during the Blitz in the second World War.

Today the opportunities for hemp are more varied, and include hempcrete, hemp insulation, and formaldehyde-free hemp panels for construction, alongside hemp-based composites to replace glass fibre in car parts. Much of our textile waste is exported, burned or downcycled. We now have an opportunity to reuse this waste and move it up the value chain. With consistent demand and a supportive policy framework, Ireland could once again be a world leader in natural fibres.

Stuart Mathieson is research manager with InterTradeIreland

]]><![CDATA[I’m giving my son a €490,000 property. Can I cut tax bill by giving part of it as a loan? ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/12/im-giving-my-son-a-490000-property-can-i-cut-tax-bill-by-giving-part-of-it-as-a-loan/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/12/im-giving-my-son-a-490000-property-can-i-cut-tax-bill-by-giving-part-of-it-as-a-loan/Thu, 12 Nov 2026 05:00:00 +0000Q. I want to give my €490,000 investment property to my son. I’ve read it’s possible to use my capital gains tax bill on the transaction as a credit to reduce his capital acquisitions tax bill.

If I give just part of the value of the property to him, with the remaining €290,000 repayable as a loan, can I still get this tax credit?

A. Transferring the property in a part-gift, part-loan arrangement works legally, but it may not be the most tax efficient option, says Carl Donnelly, head of tax at accountancy firm Cronin.

“You may end up paying more in total tax than if you made an outright gift,” says Donnelly.

In transferring the property to his son, the father will be liable for capital gains tax (CGT) as though he were selling it at its full market value of €490,000. This is regardless of whether the transfer is, in part, structured as a loan, says Donnelly.

“CGT of 31 per cent is due on your whole gain, whether you make an outright gift or a part-gift,” he says.

The father is right. The law will let him use the CGT he owes as a credit against any capital acquisitions tax (CAT) arising for the son. This is because both taxes arise on the same event and the same property, says Donnelly.

A part-gift still qualifies for this offset. However, Revenue practice is to only give credit for the share of the CGT that relates to the gift element – €200,000 in this case.

“That amounts to 200/490ths of the CGT he owes on the property,” says Donnelly.

Also, the credit cannot be more than the CAT the son might owe on the “gifted” element of the property, says Donnelly.

Landlord? Self employed? Got deposits abroad? Tips to save money this tax year

A child can receive up to €420,000 tax-free from his parents before CAT of 33 per cent kicks in. This threshold is cumulative, so it is reduced by any earlier gifts or inheritances from either parent.

Provided the son has enough of his parent-child tax-free threshold unused, a €200,000 gift creates no CAT liability for him at all, so the credit has nothing to reduce and goes to waste, says Donnelly.

“The father’s CGT bill stays the same.”

Gift the property outright instead, and the son would have received €67,000 over this tax-free threshold, factoring in the annual small gift exemption of €3,000.

Marrying after retirement will deprive spouse of survivor’s pension

CAT on this at 33 per cent is €22,110. The full CGT paid by the father could be set against it.

“If the father’s CGT is €22,110 or more, the son pays no CAT at all,” says Donnelly.

If the family goes the part-loan route, however, each write-off above the €3,000 annual small gift exemption is regarded as a new gift that uses up the son’s threshold, he says.

“No CGT arises on a write-off so there is no credit to off-set it against.”

If the loan is interest-free, the interest the son would otherwise pay also counts as a gift to him each year, although the €3,000 annual gift exemption may cover it, he says.

If you are doing a loan, make sure it’s documented with clear repayment terms, Donnelly advises.

100 Irish websites for Christmas presents, from painted chocolates to ‘panoramic socks’

Overall, the part-gift, part-loan route works legally, but it may not be the most tax-efficient route.

“For many parents, an outright gift is the better choice because it puts the full CGT credit to use. But the right answer for you depends on your actual gain and your son’s prior gifts, so I’d recommend getting the numbers checked by a tax adviser before you go ahead.”

The family should also be aware that if the son sells or otherwise disposes of the property within two years, the CGT credit is withdrawn.

The son will also have to pay stamp duty, charged on the full €490,000 market value, not just the gifted part. For a residential property, the rate is 1 per cent.

The name of the reader who submitted the question is not being published to protect the identities of those involved.

]]>Rawpixel<![CDATA[Panic over cyberattacks plays straight into the hands of those behind them]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/2026/11/12/panic-over-cyberattacks-plays-into-hands-of-those-behind-them/https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/2026/11/12/panic-over-cyberattacks-plays-into-hands-of-those-behind-them/Thu, 12 Nov 2026 05:00:00 +0000Put the kettle on. Right now, everyone would benefit from sitting down and taking a few minutes to have a cup of something.

My weekend was largely spent calming people down after last week’s cyberattacks. Supermarket fridges got hacked, there were bomb threats to airlines and the week ended with several media organisations being evacuated due to more bomb threats.

Plenty of otherwise rational people took this as a reason for all-out panic and as a sign of the need to prepare for the end of time. Civilisation isn’t about to collapse and it’s time you had that cuppa.

All of the recent attacks or threats were designed to disrupt. That is in keeping with the experience of countries that previously held the presidency of the Council of the EU.

There was certainly some fiscal impact but the core goal was to cause disorder. Some stock was lost from fridges, some flights were rescheduled and David McCullagh regretted not grabbing his jumper.

Many people became preoccupied with thoughts of, “if the hackers could do this, then what else are they capable of?”.

That’s the wrong question to ask. They are capable of far worse, but you should be asking if doing so is really in their interest.

The big fear I kept hearing about was a national blackout. At their operational best, the most sophisticated hackers could knock out power in Ireland for about 12 hours. Weather is a far more powerful and probable threat to the grid than any malicious actor.

The goal of these disruptions, which are almost always caused by state-backed actors, is to cause fear. It may be Russia today, North Korea tomorrow or the Federated States of Micronesia at the weekend. Instilling fear and uncertainty is a key part of the package.

It probably doesn’t help that these attacks are usually backed up by disinformation campaigns. We need only look at how effective Russia’s disinformation campaign in Poland has been in damaging public support there for Ukraine to see how effective this can be.

The playbook is awfully similar to what we’re seeing here. Some legitimate concerns – which we have had in Ireland following these attacks – are exaggerated to exacerbate fear.

Having a range of goals also works in favour of cybercriminals. Some want to disrupt, some want to stoke fear, others want to steal information or money and quite a few have a cocktail involving elements of all of these. Variety of motive makes it tougher to defend as the method of attack will vary.

No matter what the goal is, it is most unlikely that an all-out attack on Ireland’s core systems is uppermost in the mind of any attackers. The truth is that it does not make sense on a cost-benefit analysis to engage in something at that level.

Attacking the fridges was a good test to see what could be done. Using anonymous accounts to spread bomb threats en masse was a low-to-no-cost means of causing disruption. Taking out the grid or worse? That involves a real commitment and potential blowback. Not from Ireland, oh no, but from those outside Ireland who would be irked.

Multinational data centres and other tech infrastructure here make for tasty targets. Attacking one or a few is certainly a reasonably likely scenario that state-backed cyber attackers will consider. Going for a true shutdown? That gets the Americans angry because it disrupts their businesses. The US government is more than capable of striking back in kind.

Ukraine blowing up three Yandex data centres caused chaos in Moscow. Cyber retaliation by the US government to a cyberattack on their tech giants would make that look like a nosebleed.

Even if the US threat wasn’t there, while Ireland may punch above its weight for its population and economy size, we are far from the juiciest target in the EU, let alone globally.

Besides, with far less risk and at far lower cost, those who caused chaos with our fridges, flights and media last week can get a great return on investment.

They have already got plenty of people afraid. People are fretting about what they might need to do for an improbable attack. Many are realising that they aren’t really capable personally of doing much about it if anything did happen.

Having a torch or a charged power bank is sensible at the best of times. As I said earlier, weather is a real threat to power in this State and winter is coming.

There comes a point where obsessing over being ready for a threat you cannot do much about becomes unhealthy. It doesn’t take long for many people to hit that point.

Between two decades of covering cybersecurity and a lifelong interest in dystopian fiction, I’ve done my share of thinking about worst-case scenarios. Dying carefree beats the hell out of living in fear.

Yes, Ireland had a few mad days of it. It’ll have a few more wild ones in the days and weeks to come but UCD got promoted to football’s top domestic tier and you’ve made yourself a cuppa. Enjoy the good things and relax.

]]>Collins Photos<![CDATA[‘Good admin isn’t sexy, but saves lives’: Start-up uses AI to cut healthcare administration burden]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/innovation/2026/11/12/good-admin-isnt-sexy-but-saves-lives-start-up-uses-ai-to-cut-healthcare-administration-burden/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/innovation/2026/11/12/good-admin-isnt-sexy-but-saves-lives-start-up-uses-ai-to-cut-healthcare-administration-burden/Thu, 12 Nov 2026 03:00:00 +0000Most clinicians would prefer to spend more time with their patients and less time on paperwork. But good follow-up is vital to good outcomes, so they grit their teeth and get on with it.

Help is at hand, however, in the shape of artificial intelligence (AI). That’s what is powering MedWrite, a new clinical documentation platform designed to relieve the administrative burden on hard-pressed healthcare professionals.

MedWrite (with human oversight) captures, drafts and sends the notes, care plans and reports that form a vital part of patient care and significantly cuts the amount of time clinicians need to spend on administration.

The idea for the platform started to take shape in 2023 when Seán Kirwan, Ahmad Albarqawi and Ruth MacIver worked together at pharma giant Novartis. Forward thinking was part of their remit, and as the possibilities of large language models became apparent, they teased out how the technology could be applied in healthcare settings.

“Around this time, my brother was diagnosed with lung cancer and was being treated in Germany. Our family was trying to follow his care from abroad, in a language that wasn’t ours, and it was really difficult. So we started with a simple question: could technology help patients and their families understand their care more clearly?” Kirwan says.

“As we worked on that problem, we began to see just how much time doctors were spending on patient-related paperwork, with writing up documentation for heavy caseloads often spilling over into evenings and weekends. This is what ultimately led us to develop MedWrite,” says Kirwan, whose fourth co-founder is Dr David Menzies, a consultant in emergency medicine and clinical professor at UCD School of Medicine.

“We already knew first-hand how difficult digital health solutions can be to implement, but when the large language models began to emerge, it was clear that something fundamental was changing. With that came the opportunity to apply the technology to healthcare,” Kirwan says.

“Clinical teams are overwhelmed by documentation and fragmented systems, and many of the AI solutions available are generic, retrofitted or adapted from consumer platforms. We built MedWrite from scratch as an AI-native company with a focus on enterprise-scale healthcare organisations.”

Kirwan adds the hitch with many digital health solutions is that clinicians are so pressed for time. So, while developing a companion app for someone with a chronic disease might sound good in theory, a doctor with 15 minutes for a consultation doesn’t have time to go through the ins and outs of what the app is recording.

“I was very aware of the problem from working at Novartis where we killed more projects than we started because of it,” Kirwan says.

“When AI came along, it was actually the first time we could really see how it could be used to ease the burden on doctors. David Menzies identified the patient discharge process as a real problem, so we did a comparative study of manual discharge versus using AI, and the AI came out on top. That convinced us we were on to something.”

Artificial intelligence has already made its way into healthcare, but Kirwan says that existing products generally do one thing for one clinician.

MedWrite is a single solution for the whole organisation as it can handle all the different clinical and administrative workflows that typically make up a busy hospital.

“Our technology has been developed alongside clinicians and can adapt to an organisation’s individual requirements so each department has exactly the type of AI set-up they want. This flexibility is really important because an emergency department works very differently to an ICU or a cardiac team. Our system allows each department to maintain its unique operating processes,” says Kirwan, who adds that the platform’s other sweet spot is that it gives the information technology (IT) team full control of the system.

“Clinicians want access to AI tools, but IT departments do not want dozens of separate applications operating across their organisation,” he says.

“MedWrite gives them one governed platform through which they can manage different AI services, integrations, access and oversight. It also gives hospitals visibility over the cost of AI, meaning usage can be measured and linked back to budgets.

“One of the other features of the platform is ambient documentation,” Kirwan adds. “With the patient’s permission, it listens to the clinical consultation and prepares the documentation the clinician needs afterwards. The clinician reviews the output, makes any necessary changes and signs it off.”

The company’s main customers are hospitals and healthcare facilities, but there is also a version for consultants operating in private practice. The system went live in July 2025, and MedWrite is currently being used by the Mater Private Hospital, St Vincent’s Private Hospital and Charter Medical. The company makes its money through a combination of licence and transaction fees. “It’s very much value-based pricing,” Kirwan says. “An organisation only pays for what it uses.”

Kirwan estimates the development costs to date at about €1.3 million, which includes private investment and €250,000 from Enterprise Ireland through its pre-seed and HPSU (high-performance start-up) funds. Wicklow Local Enterprise also supported the venture in its early days. The next financial milestone will be the launch of a funding round of approximately €2 million to drive expansion in the UK and the Gulf markets. MedWrite has a distributed team of 18 split between Ireland and the Middle East.

“A significant part of the investment to date has gone into AI research and development, building our data science and engineering capability and validating how the technology performs in real clinical settings. This has included clinical studies with Irish hospitals examining the accuracy, safety and time savings delivered by the technology,” Kirwan says. “We have also invested heavily in the software around the AI, building the MedWrite platform across web, mobile and desktop and integrating it into the systems hospitals already use.

“The third major area has been security, clinical governance and regulatory compliance,” he adds. “Healthcare has a very high bar for introducing new technology, particularly technology handling patient information, so we have built those requirements into the MedWrite platform from the outset.”

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3448102/">
   <title>U2 sind wieder fast die Alten</title>
   <description>Im 50. Jahr ihrer Bandgeschichte meldet sich die irische Band U2 nach langer Schaffenspause mit einem neuen Album zurück. <item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3448087/">
   <title>Trotz laufender Angriffe fehlt USA Strategie</title>
   <description>Die Lage in der strategisch wichtigen Straße von Hormus hat sich zuletzt wieder verschärft. Am Freitag fuhr nach Angaben der iranischen Revolutionsgarde ein Flüssiggastanker auf eine Seemine, er habe sich auf einer nicht genehmigten Route befunden und Warnungen ignoriert. Es war der vierte Tag hintereinander mit Zwischenfällen in der Meerenge. Währenddessen trägt sich im Weißen Haus nach der Wahlschlappe der Republikaner bei den Midterms ein Konflikt  um das Ende des Iran-Krieges zu.</description>

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3448115/">
   <title>EU-Einigung auf breites Verhandlungsteam</title>
   <description>Die Staats- und Regierungschefs der EU haben sich darauf geeinigt, wer Europa bei künftigen Gesprächen über ein Ende des Ukraine-Krieges vertreten soll: Das „europäische Verhandlungsteam für den Frieden in der Ukraine“ werde „aus den Institutionen der Europäischen Union und den E5“ bestehen, sagte EU-Ratspräsident Antonio Costa am Freitag nach dem informellen EU-Gipfel in Dublin. Bei den E5-Ländern handelt es sich um Deutschland, Großbritannien, Frankreich, Italien und Polen.</description>
