<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3448080/">
   <title>Langsame Erholung bei Microsoft-Diensten</title>
   <description>Microsoft hat auch am Freitag versucht, die seit Donnerstagabend aufgetretenen  Ausfälle bei Diensten aus dem Cloud-Paket Microsoft 365 zu beheben. Es gebe weitere Fortschritte, hieß es am Nachmittag, nun arbeite man an der Stabilisierung und Erhöhung der Kapazitäten. Der Datenverkehr wurde inzwischen wieder schrittweise aufgenommen, die Störung betraf Nutzer und Nutzerinnen weltweit. Freitagabend teilte der Konzern mit, dass die Störung auf ein hausgemachtes Problem und nicht auf eine Cyberattacke oder KI-Aktivität zurückgehe.</description>

A new hub has opened at the University of Oxford to support research cooperation with Poland, offering grants for academic projects, visits, training and workshops.

The Oxford Poland Hub, which its organisers describe as Poland’s first initiative of its kind anywhere in the world, will also hold public events exploring Polish history, language and culture.

We’re proud to have worked on the Oxford-Poland Hub & helped make it a reality together with great partners 🇵🇱🇬🇧

Huge thanks to:
🔹 @UniofOxford & @JesusOxford, esp. Prof Paulina Kewes & Dr Marek Naczyk
🔹 Ministry of Science and Higher Education & Minister @MarcinKulasek 🧵 pic.twitter.com/LghfpOhptC

— Polish Embassy UK 🇵🇱 (@PolishEmbassyUK) November 12, 2026

“The launch of the Oxford-Poland Hub is an exciting new chapter in Oxford’s longstanding relationship with Poland,” said the University of Oxford’s vice-chancellor, Irene Tracey. “[It] will create new opportunities for academic exchange, collaborative research and partnership between Oxford and Poland.”

The centre is initially funded for three years by Poland’s National Agency for Academic Exchange (NAWA), with support from the science and higher education ministry. It will operate within The Oxford Research Centre in the Humanities (TORCH).

“The Oxford Poland Hub…gives us a permanent institutional presence at one of the world’s leading academic centres,” said Wojciech Karczewski, NAWA’s director general.

“We see it as an investment in long-term partnerships that will enable researchers from Poland and Oxford to tackle increasingly ambitious research challenges together.”

 

The University of Oxford is the oldest university in the English-speaking world and one of the most prestigious. It ranked first globally in the latest Times Higher Education World University Rankings.

The new centre will offer grants of up to £5,000 (26,400 zloty) to support research projects or academic visits and up to £10,000 for academic workshops. Training scholarships are due to be introduced from the hub’s second year.

All researchers affiliated with the University of Oxford will be eligible to apply for funding if their work involves collaboration with researchers based in Poland. The hub will focus on humanities and social sciences as well as cooperation with Oxford’s libraries and museums.

The hub will also organise public lectures, exhibitions and events related to Polish history, language and culture for the academic community and Oxford’s residents, including its Polish community.

🇵🇱🇬🇧 Oxford-Poland Hub oficjalnie otwarty! Polska nauka zyskuje nowe możliwości współpracy z Uniwersytetem Oksfordzkim.

W uroczystym otwarciu wziął udział minister nauki i szkolnictwa wyższego Marcin Kulasek. Centrum powstało dzięki współpracy Ministerstwa Nauki i Szkolnictwa… pic.twitter.com/bZaCdM3Y53

— Ministerstwo Nauki i Szkolnictwa Wyższego (@MNiSW_GOV__PL) November 10, 2026

The hub was inaugurated on Monday at Jesus College, one of Oxford University’s colleges, with Poland’s science and higher education minister, Marcin Kulasek, and Rafał Wiśniewski, chargé d’affaires at the Polish Embassy in London, among those attending.

“Poland and the United Kingdom have for many years developed strong cooperation in science and higher education through joint research projects, academic mobility programmes and institutional partnerships,” Kulasek said. “The Oxford–Poland Hub opens a new chapter in this cooperation.”

The centre is directed by Paulina Kewes, a professor of English literature at Oxford who was born in Poland. Professor Norman Davies, the renowned historian of Poland and an honorary fellow at St Antony’s College, Oxford, attended the launch.

The inaugural lecture, given by Dariusz Wójcik, a professor at the National University of Singapore and honorary research associate at the University of Oxford, discussed Maria Czaplicka, the renowned Polish academic who in 1916 became Oxford’s first female lecturer of anthropology.

A Belgian court has overturned an order to seize funds from Poland’s air-traffic control agency, PANSA, as part of pharmaceutical giant Pfizer’s efforts to enforce a €1.3 billion claim for COVID-19 vaccines Poland ordered but later refused to receive and pay for.

The ruling, issued on Thursday, followed a legal challenge by PANSA to the freezing of its funds. It argued that it was not a party to the dispute between Pfizer and the Polish state.

❗️Dziś Francuskojęzyczny Sąd Pierwszej Instancji w Brukseli wydał korzystny dla strony polskiej wyrok w sprawie zajęcia opłat trasowych należnych @PANSA_PL , pobieranych za pośrednictwem EUROCONTROL.

Sąd uznał zajęcie za bezzasadne i uchylił postanowienie, na podstawie którego… pic.twitter.com/EHvHZnL6ab

— Ministerstwo Zdrowia (@MZ_GOV_PL) November 12, 2026

In July this year, PANSA announced that it had been cut off from the fees paid to it by the European Organisation for the Safety of Air Navigation (Eurocontrol), which manages air traffic in Europe. Around 80% of PANSA’s revenue comes from those fees.

Eurocontrol is based in Belgium, which is where Pfizer has been fighting its legal battle against Poland over the unpaid vaccines. The move to freeze PANSA’s funds was part of Pfizer’s efforts to claim money it had been awarded from Poland by a Belgian court in April this year.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk pledged government support to ensure PANSA had sufficient funds to maintain its operations and assured that air safety would not be compromised.

Poland’s air-traffic control agency has been cut off from most of its revenue as part of efforts by pharmaceutical giant Pfizer to enforce a Belgian court ruling requiring Poland to pay €1.3bn for Covid vaccines it ordered but then refused to receive https://t.co/Nd9IyLqmmf

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 11, 2026

On Thursday this week, PANSA announced that its legal challenge to the seizure of its assets by bailiffs had been successful, though it noted that the ruling can still be appealed.

Poland’s health ministry, which has been involved in overseeing the legal battle with Pfizer, said that the Belgian court had confirmed that PANSA’s funds belong to the agency itself, not to the State treasury.

“The agency is a separate legal entity; it possesses its own assets and manages its own finances independently. It is not liable for the obligations of the State treasury; therefore, its funds cannot be used to satisfy Pfizer’s claims against Poland,” wrote the ministry.

 

In comments to Polish Radio, PANSA chief Magdalena Jaworska-Maćkowiak said the agency had become a hostage in a case “that did not, in fact, concern us”.

“It stemmed from an entirely separate dispute,” she noted. “This created extreme difficulties, as we were relying on a ‘bridge’ financing arrangement that, under current law, could not provide us with long-term stability.”

Pfizer, meanwhile, said Thursday’s court decision affected only one avenue of its efforts to enforce payment of the April ruling. “We are taking ​appropriate steps through ​established legal ⁠and contractual mechanisms to ensure compliance with the court’s [April] decision,” it added, quoted by Reuters.

Sąd w Brukseli uznał sprzeciw PAŻP wobec zajęcia komorniczego dokonanego na wniosek Pfizer za zasadny i uchylił postanowienie z 25 czerwca 2026 r., stanowiące podstawę zajęcia komorniczego. Rozstrzygnięcie jest zatem korzystne dla PAŻP, ale wyrok nie jest jeszcze prawomocny.

— PANSA (@PANSA_PL) November 12, 2026

The dispute stems from Poland’s refusal in 2022 to accept and pay for COVID-19 vaccine doses ordered from Pfizer under European Union procurement agreements.

In April 2022, the then health minister, Adam Niedzielski, invoked a force majeure clause following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022

Poland, which by then had already sold or donated some of its surplus vaccines, argued the mass influx of Ukrainian refugees strained its public finances, while its cases of Covid infections had dropped.

Romania later made a similar decision to not comply with the contract. In 2023, Pfizer sued both countries in Belgium, the country where the contracts were signed. Over the course of the case, Poland also argued that Pfizer had potentially abused its market position.

A Belgian court has ordered Poland to pay US pharmaceutical giant Pfizer around €1.3 billion for Covid vaccines ordered by the European Commission on behalf of member states during the pandemic but which the Polish government later refused to receive https://t.co/1ZtPgl8Y3o

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 2, 2026

But in April, a Belgian court rejected those arguments and ruled in Pfizer’s favour, ordering Poland to accept approximately 64 million vaccine doses and pay more than 5.6 billion zloty, plus interest and legal costs.

Poland appealed against the judgment in August 2026. The health ministry said on Thursday it would not disclose details of its legal arguments or planned procedural steps while the proceedings remain ongoing.

]]> Temporary no longer: Ukrainian refugees in Poland confront the long term https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/13/temporary-no-longer-ukrainian-refugees-in-poland-confront-the-long-term/ Fri, 13 Nov 2026 12:38:06 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=106719 Leo Greenberg Ukraine needs its refugees back, but conditions make that impossible.]]>

By Leo Greenberg

Speaking to Fox News in late October, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky admitted a widely known but uncomfortable truth: Ukraine needs its refugees back.

“We need 9.5 million people – who lost their homes, who are abroad, everywhere – we need them to come back to Ukraine…to rebuild their country,” he said.

Zelensky:

We need 9.5 million people who lost their housing, who are abroad everywhere — we need them to come back to Ukraine, just to live and to build their country. pic.twitter.com/Xu2Ld4eGOu

— Clash Report (@clashreport) October 21, 2026

Unfortunately for Ukraine, all signs point in the opposite direction: Ukrainians abroad are deferring or abandoning thoughts of return.

A large proportion of those refugees – almost one million of them – live in Poland, where Ukrainians, including migrants who arrived before 2022, have provided an economic and demographic boon. But their continued stay has also posed social and political challenges, as a country with no history of mass immigration grapples with the new reality of a sizable non-citizen minority.

This has left the refugees themselves in a state of limbo: torn between a homeland that wants them back, and to which many would like to return, but where conditions do not allow for it; and an adopted home where they have created new lives but where social tensions and logistical hurdles have meant persistent uncertainty.

A new reality sets in

When Solomiia Pischana, a Ukrainian woman in her late twenties, fled from Kyiv to Poland in the wake of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, she hoped to go back that same year.

When Kyiv was secured by Ukrainian forces, a return seemed possible. In late 2022, Pischana started travelling back home to see family and friends. “I was really living between two countries. I thought a lot about going back.”

Yet quickly, a new reality set in on her visits: “In winter it became basically impossible to stay there – the constant explosions.” In Poland, by contrast, “everyone put the emphasis on helping me, on helping Ukrainians.”

In a photo essay, we look at the lives of three of the million or so Ukrainian refugees who remain in Poland one year on from Russia's invasion: Liudmyla, a mother; Vlad, an amputee soldier; and Viktoria, a high-school student https://t.co/kdOpEgt2LB

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 21, 2023

For many Ukrainians, Pischana’s story will feel familiar. When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Poland became the main waystation for Ukrainians on their way out. Millions crossed the border, and while many went on to other destinations in Europe and beyond, initially more than one million remained in Poland.

The Polish state reacted quickly, assigning more than a million special identification numbers for Ukrainian refugees – known as “PESEL-UKR” – and enrolling them in the same housing and benefits systems used by Polish citizens.

So too did Polish society, with a majority of Poles working in some way to assist Ukraine or arriving refugees, and many hosting refugees in their homes.

Around 77% of Poles have been involved in helping refugees from Ukraine, for which purpose they spent around €2 billion out of their own pockets, a new study by @PIE_NET_PL has found https://t.co/xWu8JWNMui

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 28, 2022

For Ukraine, the exodus of around six million refugees meant a raft of problems. Some 650,000 military-age men left the country, while schools had to figure out how to provide remote instruction for two million children abroad.

Most of all, the refugee crisis worsened Ukraine’s demographic challenges. Before 2022, Ukraine’s population of 42 million had already been shrinking and ageing. Now, Ukraine’s minister for social policy estimates that just 22-25 million people remain in Ukrainian-controlled territory. Two thirds of Ukrainian businesses are short of workers.

Initially, many hoped for a brief war. But, as the reality of a long, grinding conflict dawned, it became clear that Ukraine could no longer plan for an imminent influx of able-bodied adults: surveys by Kyiv’s Centre for Economic Strategies show that the proportion of refugees intending to return dropped from 74% in November 2022 to 43% in January 2026.

“Rather chaotic” attempts to connect with refugees

This reality has meant that, while Ukraine needs its people back, it also knows that it cannot compel people to return to a life defined by rolling blackouts and the ever-present threat of drones and ballistic missiles.

As a result, Ukraine’s efforts to encourage and support refugee return have been haphazard and limited.

Ukraine has one deputy minister, Ilona Havronska, who is armed with just 150 million hryvnia (13.1 million zloty, €3 million) in this year’s state budget to maintain connections with refugees abroad and support their return.

Havronska has sought to create a network of “Unity Hubs,” paid for by foreign governments, where Ukrainian refugees can confer with trained consultants about returning home. Such facilities have opened in Stockholm, Prague and Berlin, with the latter receiving 5,000 visits since opening in May.

⚡️Ukraine, Germany agree to open 'Unity Hub' for Ukrainian refugees in Berlin.

"This is a professional space that brings together community, business, and cultural initiatives," National Unity Minister Oleksii Chernyshov said.https://t.co/rlTq3MpOd0

— The Kyiv Independent (@KyivIndependent) February 15, 2025

So far, however, no hub has opened in Poland, whose interior ministry told Notes from Poland: “To be frank, the Ukrainian side, Minister Havronska, they haven’t approached us much about this recently.”

Ukraine’s other major effort, a digital platform called “Dodomu” (“Homeward”), allows users to make a return plan and check off items on a digital to-do list, such as transferring medical files, verifying IDs, and registering children in Ukrainian schools.

Since launching in June, Dodomu has been used by 4,500 people in Poland, of whom 600 have completed a questionnaire about their possibility of return.

Ukraine’s efforts to reach out to refugees abroad have been “rather chaotic”, according to Olena Babakova, a Polish-Ukrainian journalist and researcher who studies migration.

 

However, a survey by the UNHCR suggests that it may not make much difference: Ukrainian refugees ranked “support for return” as less important to their decision-making than security, economic opportunities, and housing in Ukraine. Nevertheless, for older refugees and those from now-occupied territories in eastern Ukraine, large numbers cited additional information as one of their key needs.

Valentina Bryl, a Ukrainian who has lived in Poland since before 2022 and is now an HR specialist in Wrocław, notes that returning to Ukraine would mean she would have to “start everything from the beginning – my job, my life. It’s not just about safety.”

So while Bryl says that she visits Ukraine often – taking the 25-hour rail journey from Wrocław to Kharkiv to see her husband, who is serving at the front – she hasn’t made use of Dodomu or thought about the Unity Hubs. She has no intention of moving back.

From welcome to wariness in Poland

Yet for the million or so Ukrainian refugees in Poland, as well as the hundreds of thousands of Ukrainian economic migrants who came before 2022, a growing consideration is not only the conditions in Ukraine, but also the environment they face in their adopted homeland.

Poland welcomed refugees in 2022 and has supported them since. It has also benefited economically from their presence, with Ukrainian refugees estimated to have raised national GDP by 2.4% in 2025.

Ukrainian refugees boosted Poland’s GDP by 2.4% in 2025, the equivalent of €21.5bn, according to a report by the UN @Refugees agency and @Deloitte

At the same time, their growing presence in the labour market had no negative impact on employment or wages https://t.co/lcsuIwBzpy

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 8, 2026

However, there have been growing social and political tensions. During the 2025 presidential election, even liberal candidates proposed restricting child benefits for Ukrainian refugees.

The eventual winner, right-wing candidate Karol Nawrocki, in one of his first acts as president, vetoed an extension of Ukrainians’ temporary protections, before signing a revised extension that restricted benefits.

Those political changes reflect shifting attitudes in society. A June 2026 report from the Institute of Political Critique (IKP) described last year’s election campaign as a “Rubicon”, citing testimony from Ukrainian refugees that the public environment had become more hostile and historical issues had surfaced.

Pischana told Notes from Poland that, while she is “surrounded by good people” in Poland, she has noticed that “old topics like the Volhynia massacre are coming up much more”, referring to the mass slaughter of Poles by Ukrainian nationalists in World War Two. “Just walking down the street and speaking Ukrainian, it’s started to feel a bit more dangerous,” she added.

Police data show that the number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland was 30% higher in the first half of this year than in the same period of 2025.

The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland is up 30% so far this year, police data show.

The figures come following recent high-profile cases of verbal and physical attacks against Ukrainians, who are Poland's largest immigrant group https://t.co/pcTsJddDz7

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026

Myroslava Keryk, who leads Ukraiński Dom, a hub that provides services to Ukrainian refugees in Warsaw, told Notes from Poland that her staff have faced growing harassment.

She described a slew of AI-generated videos depicting them demanding Poles pay greater taxes to support refugees, as well as sexualised, fake accounts made of her employees on online apps.

Poland’s government has condemned the recent spate of hate crimes and accused the opposition and Nawrocki of stirring up such social vitriol. Meanwhile, it has begun preparing for Ukrainian refugees’ longer-term stay.

Ukrainian refugees’ current PESEL-UKR status is tied to the EU’s temporary protections, now set to expire in March 2028. So this year, the government introduced a new “CUKR” status, valid for three years of residence after it is granted. Some 75,000 Ukrainians have already submitted applications.

President Nawrocki has signed into law a government bill ending the special status granted in 2022 to Ukrainian refugees, who will now be treated on the same legal basis as other foreigners.

Nawrocki said he is "ending the era of unconditional privileges" https://t.co/BzY7wrdl49

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 20, 2026

This new status, however, is only a step on the path to long-term stability. CUKR, unlike most refugees’ current “UKR” status, counts toward the five years of legal stay required to apply for long-term EU resident status. However, its three-year duration means holders need to secure two additional years of legal protection in Poland before applying for long-term residency.

Polish state policies have not always made things easy for refugees. New restrictions on benefits and on travel outside of Poland have made refugees careful. Despite that, many appreciated the legal and logistical clarity of Poland’s approach, typified by the new CUKR status.

Refugees’ primary fears have concerned their social environment, not their legal status. Babakova put it neatly: “Ukrainians in Poland feel very connected to Ukrainian society, but not the state. At the same time, they have come to trust the Polish state, but not Polish society.”

The citizenship question

At the same time, a growing number of Ukrainians are thinking of obtaining citizenship, which would allow them to travel more freely and vote in Polish elections.

An August survey of Ukrainian refugees in Poland found that a plurality (35%) listed obtaining citizenship as the “most desired form of assistance” to make their lives easier.

In 2025, a record 19,000 foreigners, more than half of whom (10,000) were Ukrainian, were granted citizenship in Poland.

Poland granted citizenship to a record 19,135 foreigners in 2025, up 17% from the previous year and almost five times higher than a decade ago.

Over half of recipients were Ukrainians, followed by Belarusians, Russians, Vietnamese and Turks https://t.co/FoyWd5UPJx

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 15, 2026

But since then, Poland has moved to restrict access to citizenship – to make it “an earned privilege, not a formal certificate”, in the words of the interior ministry.

The plans include extending the required period of legal residence from five to eight years, requiring a loyalty declaration, mandating advanced knowledge of Polish, and introducing an exam on Polish history and values.

Pischana wants to become a Polish citizen: “I’ve thought that it would be logical […] I’ve lived for years in Poland. I know the language.” She added that her university thesis focuses on Polish history: she’s writing a comparison of Ukrainian and Polish songs with political or social themes, from the 1980s to the present day.

Kamil Kisiel, deputy director for the department of internal affairs and migration at Poland’s interior ministry, told Notes from Poland that the new citizenship laws, soon to be announced, will be tough: “For now, being more restrictive is the way to go, so that we can manage people’s expectations”.

The proportion of Poles who hold a negative view of relations with Ukraine has risen to the highest level ever recorded by state research agency CBOS

Meanwhile, the proportion who believe reconciliation with Ukraine is possible is at its lowest ever level https://t.co/YYBCFkVxNr

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 12, 2026

Kisiel was also up front that the Polish government does not envision many Ukrainians in Poland becoming citizens. No more than a few tens of thousands of Ukrainians have obtained Polish citizenship in the past decade, and those who arrived in 2022 are not yet eligible to apply.

Instead, Kisiel highlighted, “long-term EU residence is…the sort of stability people should expect”.

Karina, a Ukrainian woman who has been in Poland since she was 15 and did not want her surname published, says that she wants Polish citizenship as it offers “a chance to travel around the European Union, go to Spain. You can also go to America, because a Polish passport gives you visa-free travel; unfortunately, with a Ukrainian one you can’t.”

Head in Poland, heart in Ukraine

Barring a major change in the course of the war, Ukraine may even become one of the countries, including Ireland and Armenia, whose diasporas are as large or larger than their domestic population – a scenario that Havronska, the Ukrainian deputy minister, told Notes from Poland she is planning for.

At the same time, social tensions and citizenship restrictions in Poland reflect the fact that refugees are challenging Poland’s identity: since the eradication and movement of Jews, Ukrainians and Germans during and after World War Two, Poland has been a largely monoethnic nation, accustomed to one language, one faith, and one national identity. The approximately 1.5 million Ukrainians in Poland have changed that.

For Pischana, her head is in Poland while her heart remains in Ukraine, saying that she feels more attached to the culture of her homeland. “It’s a pity I can’t develop in my own country, because there’s room to do it there,” she says.

For Bryl, it’s been harder to keep close to Ukraine: “I have work, I have other responsibilities…You no longer want to read, you don’t want to get angry at some bad news”.

At the beginning, she said, she felt she had a fully Ukrainian life – just one that was put on pause. But, she adds, “when it’s already been going on for five years, and it’s still unknown how long it’ll go on, well, it’s hard to keep it on pause.”

After Russia announced that it had dismantled a Polish spy network and arrested two alleged agents, Poland has dismissed the claims as “disinformation” and a “provocation”.

On Wednesday, while Poland was celebrating its national Independence Day, Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) announced that it had “disrupted the activities of an intelligence network of the Polish special services operating in Kaliningrad”, a Russian exclave that borders Poland.

It claimed to have detained two “agents”- one working for Poland’s Military Intelligence Service (SWW), the other for the Internal Security Agency (ABW) – who had been “collecting and transmitting information about military personnel and facilities” and “the socio-economic situation in the Kaliningrad region”.

 

The FSB added that seven Polish citizens and three Russians who had had contact with Polish intelligence agencies had been “officially warned”, and that the Polish citizens had been banned from entering Russia.

The suspects were detained by Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW) on 3 November in Mińsk Mazowiecki, a town just outside Warsaw, the capital. ABW officers also searched their residences and other locations connected to the investigation, seizing data storage devices and narcotics.

According to investigators, the suspects were tasked with setting vehicles on fire after changing their licence plates to ones used by Ukrainian military vehicles. This was “aimed at fueling anti-Ukrainian sentiment”, says the National Prosecutor’s Office.

Prosecutors have charged the men under Poland’s espionage law with working against Poland on behalf of a foreign intelligence service – a crime that carries a minimum prison sentence of five years – and sabotage on behalf of foreign intelligence, which is punishable by 10 years to life.

At the prosecutor’s request, a court ordered both suspects to be placed in pretrial detention for three months.

 

In recent years, Poland has seen a huge rise in cases of espionage and sabotage carried out on behalf of Russia.

The ABW launched 48 investigations related to espionage last year, more than twice as many as in 2024. In those two years taken together, there were more espionage investigations than over the previous three decades combined.

Earlier this year, the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism published a report identifying Poland as the “primary focus” of Russia’s campaign of sabotage in Europe.

Shortly afterwards, the trial began of four men – three Ukrainians and one Belarusian – accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on Russian orders.

In July, a Russian married couple with refugee status in Poland were convicted of working as spies on behalf of Moscow. In October, a member of Poland’s military reserve, who holds both Polish and Ukrainian citizenship, was detained on suspicion of espionage.

By Aleks Szczerbiak

Poland’s escalating Constitutional Tribunal (TK) dispute is no longer simply a legal argument about contested appointments but a struggle over who defines constitutional legitimacy.

As the liberal-centrist government and right-wing opposition and president advance rival rule-of-law claims, the conflict risks entrenching a system of legal dualism in which judicial authority depends on political allegiance rather than broad constitutional consent.

The roots of the crisis

Poland’s 15-member TK is a powerful body that rules on the constitutionality of the country’s laws. The roots of the current dispute trace back to late 2015 and began immediately prior to the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS) party taking office following its October parliamentary election victory.

In its final weeks in power, the outgoing government, led by the liberal-centrist Civic Platform (PO, now Civic Coalition: KO), fast-tracked the appointment of five tribunal members who were replacing those whose terms were set to expire in November and December.

Upon winning an outright parliamentary majority, the incoming PiS-led government refused to recognise these appointments, elected a slate of five new tribunal members, and party-backed President Andrzej Duda swore them in.

Fifteen months since the change of government, Poland's rule-of-law crisis continues – indeed, many Poles think the situation has got worse.@J_Jaraczewski explains the roots of the crisis, what its impact has been, and how it might be resolved https://t.co/7KOCURV3dU

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025

The tribunal (still largely composed of pre-2015 judges) ruled that three of the outgoing parliament’s appointments were lawful, so only two of the new ones could stand. PiS refused to accept this, creating the so-called “understudy” judges (dublerzy) controversy.

As further vacancies arose, the new parliament gradually installed its nominees, culminating in the appointment at the end of 2016 of one of them, Julia Przyłębska, as tribunal president. Przyłębska’s leadership was contested on procedural grounds, as was that of her 2024 successor Bogdan Święczkowski, a former senior prosecutor closely aligned with the 2015-23 PiS administration.

All of this led to the then-opposition parties and much of the Polish legal and the EU political establishments denouncing the tribunal as legally compromised and politically captured.

Total non-cooperation

Following the autumn 2023 parliamentary election, a new coalition government headed up by KO leader Donald Tusk embraced a policy of total non-cooperation with the tribunal, refusing to publish its rulings.

The battle for control took a new turn when, after initially not filling any tribunal vacancies, from March 2026 onwards the new parliament elected successive waves of new members, reaching eight by September.

However, PiS-aligned President Karol Nawrocki (who succeeded Duda in August 2025) refused to swear in five of these nominees, including former minister and close Tusk ally Maciej Berek. In response, the government took the unprecedented step of swearing in the contested nominees directly in parliament, a move that both Nawrocki and Święczkowski rejected as illegal.

The standoff between the government and president over Poland’s constitutional court deepened today, as Maciej Berek, whom the prime minister recently described as his “right-hand man”, took his oath as a new judge without the presence of the president https://t.co/MrExiJRsEN

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 14, 2026

The conflict escalated sharply at the end of last month, when, backed by the government and tribunal members elected by the current parliamentary majority, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, one of the five contested nominees but having the longest judicial tenure, asserted her seniority to order a one-month suspension of Święczkowski and his deputy Bartłomiej Sochański in their official duties and assumed temporary control.

Justice minister Waldemar Żurek submitted requests to lift Święczkowski and Sochański’s immunity as the newly appointed members, and the new nominees entered the tribunal building under State Protection Service (UOP) escort.

This triggered protests by right-wing opposition supporters at the building’s gates, prompting a heavy police presence and tense stand-off. The severity of this was underscored when Nawrocki cut short an official visit to Senegal mid-flight, returned to Warsaw and entered the tribunal building in the early hours, condemning what he described as a violation of the constitutional order.

During a visit to the Constitutional Tribunal last night, President Nawrocki clashed physically and verbally with judges involved in an attempt to take control of the court.

The president is today seeking talks with political leaders to discuss the crisis https://t.co/7HmBnuIaDG

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 31, 2026

Korwin-Piotrowska then convened a tribunal general assembly which critics argued lacked the legally required two-thirds quorum because only eight of its 15 nominal members (the newly elected ones, including the five who had not taken the presidential oath) attended.

Her supporters maintained that the quorum was met because the suspension of Święczkowski and Sochański, and exclusion of the last remaining “understudy” judge, reduced the pool of eligible members to 12.

The government’s “transitional justice” logic

For the Tusk government and its legal defenders, these exceptional executive and parliamentary countermeasures were framed through the logic of “transitional justice”: as painful and extraordinary but necessary to restore the rule of law after PiS had violated the constitution and European standards, systematically packing the tribunal with political loyalists.

Justifying its non-recognition of tribunal rulings, the government argued that the presence of three defectively elected “understudy” members and their successors, together with Przyłębska’s and Święczkowski’s procedurally flawed presidential appointments, fundamentally “contaminated” the entire body, thereby invalidating its rulings.

In its efforts to restore democracy, the government may sometimes take actions that are “not fully compliant with the law”, admits @donaldtusk.

But he says this is because of the legal chaos deliberately created by the former PiS government https://t.co/AWlM6hRLie

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 11, 2024

To provide what it argued was authoritative external confirmation of this defect, the government relied heavily on landmark European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) and EU Court of Justice (CJEU) rulings which determined that, thus constituted, the tribunal could no longer be considered a legitimate body established by legal standards.

From this perspective, refusing to recognise the tribunal’s allegedly unlawful rulings was framed as the only available mechanism to neutralise a partisan weapon that PiS had left behind to block the government’s legislative agenda.

Alternative parliamentary swearing-in procedures were justified on the grounds that the president’s role in receiving oaths was purely ceremonial, not a constitutionally mandated requirement.

 

Despite his recent political role, Berek’s appointment was defended on the basis that he played more of a technocratic-expert role within the government, and was highly qualified to undertake the extraordinary transitional measures required to repair a damaged institution.

Defenders of the tribunal leadership’s suspension and occupation of its headquarters argued that by blocking the new nominees from taking up their roles, Święczkowski had paralysed the institution and decisive measures were necessary to restore its proper functioning.

A “coup d’état”?

PiS and Nawrocki, on the other hand, maintained that the Tusk government’s actions amounted to an authoritarian attempt to operate completely outside of constitutional powers, treating legality as an option when it conflicted with its political agenda.

They insisted that all of its 2015 appointments were in full accordance with the law, correcting an improper attempt by the outgoing PO-dominated parliament to entrench its influence after electoral defeat, and that the tribunal’s ruling on the legality of these three “understudy” judges went beyond its jurisdiction.

Successive tribunal general assemblies, they argued, validly and legally selected Przyłębska and then Święczkowski as presidents, and the Tusk government had no constitutional right to pick and choose which tribunal rulings it would recognise. They said that, by delaying the election of some new members when vacancies arose, the government violated existing procedures.

The constitution, they said, explicitly required these new nominees to take their oaths directly “before the president” and that by conducting improper parliamentary swearing-in ceremonies they had effectively renounced their offices.

The International Commission of Jurists has criticised the takeover of Poland’s constitutional court, saying it “contravenes international standards on the independence of the judiciary”

But it also criticised the president for refusing to swear in judges https://t.co/2kBv3GT20d

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 4, 2026

The candidacy of Berek, a recently active politician with doubtful professional qualifications, they said represented its own form of institutional capture and selective legality.

The suspension of the tribunal leadership and occupation of its headquarters amounted to an unlawful power grab or “coup d’état” that completely disregarded established constitutional procedures.

PiS rejected the “contamination” thesis and argued vigorously that Poland had never transferred jurisdiction over the organisation of the national judiciary to EU institutions and European courts, who had no authority to evaluate the legality of tribunal appointments.

They accused the EU political establishment of double standards, weaponising “rule-of-law” arguments to help a politically aligned government while ignoring the Tusk administration’s own executive overreach.

PiS also argued that by delegitimising a tribunal which had in the past ruled that the Polish Constitution superseded EU law, the Tusk government was paving the way for controversial social and economic policies to be pushed through without any domestic judicial oversight.

Tusk’s liberal critics

On the other hand, more ideologically supportive liberal critics of the Tusk government’s approach acknowledged the original 2015 irregularities but warned that selective non-recognition of an entire institution, combined with attempts to install a new tribunal without presidential participation, risked creating the same dual legitimacy problem that they accused PiS of having started.

They stressed that lasting repair required broad political consensus and careful adherence to formal procedures so that future majorities did not simply invert the non-recognition tactic. They noted the tension with earlier condemnations of PiS for elevating politically aligned figures or recently active politicians.

While sympathetic to the goal of reforming what they believed was a deeply compromised tribunal, these critics argued that, by employing legally questionable shortcuts and executive force, the Tusk government risked setting dangerous precedents and deepening the very disorder that it was claiming to correct.

Interestingly, the government’s broader “transitional justice” justificatory logic – that ordinary procedures would not adequately address a systemic capture and the priority had to be functional restoration rather than abstract purity – mirrored the arguments PiS itself advanced for its own judicial reforms after 2015.

The right-wing party argued that the post-1989 judiciary remained dominated by a post-communist elite that required deep structural overhaul rather than incremental change.

A high-risk escalation

The latest escalation is likely to entrench and intensify the profound systemic polarisation that characterises the Polish political scene, for a long-time embodied in the KO-PiS duopoly, with the conflict framed in existential terms of either “restoring the rule of law” or “defending the constitutional order”.

This fierce dispute lies at the heart of the Tusk government’s broader political “reckoning” (rozliczenie) agenda involving visibly removing PiS’s influence from key institutions.

For the ruling coalition, this was a central 2023 election campaign message, and being seen to deliver on it is an absolute political necessity to satisfy and mobilise its electoral base. A confrontational approach thus serves to consolidate the government’s support among these core voters, who have grown increasingly impatient and want to see decisive action.

However, the government’s strategy is fraught with political risk. High-stakes tactics risk uniting its right-wing opponents and alienating moderate voters increasingly exhausted by endless, hyper-partisan institutional confrontation, legal brinkmanship and the optics of police deployments around a key state body.

They provide the president and right-wing opposition with a powerful counternarrative of constitutional vandalism ahead of the next parliamentary election.

Escalation is also straining relations within the ruling coalition, especially among more conservative or legalistic coalition partners who believe that a more fundamental constitutional “reset” based on a cross-party settlement is required to break the impasse in the longer term.

The leader of one of the parties in Poland’s ruling coalition has proposed a “constitutional reset” to resolve the crisis around the country’s top court.

It would involve removing all current judges and choosing new ones in a more consensual process https://t.co/xDwpRUVHxG

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 6, 2026

Internationally, although the EU political establishment remains supportive of the Tusk government’s actions, they invite uneasy scrutiny of the stability of Poland’s legal system and have drawn explicit criticism from the US embassy.

The reliance on a “transitional justice” framing that echoes PiS’s earlier justifications for systemic change, combined with the appointment to the tribunal of a recent minister despite prior criticisms of politicised nominations, also undercuts government claims of consistent principle and provides the right with a powerful narrative of hypocrisy.

Legal dualism

Ultimately, this bitter dispute has paved the way for a protracted and deeply destabilising “legal dualism” that could plague the Polish state for years to come, with a tribunal simultaneously legitimate and illegitimate depending on who holds power.

By treating the tribunal as an illegitimate entity when its nominees did not control it, the current government has established a precedent.

Even if it now appears to have secured a clear majority for its own nominees, a future right-wing government and sympathetic president will have every incentive to use the exact same playbook: treating the reconstituted tribunal as a captured instrument of the liberal establishment, and regarding it as no more legitimate than the Tusk government did the PiS-era one.

Consequently, the tribunal’s authority, and legal certainty in Poland more generally, have been further eroded, leaving the country without a widely accepted arbiter to resolve constitutional disputes. There are no immediate prospects for a durable resolution of this conflict.

Thousands of soldiers from 11 countries began military exercises in Poland today. They are the first organised by the so-called Coalition of the Willing, with the aim of preparing for a role in supporting Ukraine following a potential future peace deal with Russia.

The manoeuvres, which are being jointly led by France and the UK, are taking place in Nowa Dęba, around 100 kilometres from the Ukrainian border, and will last until 22 November.

The development has been condemned by Russia, which says it shows that Western countries are ignoring Moscow’s “legitimate security concerns” and “fueling the spiral of escalation”.​

🇫🇷🇬🇧 KOALICJA: The MNF-U is training to ensure a solid and lasting peace in Ukraine

The Multinational Force-Ukraine (MNF-U), formed from the Coalition of the Willing and under 🇫🇷🇬🇧command, is launching its first major exercise: KOALICJA

📅 November 9–22, 2026
📍In Poland,… pic.twitter.com/Ikcl1uY8N2

— The 🇫🇷 Joint Staff – Military operations (@FrenchForces) November 7, 2026

The plans were first announced in July by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk following a summit of the Coalition of the Willing in Paris. The exercises, taking place on land, in the air, and at sea, are being conducted by the Multinational Force Ukraine (MNF-U), which serves as the military component of the coalition.

“This exercise will show that the Multinational Force-Ukraine is a real, capable, readily deployable force that represents a serious commitment from Coalition of the Willing nations to Ukraine’s long-term stability and security,” said Tom Bateman, the British lieutenant-general commanding MNF-U.

The British Ministry of Defence says that the exercise, which has been named “Koalicja” (meaning “Coalition” in Polish), “will test Allies’ readiness to support Ukraine and rebuild their Armed Forces once the conflict ends”.

France’s armed forces ministry, meanwhile, says that the aim is to ensure that MNF-U is “ready to deploy at the request of the Ukrainian government” in order to help “guarantee a robust and lasting peace in Ukraine”.

 

Around 2,800 troops are being deployed for the manoeuvres, with AFP reporting that this includes 1,100 from France alone. The British defence ministry says it has sent 300 personnel, as well as Typhoon and Voyager aircraft.

In addition, just under 2,000 Polish troops will take part, bringing the total to almost 5,000 personnel, reports Polska Zbrojna, a publication linked to the Polish defence ministry. Other countries taking part are Belgium, Estonia, Germany, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Spain, Sweden and Turkey.

Poland’s defence ministry says the exercises will “demonstrate how quickly participating nations can mobilise and establish forces capable of supporting Ukraine after the end of the war”.

However, although Poland is hosting the manoeuvres, the defence ministry reiterated the country’s position that “it would not send its own soldiers to Ukrainian territory” as part of any postwar settlement. Poland has made clear it intends instead to help provide logistical support.

Nederland doet met enkele honderden militairen mee aan oefening Koalicja in Polen. De Coalition of the Willing traint er met 11 landen op snelle verplaatsing, commandovoering en bevoorrading ter voorbereiding op mogelijke steun aan Oekraïne na beëindiging van de oorlog. pic.twitter.com/JLE6W91HnZ

France says that the deployment of forces to Ukraine would include sending instructors to help the country rebuild and strengthen its armed forces, while air missions would enable civlian aircraft to resume flying in Ukrainian airspace.

At sea, MNF-U forces could help clear mines from shipping routes in the Black Sea. The maritime component of the current exercises is being led by Turkey through a simulated operational exercise, without deploying troops to Poland itself.

France, the UK and Poland have emphasised, however, that the MNF-U forces would only be deployed once fighting in Ukraine has ceased and would not carry out peacekeeping or ceasefire-monitoring duties.

Poland will host military exercises later this year with France and the UK to prepare for providing future security guarantees to Ukraine, says PM @donaldtusk.

He also declared Poland's willingness to permanently host more troops from its European allies https://t.co/couian4FrP

On Saturday, the spokeswoman for Russia’s foreign ministry, Maria Zakharova, condemned the exercises, saying that they make “absolutely clear that the West remains unwilling to take Russia’s legitimate security concerns into account and continues to fuel the spiral of escalation”.

She described the deployment of any foreign armed forces to Ukraine as “absolutely unacceptable” and said they would “create additional threats to Russia’s security”.

“Any military units in Ukraine will be regarded by the Russian armed forces as legitimate targets, with all the risks and consequences that entails,” warned Zakharova.

Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova’s answer to a media question in connection with the first military exercises of the so-called Multinational Force – Ukraine under the Coalition of the Willinghttps://t.co/GiouEAmT6J

— Jeff Franzius (@jk55044) November 9, 2026

The exercises come as Ukraine and Russia meet the United States and others for peace talks in Abu Dhabi this week. Ukraine has repeatedly insisted that European security guarantees would be necessary for any peace agreement.

British defence secretary Wes Streeting suggested the exercises forecast precisely such a scenario: “This isn’t a hypothetical plan, it’s a real force, ready to help Ukraine once the fighting stops.”

Zakharova, however, says that the exercises are “yet another confirmation that the Europeans have no place at the negotiating table”.

Chelsea FC have opened a pop-up store in Covent Garden in a bid to capitalise on Christmas shopping and festive tourist footfall.

The shop on Monmouth Street stocks club merchandise, including replica kits, Christmas jumpers and gifts and will be open seven days a week until 21 December.

It makes Chelsea the third football club with a retail outlet in central London, after Premier League rivals Liverpool and European champions Paris Saint-Germain.

“There is nowhere quite like Covent Garden during the Christmas season, which makes it the perfect home for Chelsea’s festive pop-up,” said the club’s lifestyle director Alexandra Currie. 

“We want supporters and shoppers alike to enjoy a little Chelsea magic this season, whether that means the latest kit, a gift for the Blues fan in the family or a piece from our festive collection.”

It follows the launch of the club’s festive range, That’s Proper Chels, which includes Christmas jumpers and pyjamas based on popular retro kit designs.

A percentage of sales will go to tackling loneliness in London through partnerships between the Chelsea Foundation and charities including Age UK Kensington & Chelsea, Katherine Low Settlement and Fulham Good Neighbours.

Football clubs in high streets across the world

Paris Saint-Germain led the way in establishing a bricks-and-mortar retail presence in central London when they opened a store on Oxford Street in 2023. 

Liverpool followed suit in May this year when they opened a club shop, also on Oxford Street, becoming the first Premier League club to do so.

PSG have club shops in 10 cities around the world, including New York City, Miami, Tokyo and Doha, while Liverpool boast more than 20 outlets from Chester and Dublin to Kuala Lumpur and Cape Town. 

Arsenal and Manchester City both have retail presence in New York, with the latter also in Abu Dhabi, home of their ownership.

Real Madrid have three stores in Barcelona – home of their fierce rivals, who have shops in the capital – as well as sites in Dubai, Mexico City and Bogota.

Nvidia shares fell more than two per cent as Wall Street opened on Friday, extending a bruising week for the chip giant after Jensen Huang’s resignation and pushing its market value below $4 trillion.

The AI heavyweight slipped 2.5 per cent to around $162 in early trading, having initially risen in pre-market dealings, as investors continued to assess the fallout from the departure of its founder and chief executive after 33 years. He stepped down following reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including a relationship with a woman suspected by US intelligence officials of spying for China.

The decline followed Thursday’s volatile session, when Nvidia shares plunged more than 13 per cent at the opening bell before recovering to close just over four per cent lower.

The scandal has raised questions over Nvidia’s leadership and corporate governance, with chief financial officer Colette Kress taking over as interim chief executive while the board searches for a permanent successor.

Tech stocks retreat as Wall Street opens mixed

The wider US market opened mixed on Friday, with the S&P 500 edging up 0.15 per cent to 7,603.78 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average gaining 0.27 per cent to 52,438.13.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite slipped 0.07 per cent to 25,347.59 as selling pressure continued across semiconductor stocks.

Nvidia’s rivals also lost ground, with AMD, Broadcom and Intel falling around two per cent, reversing some of Thursday’s gains as investors reassessed the sector’s outlook.

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, which produces Nvidia’s chips, slipped less than one per cent, while Dutch chip equipment maker ASML was little changed.

Memory chipmakers Micron Technology and SK Hynix also declined, alongside storage manufacturer SanDisk.

The losses followed a difficult session for Wall Street on Thursday, when the S&P 500 fell 0.35 per cent, and the Dow shed 189 points as Nvidia’s leadership crisis weighed on sentiment.

Despite the sell-off, some analysts believe the chipmaker’s falling valuation could present an opportunity for investors. James Demmert, chief investment officer at Main Street Research, said sentiment towards Nvidia had become “extremely negative”, but suggested the shares could find support around $165.

“We think the stock has support at $165 per share, and sentiment is extremely negative,” he said on Friday morning.

Nvidia is trading at around 13 times forward earnings, according to market estimates, despite revenue growing approximately 60 per cent year on year.

However, GF Securities downgraded Nvidia on Friday, following a separate downgrade by Oppenheimer to Perform, as investors weighed the potential consequences of losing one of the technology industry’s most influential executives.

The UK capital attracts three times as many European headquarters as any other European city, according to new research by the London Property Alliance (LPA), which represents [...]]]>

London’s status as Europe’s go-to destination for corporate headquarters is at risk, top developers and investors warn, as the City of London faces a growing office space shortage.

The UK capital attracts three times as many European headquarters as any other European city, according to new research by the London Property Alliance (LPA), which represents leading property owners, developers and investors. 

The number of head offices in London surged by 84 per cent between 2019 and 2025, according to the LPA. The city attracts three times as many European HQs as any other on the continent.

London ranks second only to Singapore in the world for the value of foreign investment in headquarters between 2003 and 2025, attracting $13.9bn. 

The capital hosted 3,185 head offices as of last year, compared to 1,735 in 2019. The number of people employed in London’s headquarters surged by 64 per cent between 2019 and 2023, according to the LPA, compared to a 10 per cent jump in employment in the city as a whole.

Howard Dawber, London’s deputy mayor for business and growth, said: “The Mayor and I are proud that London remains Europe’s leading corporate headquarters destination, a place where businesses want to invest in offices for people to do important work but also enjoy the wider cultural offer of our great city.”

These figures are “a huge vote of confidence in the capital’s future, and a testament to our enduring status as a global centre for innovation and enterprise,” he added.

But the LPA warned that London’s position as a hub for global headquarters is at risk from the growing shortage of office space in the capital’s most in-demand areas, like the Square Mile and Canary Wharf. 

London offices are ‘in short supply’

Office vacancy in London’s most sought-after locations ranges from zero to 0.8 per cent. Property developers have warned that this leaves global firms with few options to expand their existing headquarters or find new office sites. 

James Raynor, chair of the Westminster Property Association, which is part of the LPA, said: “Businesses continue to choose the capital to invest, expand and grow. But in an increasingly competitive global market, we cannot afford to become complacent.”

The LPA, which also includes the City Property Association, has urged the government to designate key office developments as critical economic infrastructure to fast-track their planning approval.

The property developers also urged the government to address rising building costs and the red tape that blocks construction projects. Multiple builders have warned in recent months that projects in London are becoming unviable.

Raynor said: “The modern offices that international businesses want, in the locations they want to be, are in increasingly short supply. We urgently need to address the rising costs and barriers holding back development and unlock investment in new and upgraded workspace.”

London-listed technology trusts suffered another bruising sell-off on Friday, after Nvidia’s shares were thrown into turmoil once more by Jensen Huang’s dramatic departure.

Nvidia shares opened 2.3 per cent lower upon Friday’s opening bell, having plunged as much as 14.3 per cent on Thursday, following the resignation of its chief executive after 33 years at the helm.

The losses dragged the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index down 0.3 per cent, while the S&P 500 shed 0.1 per cent.

Losses were exacerbated by revelations of a third extramarital affair involving Huang, following news of one with a woman who is suspected to be a Chinese spy by the US government and Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare.

Betting big

The crisis surrounding Huang has dealt a heaby blow to a number of London-listed technology investment trusts who bet big on the chipmaker long deemed essential to the AI trade.

Manchester & London Investment Trust which has Nvidia alongside fellow US chip firms Micron and Broadcom, account for about a third of its portfolio, has lost nearly a fifth of its value over the last month.

Allianz Technology Trust has seen its share price tumble 13.2 per cent, while Polar Capital Technology Trust, has lost 13.3 per cent. Both boast Nvidia as their largest holding.

On Friday, following US market open, Manchester & London’s daily losses extended to 1.5 per cent.

Polar Capital plunged 1.5 per cent and Allianz shed 1.2 per cent.

Concentration woes

Over 40 per cent of Polar Capital’s portfolio is exposed to semiconductor stocks. Micron and Broadcom also present as a top ten holding alongside Microsoft which suffered a global outage on Thursday and plunged critical services across the UK into the dark.

All three investment trusts are highly concentrated in the US market, led by Manchester & London which has 92.6 per cent of its equity exposure in North America, leaving it particularly vulnerable to the mass sell-offs plaguing the sector over the past week.

Away from Huang, concerns over debt-fuelled hyperscaler data centre build-out coupled with the Democrat’s resounding midterm victory has left investors questioning the longevity of the AI boom.

In contrast, trusts with minimal to no exposure to US-listed tech have seen their share prices rise. Finsbury Growth & Income Trust, led by notable fund manager Nick Train, has increased 3.1 per cent in the last week, while UK small-cap stockpicker Onward Opportunities rose 1.9 per cent.

Asda’s food sales slowed in the weeks before Allan Leighton stepped back from leading the grocer’s turnaround, to be replaced by a former Morrisons and Tesco boss.  The discount supermarket grew its like-for-like food sales by 0.1 per cent in its third quarter, marking a slowdown from the significant uplift in sales it had seen [...]]]>

Asda’s food sales slowed in the weeks before Allan Leighton stepped back from leading the grocer’s turnaround, to be replaced by a former Morrisons and Tesco boss. 

The discount supermarket grew its like-for-like food sales by 0.1 per cent in its third quarter, marking a slowdown from the significant uplift in sales it had seen at the start of this period.

The group had already disclosed 0.7 per cent like-for-like sales growth in food for the seven weeks to mid-August, but Friday’s figures, which cover the full 13 weeks to the end of September, show this uplift has since tailed off.

Asda has been pushing for a turnaround since appointing Allan Leighton, who led the grocer to its 1990s heyday, as executive chairman in November 2024. 

He stepped back into a non-executive role last week, and was replaced by former Morrisons boss David Potts, who took up the reins as chief executive on Tuesday. 

Leighton said in August that the group was in the “foothills of recovery” after it reached like-for-like sales growth for the first time in more than two years.  

Asda’s overall revenue, including fuel, grew 3.1 per cent year on year in the 13 weeks to September, as online sales were a key driver, up 6.9 per cent like-for-like.

The discount grocer said it is working to keep prices low to draw in customers battling a squeeze on their budgets. British families’ budgets are at a six-month low, according to Asda’s income tracker.

Asda loses ground on rivals

Michael Gleeson, Asda’s finance chief, said: “The work we’ve done through the period to deliver against our strategy was reflected in our third-quarter performance. 

“Asda’s key strength is the breadth of our business, spanning food, clothing, fuel, pharmacy and other services. This means we can meet more of our customers’ everyday needs and gives us more opportunities to grow. 

“Our disciplined approach to managing costs and cash means we can keep investing in value today and in sustainable growth in the long-term.”

Asda’s slowdown in sales growth revealed on Friday comes amid suggestions that the grocer’s takings have slumped back into negative territory in recent weeks. 

The discount grocer’s total sales came in at £4bn in the 12 weeks to November, according to the latest figures from Worldpanel, marking a 0.5 per cent decline from the same time last year. 

During this period, takings grew at each of Asda’s competitors, including a 6.6 per cent uplift at Lidl and a two per cent jump at Morrisons. 

Since taking charge of the grocery giant, David Potts, who was chief executive of Tesco’s Asian business before joining Morrisons in 2015, has told Asda’s staff to focus on improving the in-store experience for shoppers.

He has instructed the group’s general managers to make more staff-operated checkouts available at its stores. He told staff: “We’re making it harder than it should be for customers to get what they want, move around the store and pay for their shopping. We need to change that, starting now.”

On Thursday, Potts announced Asda would cut 4p per litre from the price of petrol and unleaded diesel at its 321 fuel forecourts. The measure will save the average family £2.20 per tank, the grocer said.

Nvidia chief’s defenestration underlines the importance of governance ESG’s overlooked category, Ali Lyon writes in today’s Midday Markets newsletter.

At City AM, we pride ourselves on making the cross-pollinating worlds of business, finance, economics and wealth, fun. Indeed, so averse are our higher-ups to conforming to the industries’ love of complexity, jargon and – dare we say – pretence, that ‘business with personality’ has been the paper’s strapline for the entirety of its 21-year existence.

And so when, today, I suggested devoting this newsletter to the the subject of ‘governance’ I was met with more than a few raised eyebrows.

I’ll concede, 700 words on the processes and structures that a company implements to protect the long-term interests of its stakeholders doesn’t scream ‘business with personality’.

But this week’s defenestration of Jensen Huang – the scandal-hit co-founder of chip giant Nvidia – has thrust the thorny, unsexy issue firmly into the limelight, and thrown up some interesting talking points, to boot.

To many in the public and among some of the company’s shareholders, Huang was not the face of Nvidia; he was Nvidia. And for good reason: the leather jacket-toting, ever-energetic ‘AI rockstar’ had been both chief executive and president of the semiconductor colossus for more than 30 years.

He oversaw its evolution from niche computer-gaming chipmaker to the undisputed weathermaker of the AI evolution. And now, he’s gone, leaving a vacuum of leadership, not just at the world’s second-largest company, but at the heart of the most financially consequential industrial revolution in history.

This is, to borrow a technical phrase, not good. Nvidia’s shares are down 10 per cent since the start of the week, and 20 per cent in the past month. In one day, they shed more value than the total market capitalisation of HSBC, the FTSE 100’s most valuable company, all because of the poor judgement of a single, highly consequential individual.

UK Corporate Governance Code, I was not familiar with your game

The unseemly episode has laid bare the sheer amount of power and influence wielded by those at the top of the largest companies in history. In Nvidia’s case, Huang reportedly had up to 60 executives reporting directly into him at any one time. And despite the totemic founder’s multi-decade tenure, Nvidia’s toothless – and, until this week, chairless – board appears to have done next to no succession planning.

As Imperial Business School associate professor Dr Porneetha Luthra wrote in the pages of City AM this week: “While charismatic’ leaders can seem intoxicating – admired, respected and sometimes loved – this is a very dangerous hierarchy.”

It’s worth noting that, had the same indiscretions been committed by any of the other founder-led tech giants, things would have been even worse. Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, SpaceX and Tesla’s Elon Musk and Palantir’s Alex Karp are all, essentially, impossible to fire, thanks to the company’s dual-share structure.

And to a number, those emblematic entrepreneurs also personally own much more of the company than Huang’s 3.6 per cent. Just imagine the chaos had it been Elon Musk – who owns a fifth of Tesla and nearly half of SpaceX – who fraternised with an alleged Chinese spy.

In the good times, this concentrated power is a blessing. It allows for fast, bold decision-making unhindered by pesky shareholder votes and board oversight. When you’re dealing with some of the biggest brains in the world, who know their company and industry back to front – those decisions are more often than not, correct and lucrative. But either in – or in the run-up to – crises, robust governance is worth its weight in gold.

Which is why, today at least, we should be grateful for the UK’s rather old-fashioned approach. Thanks to the UK Corporate Governance Code, there is not a single FTSE 100 chief executive who also serves as chair of their company’s board (on the US’s S&P 500, more than four in 10 do). Under London-listing rules, any public company that allows its most senior executive to serve in both roles must explain its rationale to shareholders every year.

In a recent overhaul, the London Stock Exchange chose to water down some of its rules in what is, so far, a vein attempt to attract founder-led fintech and tech unicorn IPOs. But those changes don’t come close to mirroring the free-wheeling approach adopted by the bourse’s counterparts across the pond. And after this week’s Nvidious episode, that is probably no bad thing.

]]> 2477698Ali Lyon Ali Lyon Davina McCall lights up London’s tallest Christmas tree, then belts out Mariah Carey https://www.cityam.com/davina-mccall-switches-on-londons-tallest-christmas-tree/ Fri, 13 Nov 2026 12:50:45 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2477725

Davina McCall switched on the 67ft Eastern City tree outside Pan Pacific London, then joined a singalong of Mariah Carey’s Christmas classic]]>

Last night Davina McCall switched on the lights on London’s tallest Christmas tree, a 67ft installation outside the Pan Pacific Hotel near Liverpool Street.

Dickensian figures and the world’s biggest wreath

The mammoth tree, which is sponsored by the Eastern City Business Improvement District (BID), features more than 100,000 lights and, in a nod to the Square Mile’s literary history, is surrounded by six Dickensian figures. Opposite the tree you can spot the world’s biggest Christmas wreath in the window of the hotel.

The lighting ceremony was accompanied by stilt-walking nutcracker characters, a gospel choir and stands offering mulled wine and mince pies. After switching on the lights, McCall joined Eastern City BID CEO Kate Hart on stage for a rendition of Mariah Carey’s All I Want For Christmas.

Davina McCall: ‘It means we’re allowed to play Mariah!’

McCall said: “I love it when the lights start going on – it means that we’re allowed to play Mariah!

“Christmas is a time to reflect on what happened to us last year, for some of us. That might be quite difficult, but it is also a time where you can learn from it, and then you can let it go and move on.

“It’s a great time of hope and coming together, and it doesn’t necessarily have to be friends and family – it can just be remembering to give someone a smile on the street.

“If we look too much at social media, we think, oh, the world is full of horrible people and hatred. But I’m looking around here and I disagree: it’s full of hope, and it’s full of love and beautiful people. So let’s all be kind to each other this Christmas.”

Eastern City BID: ‘It’s all about people and place’

Kate Hart said: “We are incredibly proud to deliver this fabulous festive initiative along with our friends at Pan Pacific London. Christmas is a time for community, for tradition, for celebrating the past but looking ahead to the future. It’s all about people and place.

“In the last five years we have organised over 400 events which have been attended by over 180,000 people – and with your support we hope to do so much more going forward.”

London’s tallest Christmas tree: Dates and festive events

The Eastern City Christmas tree will be on display until 9th January 2027. It is just one of the festive experiences sponsored by the Eastern City BID this Christmas. Others include:

  • A Letters to Santa scheme (16 November-20 December), allowing people to post their Christmas wishes on Birchin Lane for the chance to win a Pan Pacific London gift voucher or Christmas hamper.
  • A traditional Christmas Sweet Cart (17-19 November and 8-10 December) featuring complimentary old-fashioned sweets at various locations across the Eastern City.
  • The Eastern City Festive Fair (24–28 November) which includes traditional market stalls, seasonal treats, festive workshops and Victorian characters.
  • A series of Christmas Creative Workshops (17 November-9 December) encouraging Londoners to get creative with wreath-making, gingerbread decorating, festive calligraphy, embroidery and more.
  • Dickensian Christmas Walking Tours (26 November and 9 December) allowing people to discover the Eastern City’s festive past through historic landmarks, ghost stories and Victorian Christmas traditions.
  • A visit from Santa (10 December) during which the big man himself will visit locations around the Eastern City.

British businesses face a “bad day for UK plc productivity” thanks to Microsoft’s global outage, prompting warnings of mounting financial losses and the risks of relying on a single technology provider. The disruption, which began on Thursday evening, has left companies struggling to access Outlook, Teams and other Microsoft 365 services, affecting everything from customer [...]]]>

British businesses face a “bad day for UK plc productivity” thanks to Microsoft’s global outage, prompting warnings of mounting financial losses and the risks of relying on a single technology provider.

The disruption, which began on Thursday evening, has left companies struggling to access Outlook, Teams and other Microsoft 365 services, affecting everything from customer communications to financial transactions.

Supermarket giant Asda reported problems with online customer registrations, password resets and email changes, although City AM understands its operations have been restored.

Rail operators were also hit, with Great Western Railway warning passengers that emailed ticket confirmations were unavailable and advising customers to access tickets through its app or website.

The disruption has also affected financial services firms, including Natwest, as businesses across the City grapple with communication failures.

Riz Malik, an independent financial adviser at R3 Wealth, said: “Friday the 13th spells doom for Microsoft and many of those that rely on their services. This is a bad day for UK plc productivity.”

Businesses warn of mounting losses from Microsoft outage

The outage has raised concerns over the financial cost of prolonged disruption, particularly for smaller businesses that rely on Microsoft’s software to communicate with customers, suppliers and lenders.

Samuel Mather-Holgate, managing director of Mather and Murray Financial, warned that the disruption could become one of the “most economically damaging technology failures in history” and cost businesses billions.

The impact has been particularly acute for time-sensitive transactions, including property purchases, where delays in exchanging documents between solicitors, lenders and brokers can hold up completions.

Financial services firms also face heightened pressure to maintain access to critical information, with regulators requiring businesses to demonstrate that they can withstand major technology disruptions.

Rob Mason, director of regulatory intelligence at Global Relay, said firms could not afford to “go dark”, warning that the outage would prompt fresh questions about operational resilience and dependence on third-party providers.

The disruption has also exposed the extent to which British companies rely on a small number of American technology giants for their day-to-day operations.

Microsoft and Amazon Web Services together control an estimated 70 to 80 per cent of the UK’s public cloud market, leaving businesses heavily exposed to failures at major providers.

Mark Boost, chief executive of UK cloud provider Civo, said the concentration of services within a handful of companies meant a single outage could disrupt multiple business functions simultaneously.

“When the same company runs the cloud, email, documents and collaboration tools, a single failure takes everything down together,” he said.

However, Microsoft’s entrenched position means businesses are unlikely to abandon its services overnight.

Amish Patel, head of equity research at Raymond James, said the direct financial impact on Microsoft was likely to be negligible, given its scale and the difficulty customers face in switching providers.

“The more interesting question is whether repeated outages begin to change how businesses think about their dependence on a single technology provider,” he said.

Microsoft said on Friday that it was making “additional progress toward service recovery”, with traffic gradually being restored after disruption spread across 74 countries.
