AGN https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/ Aerospace Global News Sat, 14 Nov 2026 00:26:55 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.4 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/cropped-AGN_Icon_Jet-32x32.png AGN https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/ 32 32 What is a ground stop and why does the FAA order one? https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/what-is-a-ground-stop-faa-why-order-one Sat, 14 Nov 2026 00:07:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=56727 A single disruption can send delays rippling through the aviation network. Here's a closer look at the decisions behind keeping aircraft on the ground and how controllers manage the knock-on effects.

The post What is a ground stop and why does the FAA order one? appeared first on AGN.

]]> The last thing you want to hear when you’re about to depart is that a ground stop is in effect. But for airlines, airports and air traffic controllers, it is an essential tool for maintaining safety and managing congestion across the aviation network.

A ground stop is an air traffic management measure issued by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) that temporarily prevents aircraft from departing for a specified airport or location. Instead of allowing flights to take off and potentially join an already congested arrival queue, airlines are instructed to hold affected aircraft at their departure airports.

It does not necessarily mean the destination airport has closed. Arrivals may continue, depending on the circumstances, while flights already airborne are managed by air traffic controllers.

Read next: Breaking: All US flights grounded nationwide over major communications issue Read next: Breaking: All US flights grounded nationwide over major communications issue

Why might the FAA order a ground stop?

The most recent ground stop occurred on 13 November 2026, due to a communications issue with air traffic control.

However, weather is another common reason the FAA might issue a ground stop. Thunderstorms, heavy snow, strong winds and poor visibility can significantly reduce an airport’s capacity. An airport that normally handles dozens of arrivals an hour may suddenly be able to accept far fewer.

When this is the case, keeping aircraft on the ground is often safer and more efficient than allowing them to depart, only to spend extended periods in holding patterns or divert to alternative airports.

Operational problems can also trigger a ground stop. Runway closures, aircraft incidents, equipment failures and cyber attacks can all affect an airport’s ability to handle normal traffic volumes.

Staffing shortages may also play a part. If an air traffic control facility cannot safely manage the expected number of aircraft, the FAA can restrict incoming traffic until sufficient capacity is restored.

How does a ground stop work?

The FAA’s Air Traffic Control System Command Center coordinates traffic management across the United States, working with individual air traffic control facilities to respond to changing conditions.

When a ground stop is introduced, airlines receive instructions specifying the affected airport, which flights are covered and the anticipated duration. Departures are held at their origin airports, with airlines adjusting schedules and passenger arrangements accordingly.

Ground stops are not necessarily issued for a fixed period. The FAA regularly reassesses conditions and can extend, modify or lift restrictions as circumstances change.

Read: How much extra fuel does an airliner need to carry in case something goes wrong? Read: How much extra fuel does an airliner need to carry in case something goes wrong?

Ground stop vs ground delay programme

Although often confused, these are two distinct traffic management measures.

A ground stop temporarily prevents specified flights from departing for an affected destination. A ground delay programme takes a less restrictive approach, assigning departure delays and calculated arrival times to regulate the flow of traffic.

The FAA uses both to balance demand with available airport and airspace capacity. The appropriate measure depends on the severity and nature of the disruption.

Keeping the skies moving safely

Ground stops can cause significant inconvenience, particularly when disruption spreads across multiple airports. However, they are an important part of managing an aviation system in which a problem at one location can have consequences hundreds of miles away.

By controlling departures before congestion becomes unmanageable, the FAA can give airports and controllers the breathing space needed to restore normal operations.

Unfortunately for passengers, it may mean a rather longer wait at the gate. But for the wider aviation network, it is a practical way of putting safety ahead of schedule.

]]> What happens to planes already in the air when the FAA grounds all flights? https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/what-happens-planes-already-in-air-faa-grounds-flights Fri, 13 Nov 2026 23:33:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=56719 A nationwide grounding doesn't necessarily mean every aircraft must land immediately. Aircraft already airborne may continue to their destinations, enter holding patterns or be diverted, depending on the severity of the disruption and the availability of air traffic control services.

The post What happens to planes already in the air when the FAA grounds all flights? appeared first on AGN.

]]> When the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) orders all flights to be grounded, departures across the country can quickly come to a halt. The last major time we saw a ground stop in the US was during the 9/11 attacks.

But what happens to the thousands of aircraft that may already be airborne across US airspace?

The answer depends on the reason for the grounding and how significantly air traffic control (ATC) operations have been affected.

In most cases, aircraft already in flight are not automatically ordered to land. Instead, controllers manage each flight according to the circumstances, maintaining safe separation and determining whether aircraft can continue to their planned destinations.

Read next: Breaking: All US flights grounded nationwide over major communications issue Read next: Breaking: All US flights grounded nationwide over major communications issue

Flights already airborne can usually continue

A standard ground stop is primarily intended to prevent aircraft from taking off. It does not necessarily apply to flights already in the air.

If the disruption is relatively localised, such as a technical issue at an airport or a temporary restriction on departures, aircraft already en route will generally be allowed to continue to their destinations.

Air traffic controllers remain responsible for managing these flights, coordinating arrivals and making sure aircraft maintain safe separation. However, depending on the scale of the disruption, arriving aircraft may face delays or additional restrictions as controllers manage the flow of traffic.

Holding patterns and diversions

The situation becomes more complicated if an airport can no longer safely accommodate arriving traffic.

If an airport becomes congested, approaches capacity or experiences a significant equipment failure, controllers may instruct aircraft to enter holding patterns. This allows flights to remain in designated areas of airspace while waiting for landing clearance.

Where disruption is more serious or goes on for longer, aircraft may be diverted to alternative airports. These decisions take into account several factors, including fuel reserves, weather conditions, runway availability and the capacity of neighbouring airports to accommodate additional traffic.

One particularly serious scenario is an ‘ATC Zero’ event, where an air traffic control facility loses the ability to provide normal services. This could result from a major failure involving communications, radar or essential automation systems. With the ability to manage aircraft significantly reduced, diversions and wider airspace restrictions may become necessary.

Read: What happens when an airport loses air traffic control? Read: What happens when an airport loses air traffic control?

What happens to international flights heading to the US?

International arrivals are also managed according to the nature and extent of the disruption.

Some aircraft may be permitted to continue towards their US destinations, while others could be rerouted, placed in holding patterns or diverted to alternative airports.

For transatlantic flights, for example, decisions may need to be made before aircraft reach US airspace, potentially resulting in rerouting or holding offshore. Coordination with neighbouring air navigation service providers is essential so that aircraft can be managed safely across different areas of responsibility.

Safety is the priority

Ultimately, the response depends on the nature of the disruption, the availability of ATC services and the ability of airports to safely handle arriving traffic. For passengers already onboard, that could mean continuing to their destination, spending time in a holding pattern or being diverted elsewhere.

The priority throughout is to maintain safe and orderly operations, even when the wider aviation system is facing significant disruption.

The post Breaking: All US flights grounded nationwide over major communications issue appeared first on AGN.

]]> For only the second time since the 9/11 attacks, all flights in the United States have been ground to a halt. US Transport Secretary Sean Duffy says that the ground-stop was ordered over a communications issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centres. No additional information has been shared at the time of publication as to the nature of the issue.

Flights bound for the US are no longer allowed to depart. Although international flights that have already departed would already be en-route, the FAA says they will be managed on a “case by case basis.”

“Everybody is safe,” assures US Homeland Security secretary Markwayne Mullin. “There should be no fear to the public at all.”

Flights grounded over a “communications issue”

The advisory issued by the Federal Aviation Administration said: “Due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety. Attention all aircraft operators, by order of the Federal Aviation Command Center all airports are ground stopped. All departing traffic should remain ground stopped until further notice. Inbound international flights will be managed on a case by case basis.”

The FAA added in a statement that the decisions was taken “out of an abundance of caution” over a “temporary telecommunications outage.”

“You cannot rule out anything at this point,” Mulling added when asked whether this was AI-related disruption following rumours to that effect.

The body initially ordered all flights from Chicago’s O’Hare and Midway Airports to be suspended at 20:10 UTC over an “equipment outage.” At 20:54, the ground stop was extended nationwide.

Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said: “The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers. FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them.”

The last time flights were brought to a complete stop in the United States was on 11 January 2023, when the FAA halted all domestic operations between 07:30 and 09:00 in the morning due to a system outage.

Heavy disruption expected

Amid the ground-stop, Flightradar24 data shows just over 3,100 flights are bound for the United States. Thousands have already been delayed or cancelled as a result of the order from the FAA.

Information from aviation analytics firm Cirium shows 26,284 flights are scheduled to depart today from the United States of which 11,000 are still planned. 481 are listed a scancelled at the time of publication, though this number will increase exponentially as airlines adjust schedules to accommodate the FAA’s instruction.

A source on the ground at Chicago O’Hare tells Aerospace Global News that baggage is still being loaded onto aircraft, noting significant queues of planes across the airfield. Departure and arrival boards have now updated to account for the disruption, showing either heavy delays or cancellations.

Aircraft currently at the gates remain stationary, while passengers on other planes remain stranded on aircraft parked elsewhere across the airport. Chicago, like many other major US airports, is now nearing capacity. By 22:50 UTC, 28 flights had been diverted to Chicago, Cirium says, most of which originated there.

In any case, disruption will have knock-on effects worldwide as aircraft and crews are displaced.

Airlines begin cancelling flights

United Airlines says that all flights currently airborne will proceed as planned, but no new departures will take places. “United will work with our customers to get them to their destinations once this issue is resolved,” it adds.

American Airlines said the same, adding that it expects disruption to its schedule “for the rest of the day, depending on the length of the FAA’s nationwide ground stop.”

Canada continues to operate as normal. NAV Canada, the country’s air navigation service provider, says: “We continue to support the safe movement of air traffic in our airspace, including any aircraft that may be diverted.”

It adds that it has “implemented traffic management measures” in Toronto, Montréal, Calgary and Vancouver, with delays to be expected. NAV Canada urges customers to check with their airline directly.

]]> SpiceJet cancels Dubai flights amid dispute over unpaid airport fees, according to reports https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/spicejet-cancels-dubai-flights-unpaid-dues/ Fri, 13 Nov 2026 17:14:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=56649 SpiceJet cancelled multiple Dubai-to-India flights after airport check-in services were suspended over unpaid airport fees, according to reports.

The post SpiceJet cancels Dubai flights amid dispute over unpaid airport fees, according to reports appeared first on AGN.

]]> Four SpiceJet flights from Dubai to India were cancelled on 12 November after airport check-in services were reportedly suspended over outstanding dues of 14 million dirhams (about $3.8 million).

The cancellations affected services to Amritsar, Jaipur, Mumbai and Delhi. Two other flights, bound for Ahmedabad and Delhi, were allowed to operate, according to media reports.

The Week reported on Friday that the Indian low-cost carrier was working with the relevant authorities to resolve the payment dispute.

SpiceJet acknowledged the issue in a statement quoted by The Week.

“We are in the process of resolving the matter with the concerned authorities. We have adequate bank guarantee cover in place and are working to ensure that the issue is sorted out at the earliest,” the airline said.

The statement did not specify when normal operations would resume or explain why the outstanding payments had led to the suspension of check-in services.

The disruption extended into Friday, with The New Indian Express reporting that no SpiceJet flights departed Dubai for India today. The newspaper said ground-handling company Dnata had not allocated check-in counters to the airline because of the payment dispute.

Internal correspondence first reported by Informist Media indicated that Dubai Airports had warned SpiceJet earlier in the week that its outstanding payments had reached 14 million dirhams, with no payment received since 13 October.

The correspondence also indicated that the Dubai Civil Aviation Authority had asked the airline to arrange alternative travel and accommodation for stranded passengers.

The four cancelled passenger flights were subsequently designated as ferry flights, allowing the aircraft to return without passengers.

Financial problems deepen

The Dubai disruption comes as SpiceJet faces mounting financial and operational difficulties, including a shrinking fleet, repeated cancellations and outstanding payments to suppliers and aircraft lessors.

According to The Week, the airline told the publication that it had 12 operational aircraft, although three were reportedly grounded. This represents a sharp reduction from a fleet of around 120 aircraft in 2020.

The airline’s domestic market share fell to just 0.6% in September, according to data from India’s Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA). SpiceJet carried approximately 73,000 domestic passengers that month, compared with about 590,000 in January.

The carrier has also faced complaints from employees over delayed salaries, while former staff have alleged that their final settlements remain unpaid.

Its financial position remains difficult to assess because the airline has yet to publish its results for the final quarter and full year of the 2025–26 financial year, as well as the first two quarters of 2026–27.

The Bombay Stock Exchange stated that trading in SpiceJet shares will be suspended starting December 10, 2026, unless the airline files its overdue financial results for the March and June 2026 quarters by December 7, 2026.

SpiceJet seeks fresh capital

The airline is now considering another round of fundraising to support its operations.

In a stock exchange filing on Friday, SpiceJet said its board would meet on November 18 to consider raising fresh capital through equity shares, preference shares, debt securities or other permitted financial instruments.

The development comes as operational difficulties are affecting passengers beyond Dubai.

Delhi’s Indira Gandhi International Airport issued an advisory on Friday warning that some SpiceJet flights could be affected by operational challenges. Passengers were advised to contact the airline directly for updated flight information. The airport did not specify the number of services involved.

]]> Czech Republic considers supplying Ukraine with 16 L-39 Skyfox aircraft https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/czech-l39-skyfox-ukraine/ Fri, 13 Nov 2026 16:14:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=56566 Following Ukraine's earlier attempt to acquire four L-159 ALCA light combat aircraft, the Czech Republic is negotiating Ukraine acquiring 12 new build L-39 Skyfox drone hunters.

The post Czech Republic considers supplying Ukraine with 16 L-39 Skyfox aircraft appeared first on AGN.

]]> Following a breakdown in an effort to supply Ukraine with L-159 ALCAs from its own stocks, the Czech Republic is discussing transferring a dozen new-build L-39 Skyfox trainers, light combat, drone interceptors.

The Czech Minister of Industry and Trade, Karel Havlíček, said on Wednesday (11 November) that the Czech Republic may help to facilitate the supply of 16 Skyfox aircraft to Ukraine.

Havlíček added that four Skyfox jets have already been confirmed for delivery and that discussion is now focusing on 12 more. Funding for the first four is secure, but funding for the next 12 remains in negotiation.

At the end of July 2026, it was reported that the Czech Republic and Ukraine had jointly approached about 12 partner countries (Australia, Canada, and 10 European states) seeking financing for the purchase.

What is the L-39 Skyfox?

The Skyfox is a turbofan-powered military trainer, light combat, and drone-interceptor aircraft developed by the Czech Republic’s Aero Vodochody and is the successor to the Aero L-39 Albatros.

Aero Vodochody is the primary Czech airplane maker and is noted for producing a range of jet-powered trainers. This includes the L-29 Delfn and L-39 Albatros and the L-39 derivatives, the L-59 Super Albatros and the L-159 ALCA aircraft.

The company currently produces around 12 L-39 Skyfox jet trainers annually, with company statements suggesting it has capacity to produce up to 18 a year.

It has sold over 40 Skyfox aircraft today, and its production schedule is fully booked through to the second quarter of 2027.

Failed efforts to acquire Czech L-159 ALCAs

AGN has previously reported that Ukraine was seeking to acquire four L-159 ALCA (Advanced Light Combat Aircraft) from the Czech Armed Forces inventory.

Prime Minister Andrej Babiš rejected transferring the aircraft, arguing the Czech military needed them. AGN subsequently reported that the Czech Air Force lacks the pilots to fly them.

Ukraine intended to use them as drone hunters to help intercept masses of Russian drones being fired.

Aero Vodochody’s L-39 Skyfox lands first customers in Africa and North America Aero Vodochody’s L-39 Skyfox lands first customers in Africa and North America

Aero Vodochody’s New Drone Hunter

The Aero L-39 Skyfox is Aero’s latest aircraft, having only reached serial production in 2024. In September 2026, the dedicated Skyfox Drone Hunter version was unveiled.

That version can carry up to 28 of the cheap 70 mm laser-guided rockets used to intercept drones. It can also carry a 12.7mm gun pod.

The Czech news outlet CT24 states, “Drone Hunter has not yet been deployed operationally, and its capabilities will need to be demonstrated through further testing.”

Ukraine and other countries are currently using fighter jets to intercept drones. The Skyfox would offer significantly lower operating costs than those of a frontline fighter.

Unlike fighter jets, the Drone Hunter configuration lacks an expensive onboard search radar. Instead, it relies on external sensors for target detection and its electro-optical/infrared pod for identification and targeting.

Aeros Vodochody’s advertizing brochure claims, “Very low operational cost (less than 2000 €/FLH), Faster response time (~13 min) outperforming helicopters and turboprops, Extended endurance capability (4 h 45 min) and loiter time (3 h+).”

]]> Poland presses ahead with Port Polska hub as 2032 opening target remains in sight https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/poland-port-polska-airport-hub-2032-opening/ Fri, 13 Nov 2026 15:07:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=56563 The Port Polska project, formerly known as the Central Communication Port (CPK), is intended to become a major transfer gateway for Central and Eastern Europe.

]]> Poland is pressing ahead with plans to build a major new international airport and high-speed rail hub intended to challenge established Western European gateways, with the country’s airport operator insisting that a 2032 opening is still “achievable” despite financing and construction challenges.

The Port Polska project, formerly known as the Central Communication Port (CPK), is intended to become a major transfer gateway for Central and Eastern Europe.

Poland’s new airport moves to execution phase

Speaking to Aerospace Global News at the Routes World 2026 conference in Frankfurt, a Polish Airports (PPL) spokesperson said the project had moved beyond its initial planning and was now entering execution phase, with the focus shifting to construction contracts and securing the financing needed to deliver the airport.

“Maintaining the 2032 opening target is achievable provided we maintain strict contractual discipline and efficiently close the debt financing structure,” the spokesperson said.

The airport component is estimated to cost PLN42.7bn (€10.1bn), with the next two to three years described as critical for the project. 

Major tenders covering earthworks, the passenger terminal and airside infrastructure are due to be awarded, while negotiations continue with a consortium of commercial banks and development institutions.

Read more: Poland inducts first F-35As as Warsaw outlines plan to double fleet to 64 jets Read more: Poland inducts first F-35As as Warsaw outlines plan to double fleet to 64 jets

PPL said the final one of 18 executive design contracts covering 36 airport support facilities was completed in mid-October 2026. 

The company said there had been administrative delays affecting earthworks, and there were additional complications from the availability of construction contractors and financing negotiations.

A new transfer hub for Central and Eastern Europe

Port Polska is designed to address what PPL said was a gap in the country’s aviation infrastructure, with the absence of a large transfer hub comparable with Frankfurt or other Western European airports.

The initial development will have capacity for more than 30 million passengers annually, with a modular terminal design allowing this to increase to 45 million. 

Land will also be safeguarded for further expansion over subsequent decades.

The airport will operate 24 hours, with two parallel runways measuring 4,000m by 60m. Designed to the highest ICAO 4F classification, the facility is expected to accommodate between 80 and 90 independent aircraft movements an hour. The longer-term masterplan, extending to 2060, also reserves space for a third independent runway measuring 3,800m.

Facilitating more seamless connections

A key consideration in the design is the ability to facilitate connections between domestic, European and long-haul services. PPL is aiming for minimum connecting times of 35-45 minutes for domestic transfers and 45-60 minutes for international connections.

The airport’s development is closely linked to LOT Polish Airlines, which may use the new hub to expand its network and strengthen its hand against larger European carriers in neighbouring Germany and Scandinavia. 

Cargo is another part of the strategy. PPL wants to increase Polish air freight volumes from approximately 200,000 tonnes annually to more than one million tonnes.

The new airport will include dedicated cargo infrastructure and will be able to operate without night-time noise restrictions, which PPL believes could help it attract new freight operators.

High-speed rail links to airport

The airport is being developed as part of a wider transport programme, with a new high-speed rail network intended to connect it with major Polish cities.

Trains operating at speeds of up to 350km/h will serve a station integrated directly into the airport terminal, allowing passengers to transfer between air and rail services.

The first section of the network, linking Warsaw, the airport and Lodz, is scheduled to open alongside the airport in 2032. 

The wider Y-shaped railway network, extending to Poznan and Wroclaw, is scheduled for completion by 2035.

Chopin Airport faces capacity squeeze ahead of relocation

The transition to Port Polska will require the eventual transfer of civil passenger operations from Warsaw Chopin Airport, which handled 24.1 million passengers in 2025.

Chopin is already operating under considerable capacity pressure, with demand for slots reaching approximately 150% of available capacity, according to PPL.

The airport is undergoing a terminal modernisation and expansion programme intended to increase its annual capacity beyond 30 million passengers. 

Dual-use infrastructure to help in times of war

The project also has a strategic dimension beyond commercial aviation, given Poland’s position on NATO’s eastern border and the proximity of the war in Ukraine.

PPL argued that aviation infrastructure should increasingly be considered part of Europe’s wider security architecture, particularly in relation to military mobility, air freight and the ability to support allied forces during a crisis.

It has called on the European Commission to establish dedicated funding for dual-use airport infrastructure, particularly 24-hour cargo facilities that could support commercial logistics during peacetime and military or humanitarian operations when required.

The company also highlighted the importance of developing domestic supply chains. 

The scale of PPL’s ambitions for the country’s airports reflects the pace of growth in the Polish aviation market, which expanded by more than 14% in 2025, almost three times the European average. 

PPL forecasts that national passenger traffic will exceed 114 million annually by 2040.

]]> IATA warns too few air accident reports are made public https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/air-accident-investigation-reports-iata-icao/ Fri, 13 Nov 2026 14:21:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=56626 Only about half of aviation accidents investigated under international rules result in a published final report, an IATA safety executive has said.

The post IATA warns too few air accident reports are made public appeared first on AGN.

]]> Authorities publish final reports for only about half of aviation accidents investigated under international rules, an International Air Transport Association (IATA) executive has said. The reporting gaps make it harder for airlines and regulators to identify hazards that could lead to similar accidents elsewhere.

Mark Searle, IATA’s global director of safety, told Reuters that he saw little improvement in publication rates. “I don’t think 50% is acceptable,” he said, speaking on the sidelines of the International Aviation Safety Summit in Montreal. “It just seems ​we’re floating around that 50% and there’s no real sort of forward trajectory.”

Hassan Shahidi, president and chief executive of the Flight Safety Foundation, which organised the summit, told Reuters that investigating bodies often cite a shortage of staff with the expertise to complete reports. He said some cases are also politically sensitive, including suspected aircraft downings.

What IATA’s accident data shows

IATA’s 2025 Annual Safety Report found that investigations had been completed for 63% of the 203 accidents it recorded from 2019 to 2023. 

The association has set up a database of safety recommendations from accident investigations. 

This gives operators a way to discover findings that apply to their own fleets or procedures. For example, a report can give an airline enough detail to review whether its training addresses the circumstances that led to an accident involving another operator.

What investigators must publish after a year

The International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO) sets out the investigation process in Annex 13 to the Chicago Convention. The state conducting the investigation must make the final report public as soon as possible and, if possible, within 12 months of the occurrence.

If the final report is unavailable after 12 months, the investigating state must publish an interim statement on each anniversary. The statement should describe the progress of the investigation and any safety issues it has raised. A preliminary report shares early factual information, generally within 30 days, while investigators still gather and analyse evidence.

Before publication, the investigating state circulates the draft final report to the states entitled to participate and gives them an opportunity to comment. Investigators can issue urgent safety recommendations while that work is underway.

The final report brings together the evidence, analysis, conclusions and any safety recommendations so others can see how the findings were reached.

Air India Flight 171 final report still pending

India’s investigation into Air India Flight 171 shows how the interim reporting process works. The Boeing 787-8, bound for London Gatwick, crashed shortly after take-off from Ahmedabad on 12 June 2025. The crash killed 260 people on the aircraft and on the ground.

India’s Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau published a preliminary report in July 2025 and issued an interim statement on the first anniversary. In that update, the bureau said it was continuing to analyse evidence. As AGN reported at the time, families were still waiting for the investigators’ conclusions a year after the crash.

Reuters reported on 12 November that the timing of the final report remained unclear. When published, the findings will give families and the aviation industry the investigators’ account of what happened and set out any recommendations arising from the evidence which could prevent a similar tragedy in the future.

]]> The aerospace startup Hermeus, and the established aerospace giant Northrop Grumman, have announced a new strategic teaming agreement to advance high-Mach, unmanned aircraft.

Hermeus & Northrop Grumman agree on new strategic agreement

Under the agreement, Northrop is to provide integrated mission systems, design, development, integration, and sustainment. Meanwhile, Hermeus is to develop a next-generation reusable, unmanned high-Mach platform.

In a press release, Hermeus says these are to “deliver affordable capability on relevant timelines.” Hermeus is hailing the agreement as providing a path to equip its aircraft with sensing, comms, navigation, and command and control technologies.

These technologies will allow its autonomous aircraft to “operate more intelligently” and take on more complex missions.

The statements by Northrop Grumman and Hermeus leave open many important questions. They failed to elaborate specifically on the kind of operational missions that future Hermeus drones could perform.

It is also unclear which branches of the US military are being targeted, what the envisioned timeline is, or how much they will cost.

Building a new class of aircraft for US forces

Zach Shore, CEO of Hermeus, stated, “We’re building a new class of aircraft that gives the warfighter improved speed, range, and flexibility while integrating into the existing Force.”

He said that Northrop Grumman is able to provide the battle-tested mission systems the company needs to build aircraft that can work in real-world scenarios. This will enable Hermeus to develop its aircraft faster.

It is unclear exactly what type of aircraft Hermeus has in mind beyond its Quaterhouse in development. New aircraft are to be rapidly developed and iterated and come with an in-house mission management system (MMS) core.

This is an open and modular system designed to keep flight-critical and mission-critical functions cleanly separated. The MMS core will allow future integrations and updates in weeks rather than years.

Hermeus has previously said its goal is to develop high-supersonic aircraft and eventually hypersonic aircraft for the US military.

Watch: Hermeus achieves first supersonic flight with Quarterhorse CCA Watch: Hermeus achieves first supersonic flight with Quarterhorse CCA

Hermeus’ efforts to develop high-Mach aircraft

AGN has previously reported Hermeus is developing the F-16-sized high-Mach Quaterhorse unmanned combat aircraft as well as parasitic Ramjet-X expendable ramjet-powered autonomous vehicles to facilitate high-Mach testing.

Quarterhorse first broke the sound barrier in May, and the next version, the Mk 2.2, is expected to push beyond Mach 2. It is possible the agreement with Northrop is related to the Quarterhorse, or it could be an undisclosed programme.

Most aircraft being developed, including Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCAs), are subsonic. As much of the military sector moved toward stealth, emphasis has generally moved away from the early Cold War’s focus on higher and higher speeds.

For Hermeus, this is a mistake, and it explicitly says its mission is to reclaim the “lost art of rapid iterative prototyping to build fast and powerful aircraft on relevant timelines, delivering the high-speed systems…”

Separately, it would seem that NASA’s Administrator, Jared Isaacman, would agree. In recent months, a long-retired and displayed Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird has disappeared.

It appears NASA is planning to use the airframe as a testbed for new high-Mach engines and maybe other systems. Isaacman has cryptically teased the Blackbird, but also said it’s classified.

He has posted, “NASA is rebuilding its X-plane portfolio, and soon we’ll be flying faster and higher, just as we did in decades past.”

]]> ULA’s Vulcan rocket set for return to flight with 40 Amazon satellites https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/ulas-vulcan-rocket-flight-40-amazon-satellites/ Fri, 13 Nov 2026 13:06:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=56587 United Launch Alliance is set to return its Vulcan rocket to flight on November 13 following a nine-month hiatus, deploying 40 Amazon Leo broadband satellites in the vehicle's first six-booster heavy-lift configuration.

The post ULA’s Vulcan rocket set for return to flight with 40 Amazon satellites appeared first on AGN.

]]> United Launch Alliance (ULA) is preparing to launch 40 Amazon Leo broadband satellites aboard its Vulcan rocket today (13 November), marking the vehicle’s return to flight after a nine-month gap following an anomaly during a US military mission.

The launch, scheduled for 12:54 p.m. Eastern Time (17:54 UTC) from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida, will be Vulcan’s fifth flight and its first carrying satellites for Amazon’s planned internet constellation.

It will also be the first Vulcan launch using six solid rocket boosters, the maximum number the vehicle can accommodate.

The configuration provides the additional thrust needed to carry heavier payloads into orbit.

The mission, designated Leo Vulcan 1 (LV-01), is the first of 38 Vulcan launches Amazon has contracted with ULA to help build its satellite network.

The flight comes at an important time for both companies. ULA, a joint venture between Boeing and Lockheed Martin, is working to establish Vulcan as its principal rocket for commercial and US national security missions. Amazon, meanwhile, needs frequent launches to deploy thousands of satellites for a broadband service intended to compete with SpaceX’s Starlink.

Vulcan returns after February anomaly


Vulcan last flew on 12 February, when it carried out a national security mission for the US Space Force.

Although the rocket delivered its payload, an anomaly was observed during the flight, prompting a prolonged gap before its next launch.

“As with any new rocket, there are risks associated with every launch, and particularly as we are early in this phase of introduction of Vulcan to the market and working to a regular operational tempo. Every flight generates data and every flight teaches us something.

“And we’re going to look to this flight to get some more useful data in a flight environment on the effectiveness of the corrective action that we’ve implemented,” said Mark Peller, ULA president and CEO.

The February mission was Vulcan’s fourth flight. Its first two missions took place in 2024, followed by national security launches beginning in August 2025.

“During our first four Vulcan missions, the robustness of Vulcan served us well. It flew through some difficult environments associated with the SRB anomalies and successfully completed all of those missions, giving the spacecraft both a smooth ride and precise, bullseye orbital injections,” Peller noted.

The rocket is intended to succeed ULA’s Atlas V and Delta IV families. Delta IV was retired in April 2024, while Atlas V remains operational and has already carried Amazon satellites on eight missions.

The November 13 launch will therefore be an important test of Vulcan’s ability to resume operations while taking on a larger share of ULA’s commercial launch commitments.

The vehicle selected for LV-01 is designated VC6L. Its six solid rocket boosters provide additional power alongside two BE-4 main engines developed by Blue Origin.

The engines burn liquefied natural gas and liquid oxygen, while the six Northrop Grumman-built solid boosters provide further thrust during the initial ascent.
ULA says the configuration can carry more than 22,700kg of payload on an Amazon Leo mission.

The rocket also features a modified Centaur V upper stage, optimised for launches into low Earth orbit. The shorter version is intended to increase the number of satellites Vulcan can carry on each mission.

Its two RL10 engines use liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen to place payloads into their intended orbits.

Amazon expects subsequent Vulcan missions to carry larger satellite batches as further improvements to the rocket are introduced.

Amazon prepares to accelerate launches

The 40 satellites aboard LV-01 represent the largest single batch yet launched for Amazon Leo, previously known as Project Kuiper.

The network is designed to provide high-speed internet access to homes, businesses and communities, particularly in areas poorly served by terrestrial broadband infrastructure.

Amazon’s initial constellation is planned to comprise more than 3,000 satellites operating in coordinated low Earth orbits.

The company said it completed production of its 1,000th satellite in early September and now has hundreds of flight-ready spacecraft awaiting launch.
However, manufacturing satellites is only part of the challenge. Getting them into orbit quickly enough requires a sustained launch schedule involving several rocket operators.

Amazon has contracted launches with ULA, Arianespace, Blue Origin and SpaceX. Vulcan is expected to carry more than 1,500 first-generation Amazon Leo satellites across its 38 contracted missions.

“Larger rockets and more frequent launches are critical to scaling our constellation and getting service to customers, and the Vulcan program is designed to deliver on both dimensions,” said Melissa Wuerl, director of launch systems for Amazon Leo.

“Vulcan will launch close to half our first-generation constellation, making it our primary workhorse over the next several years, and we’re looking forward to kicking off the sprint with our partners at ULA.”

New facilities to shorten launch turnaround

Amazon has also invested in dedicated launch infrastructure at Cape Canaveral to reduce the time needed between Vulcan missions.

The facilities include a new Vertical Integration Facility, known as VIF-A, and a dedicated mobile launch platform.

They allow ULA to prepare two Vulcan rockets simultaneously rather than completing preparations for one before beginning work on another.

The second Amazon Vulcan mission, LV-02, is already undergoing preparations in another integration facility and could launch within weeks of LV-01, provided the first mission proceeds successfully.

Amazon is also preparing another Ariane 6 launch, designated Leo Europe 4, from Europe’s Spaceport in French Guiana no earlier than November 23.

The company expects to begin an initial rollout of its satellite broadband service later this year, with further launches expanding coverage and capacity.

Vulcan’s return will be closely watched by both the commercial launch industry and the US Space Force, which is counting on the rocket for future national security missions.

A successful flight would give ULA a route back to regular launches while providing Amazon with the heavy-lift capacity it needs to expand its satellite network.

]]> Wizz Air bets on downturn to accelerate its pan-European expansion https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/wizz-air-europe-expansion/ Fri, 13 Nov 2026 12:19:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=56520 Chief executive József Váradi said the retreat of rival airlines in Europe was opening up markets for the low-cost carrier to expand.

The post Wizz Air bets on downturn to accelerate its pan-European expansion appeared first on AGN.

]]> Never let a good crisis go to waste, goes the saying, and for Wizz Air that is certainly the case as it seeks to grow as competitors shrink amid the industry’s latest downturn.

Chief executive József Váradi said the retreat of rival airlines in Europe was opening up markets for the low-cost carrier to expand.

“When it’s a bad time for the industry, you have to take a different pace, and you have to take a different avenue than the rest of the guys,” Váradi said at Routes World 2026 in Frankfurt. “This is the time to act.”

Wizz Air’s plan for growth despite the headwinds

The airline expects to grow by around 20% in 2026, Váradi said, despite high fuel prices and geopolitical disruption. 

Wizz has moderated its winter growth plan from an initial 30% to 20%, but is still expanding while much of the wider industry contracts in the face of those challenges.

Váradi said that capacity cuts by other airlines were creating opportunities for Wizz to fill gaps in the market.

“We are trying to fill the void, fill these gaps created by others,” he said, describing the company as well suited to “organically consolidate” markets by adding its own capacity when rivals shrink or exit. 

He ruled out acquisitions as a central part of that approach, saying mergers and acquisitions were “counterintuitive” to Wizz’s ultra-low-cost-carrier focus on simplicity and efficiency.

Looking beyond eastern Europe

The growth push comes as Wizz is seeking to become more pan-European than it has been in the past. 

While Central and Eastern Europe remains its core market, Váradi said the airline was intent on broadening its reach. 

“Central East Europe is only 10 percent of the total European airline market,” he said. “You are not going to survive in the long run with only being focused on 10 percent” of the market.

Italy, Spain and the UK are key to that strategy. Váradi described the UK as Wizz’s first move beyond its Central and Eastern European base, Italy as the second, and Spain as the next. 

He said the airline was seeking to build on its experience in Italy, where it has established operating bases, and replicate that approach in Spain.

The shift westward, he stressed, does not mean abandoning Wizz’s established markets. 

Low-cost-carriers pick up slack where legacy airlines retreat

The airline has a 27% market share in Central and Eastern Europe, according to Váradi, and intends to strengthen that position while adding capacity elsewhere. 

He pointed to new bases and network growth in the region, alongside increasing demand from a rising middle class and more outbound leisure travel. 

Váradi said Wizz’s expansion was the latest chapter in the expansion of low-cost airlines across the continent. 

“The entire growth is coming from low-cost carriers,” he said, arguing that legacy airlines were not adding capacity at the same pace and would face declining market share. 

Hedging offers clarity on fuel costs in the short term

Fuel economics are central to his confidence. Váradi said Wizz was 85% hedged for the next six months at $800 per metric tonne, compared with a market price of about $1,500, and 50% hedged for summer 2027 at $900. 

He also cited the fuel efficiency of the airline’s Airbus Neo fleet as an advantage.

Váradi acknowledged that a sudden end to the Middle East conflict and a sharp fall in fuel prices could leave Wizz paying a premium on its hedges. 

But he said the airline was prepared to keep investing while remaining selective. Airports whose existing carriers were “wobbling”, he said, were already asking Wizz whether it could step in. 

“When everyone else is going to shrink and increase fares,” he said, Wizz believes it can “manoeuvre in that environment very well for further growth.”

 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 32px;}
.sie-dest-hero__label{display: block;
 font-size: 13px;
 font-weight: 500;
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.75);
 margin-bottom: 12px;
 letter-spacing: 0.03em;}
.sie-dest-hero__label a{color: inherit;
 text-decoration: none;}
.sie-dest-hero__label a:hover{color: #fff;
 text-decoration: underline;}
.sie-dest-hero__title{font-size: clamp(32px, 5vw, 56px);
 font-weight: 800;
 color: #ffffff;
 margin: 0 0 14px;
 line-height: 1.1;
 letter-spacing: -0.02em;
 max-width: 800px;}
.sie-dest-hero__tagline{font-size: clamp(15px, 2vw, 19px);
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);
 margin: 0 0 28px;
 max-width: 1100px;
 line-height: 1.5;
 font-weight: 400;}
.sie-dest-hero__cta{display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 8px;
 padding: 12px 24px;
 background: #1E56B0;
 color: #fff;
 font-size: 15px;
 font-weight: 600;
 border-radius: 6px;
 text-decoration: none;
 transition: background 0.2s;}
.sie-dest-hero__cta:hover{background: #163e82;
 color: #fff;
 text-decoration: none;}
.sie-dest-hero__actions{display: flex;
 flex-wrap: wrap;
 gap: 12px;
 margin-top: 4px;}
.sie-dest-hero__cta--secondary{background: transparent;
 border: 2px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.6);
 color: #fff;}
.sie-dest-hero__cta--secondary:hover{background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.12);
 border-color: #fff;
 color: #fff;}
.sie-country-heart--hero{position: static !important;
 top: auto !important;
 right: auto !important;
 padding: 10px 20px;
 font-size: 14px;
 font-weight: 600;
 gap: 8px;
 border-radius: 6px;
 min-width: unset;
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.92);
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.12);
 border: 2px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.6);
 box-shadow: none;
 backdrop-filter: none;
 white-space: nowrap;
 cursor: pointer;
 font-family: inherit;
 line-height: 1;
 display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;}
.sie-country-heart--hero:hover{background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.22) !important;
 border-color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.9) !important;
 color: #fff !important;
 transform: none;}
.sie-country-heart--hero.voted{background: rgba(239, 68, 68, 0.28) !important;
 border-color: #f87171 !important;
 color: #fff !important;}
.sie-country-heart--hero.voted i{color: #fca5a5;}
.sie-country-heart--hero .sie-country-heart__count{display: none;
 font-size: 12px;
 opacity: 0.85;}
.sie-country-heart--hero.has-votes .sie-country-heart__count{display: inline;}
.sie-dest-body{max-width: 1100px;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 24px 80px;}
.sie-dest-stats{display: flex;
 flex-wrap: wrap;
 gap: 0;
 background: #f0f4fb;
 border: 1px solid #d4e0f5;
 border-radius: 10px;
 margin: 32px 0;
 overflow: hidden;}
.sie-dest-stat{flex: 1;
 min-width: 150px;
 display: flex;
 flex-direction: column;
 gap: 4px;
 padding: 18px 20px;
 border-right: 1px solid #d4e0f5;}
.sie-dest-stat:last-child{border-right: none;}
.sie-dest-stat__label{font-size: 11px;
 font-weight: 600;
 color: #505a6b; 
 text-transform: uppercase;
 letter-spacing: 0.06em;}
.sie-dest-stat__value{font-size: 14px;
 font-weight: 700;
 color: #003B73;
 line-height: 1.3;}
.sie-admreq-cta-strip .sie-dest-hero__cta{display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 0.5rem;
 padding: 0.75rem 1.5rem;
 background: #fff;
 color: #1d4ed8;
 border-radius: 6px;
 font-weight: 700;
 text-decoration: none;
 font-size: 0.97rem;
 transition: opacity 0.2s;}
.sie-admreq-cta-strip .sie-dest-hero__cta:hover{opacity: 0.9;}

.leo-confirm-yes:hover{background:#1E3354 !important}
.leo-confirm-no{background:#fff !important;background-image:none !important;color:#12233D !important;border:1px solid #C3C9CE !important;border-radius:4px !important;box-shadow:none !important}
.leo-confirm-no:hover{border-color:#12233D !important}
.leo-sat{background:#F4F2ED !important;background-image:none !important;border:1px solid #E4E0D8 !important;border-radius:6px !important}
.leo-visit-website{background:#12233D !important;border-radius:4px !important}
.leo-visit-website:hover{background:#1E3354 !important}
.leo-score-pill{background:#F4F2ED !important;color:#12233D !important;border-color:#E4E0D8 !important;border-radius:3px !important}
.leo-ovv2{border-color:#E4E0D8 !important;border-radius:6px !important;box-shadow:none !important}
.leo-ovv2>summary{background:#F4F2ED !important;border-bottom-color:#E4E0D8 !important}
.leo-ovv2-hl{color:#12233D !important;font-family:"IBM Plex Mono",ui-monospace,monospace !important;font-weight:500 !important;letter-spacing:.06em !important}
.leo-ovv2-toggle{background:#12233D !important;border-radius:4px !important}
.leo-ovv2>summary:hover .leo-ovv2-toggle{background:#1E3354 !important}
.leo-ovv2-mapwrap,.leo-ovv2-tile{background:#FAF8F4 !important;border-radius:4px !important}
.leo-ovv2-filterbar{border-color:#E4E0D8 !important;border-radius:6px !important;box-shadow:none !important}
.leo-ovv2-search:focus{border-color:#12233D !important;box-shadow:0 0 0 3px rgba(18,35,61,.10) !important}
/* "What are you looking for?" composer: site-wide overlay (#slo-, leo-entry-overlay JS)

#slo-backdrop,.lh-chat-backdrop,.lh-chat-overlay.lh-discover-mode .lh-chat-backdrop{background:rgba(18,35,61,.55) !important;backdrop-filter:blur(2px) !important;-webkit-backdrop-filter:blur(2px) !important}
#slo-drawer,.lh-chat-drawer,.lh-chat-overlay.lh-discover-mode .lh-chat-drawer{background:#FAF8F4 !important;background-image:none !important;border-radius:8px 8px 0 0 !important;box-shadow:0 -12px 40px rgba(18,35,61,.25) !important}
.slo-orb,.lh-chat-orb{display:none !important}
.slo-brand,.lh-chat-drawer-brand{background:#12233D;margin:0 -36px 26px !important;padding:16px 36px !important;border-bottom:0 !important}

.slo-title,.lh-chat-drawer-title{font-family:"Source Serif 4",Georgia,serif !important;font-weight:600 !important;font-size:26px !important;color:#12233D !important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#12233D !important;letter-spacing:-.01em}

.slo-input-wrap,.lh-chat-drawer-inner .lh-input-wrap{background:#fff !important;border:1px solid #C3C9CE !important;border-radius:6px !important;box-shadow:none !important}

 space for unsized images. They were removed — those same images are also
 used as DECORATIVE icons sized purely by CSS (e.g. the Leonardo lynx in
 the chat header), and "height:auto" overrode that sizing and let them
 balloon to full intrinsic size. The real, measured CLS cause is the font
 swap handled above; any genuinely-unsized content image should get
 width/height attributes on the tag itself, not a blanket src selector. */
 /* Homepage auto-playing chat demo: the typing animation appends message
 bubbles and result cards, which used to GROW the demo window and push
 everything below it on every cycle (measured: CLS 0.258 on the
 homepage). Fixed internal heights make the animation play inside a
 constant-size box — newest messages stick to the bottom like a real
 chat, the results tray keeps its space reserved. */
 #lh-demo-chat {
 height: 240px;

 justify-content: flex-end;
 overflow: hidden;
 }
 #lh-demo-flow {
 height: 250px;
 overflow: hidden;
 }

 /* ── Make the search the priority, not an afterthought ────────────────
 Measured before this change at 1440x900: hero 1028px tall, search bar
 top at y=694. Tightened the vertical rhythm and moved the trust row
 below, which lifts the bar roughly 230px — comfortably in view. */
 .lh-hero.lh-hero{padding:clamp(28px,4vw,56px) 0 clamp(32px,4.5vw,64px)}
 .lh-hero .lh-hero-center{gap:clamp(16px,2vw,26px)}
 /* ⚠️ THE CAUSE OF THE BIG EMPTY GAP, and it was mine. The stylesheet sets
 .lh-hero-text{flex:1 1 380px} and .lh-portals{flex:1 1 420px}. Those were
 written for the original ROW layout, where flex-basis is a WIDTH. Turning
 the container into a column silently turned both into fixed HEIGHTS: the
 text box stayed 380px tall although its content ended after 187px, and
 the search row stayed 420px tall although the cards are 195px. That is
 ~420px of enforced emptiness. Resetting the basis is the whole fix —
 never set flex-direction on an inherited flex container without checking
 what flex-basis meant before. */
 .lh-hero .lh-hero-text{flex:0 0 auto}
 .lh-hero .lh-portals--search{flex:0 0 auto}
 .lh-hero .lh-badge{margin-bottom:10px}

 /* ── Results as a responsive grid, not a single strip ──────────────────
 .sie-res-list holds the program cards as direct children (verified live:
 18 cards, one parent, no headers in between), so one grid rule is enough.
 ⚠️ SCOPED TO THE HOMEPAGE ON PURPOSE. .sie-res-list is the shared
 SieFlowView markup — Leonardo renders into it too, with its own
 per-card animation offsets. Re-layouting it globally would change his
 results as a side effect of a homepage fix. */
 .lh-herosearch .sie-res-list{display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fill,minmax(320px,1fr));gap:16px;align-items:start}
 .lh-herosearch .sie-res-list > .program-card{width:auto;max-width:none;margin:0}

 per country. Each branch carries max-width:560px inside a 798px rail, so
 two never fit and they stack — the "single strip". Releasing the cap and
 tiling the branches gives two country panels per row at this width, and
 more on a wider screen, without touching the cards inside.
 ⚠️ Scoped to .lh-herosearch: Leonardo renders the same flow markup. */
 .lh-herosearch .sie-flow__branches{display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fill,minmax(360px,1fr));gap:18px;align-items:start}
 .lh-herosearch .sie-flow__branch{max-width:none;width:100%}
 /* ── The figures strip ────────────────────────────────────────────────
 Serif numerals, monospaced labels, hairline rules, no card, no shadow,
 no colour fill behind each figure. The register of a register. */
 .lh-stats.lh-stats--figures{background:#F4F2ED;border-top:1px solid #E4E0D8;border-bottom:1px solid #E4E0D8;padding:0}
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stats-grid{max-width:1200px;margin:0 auto;padding:0 clamp(16px,4vw,48px);display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(4,minmax(0,1fr));gap:0}
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat{padding:clamp(20px,2.4vw,32px) clamp(14px,2vw,28px) clamp(20px,2.4vw,32px) 0;border-right:1px solid #E4E0D8;text-align:left;background:none;border-radius:0;box-shadow:none}
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat:last-child{border-right:0}
 /* Every cell except the first gets inner space on its left, so each rule
 sits with equal air on both sides instead of crowding the next figure.

 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat + .lh-stat{padding-left:clamp(18px,2.4vw,34px)}

 /* #6B7A8D measured 3.92:1 against the warm band — under the 4.5:1 that
 11.5px text needs. The cool grey was fine on the old cold background and
 quietly failed when the palette warmed up; #4F5967 measures 6.2:1.
 Worth remembering when warming any other background. */
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat-label{margin-top:8px;font-family:"IBM Plex Mono",ui-monospace,monospace;font-size:11.5px;letter-spacing:1.3px;text-transform:uppercase;color:#4F5967}

 .lh-inst-body{margin:0 0 26px;font-size:clamp(15.5px,1.4vw,17px);line-height:1.65;color:#C6D2E0;max-width:54ch}

 /* ── Institutional pass, part 2 (2026-11-08, evening) ──────────────────
 Brings the sections below the hero onto the palette and type the hero
 already uses, so the page reads as one document instead of two designs
 stacked on top of each other. Everything here is homepage-only (it lives
 in this template) and is pure CSS: delete this block to revert. */
 /* The page itself: the site-wide body is cold pale blue (#E8F1FA), which
 showed through every transparent section (the institutions carousel and
 the study fields block) as a blue band between warm ones. */
 body.page-id-150{background:#FAF8F4}
 /* ⚠️ THE HEADLINE NEVER WAS SERIF. leonardo-homepage-css.min.css carries
 `.lh-wrap .lh-title{font-family:system-ui !important; font-size:44px
 !important; font-weight:800 !important; color:#003b73 !important}`, so
 the Source Serif rule earlier in this block lost on every device. Only
 !important with equal-or-higher specificity can beat it. */
 .lh-wrap .lh-hero .lh-title,.lh-wrap .lh-hero h2.lh-title{font-family:"Source Serif 4",Georgia,serif !important;font-weight:600 !important;font-size:clamp(34px,4.4vw,58px) !important;line-height:1.08 !important;letter-spacing:-.6px !important;color:#12233D !important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#12233D !important}

 EUROPE") already does that job; the extra pill only added noise. */
 .lh-hero .lh-badge{display:none}

 the screen edge while the centred text did not. Left-aligned, with the
 same 20px gutter as the rest of the page, it matches the desktop. */
 @media(max-width:900px){
 .lh-hero .lh-hero-center{padding-left:20px;padding-right:20px;box-sizing:border-box;text-align:left}

 .lh-wrap .lh-hero .lh-title{text-align:left}

 }

 Serif headings and a small monospaced label instead of the rounded blue
 pills, which were the last "app" element on the page. */

 .lh-wrap .lh-section-badge{display:inline-block;margin-bottom:14px;padding:0;background:none;border-radius:0;font-family:"IBM Plex Mono",ui-monospace,monospace;font-size:11.5px;font-weight:500;letter-spacing:1.8px;text-transform:uppercase;color:#8C5A23}
 .lh-wrap .lh-section-sub{color:#4A525C}
 /* Section rhythm: paper / white / paper, so each block has an edge. */

 .lh-wrap .lh-unis{background:#fff;border-top:1px solid #E4E0D8}
 .lh-wrap .lh-dest-section--origins{background:#fff;border-top:1px solid #E4E0D8}

 .lh-wrap .lh-dest-section--countries a[class*="card"],.lh-wrap .lh-dest-section--countries [class*="card"]{border-radius:6px}
 /* ── Study fields block (rendered by [sie_study_fields] after .lh-wrap) ─
 Six bright category colours, gradient pills and a gradient CTA made it

 The branch colours arrive as INLINE custom properties and inline
 backgrounds, so these overrides need !important to apply. Scoped to the
 homepage: the study-field pages keep their colour coding. */
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-title{font-family:"Source Serif 4",Georgia,serif;font-weight:600;font-size:clamp(28px,3vw,40px);letter-spacing:-.4px;color:#12233D}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-subtitle{color:#4A525C}

 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__junction-dot{background:#12233D}

 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__branch-count{background:#F4F2ED !important;color:#12233D !important}

 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__field-icon{background:#F4F2ED !important;color:#12233D !important;border-radius:5px}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__leo-link{color:#0B5FA5 !important}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-leonardo{background:#12233D !important;background-image:none !important;border-radius:6px}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-leo-btn{background:#fff !important;color:#12233D !important;border-color:#fff !important;border-radius:4px}
 /* Alignment: the search widget carries its own 24px side padding, so the
 bar sat indented from the headline above it; and the trust row was
 centred under a left-aligned column. Both now share the text's edge.
 Only the LEFT padding goes: removing the right one too pushed the
 "AI-enhanced matching" toggle across the seam into the navy side. */
 .lh-herosearch .sie-sps-wrap{padding-left:0 !important}
 .lh-hero .lh-trust-row{justify-content:flex-start}
 /* Institution cards: the stylesheet tints each card top a different pastel

 monogram or logo is the only thing that differs between cards. */
 .lh-wrap .lh-uni-card:nth-child(n) .lh-uni-card-top{background:#F4F2ED !important;background-image:none !important;border-bottom:1px solid #EDEAE3}
 .lh-wrap .lh-uni-cta{color:#0B5FA5 !important}
 .lh-wrap .sie-dest-hub__name{color:#12233D}
 /* Europe silhouette on the navy side. Present, never loud: a lighter blue

 DESTINATIONS PANEL  — overlay + grid
 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
 /* Outer layer: covers full viewport */
 .sie-dest-panel {
 position: fixed;
 inset: 0;
 z-index: 2147483000;
 display: flex;
 align-items: stretch;
 justify-content: flex-end;
 opacity: 0;
 visibility: hidden;
 pointer-events: none;
 transition: opacity .25s ease, visibility .25s;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open {
 opacity: 1;
 visibility: visible;
 pointer-events: auto;
 }
 /* Backdrop */
 .sie-dest-panel__backdrop {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 background: rgba(11, 55, 112, .52);
 backdrop-filter: blur(3px);
 -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(3px);
 cursor: pointer;
 }
 /* Sheet — right-panel on desktop */
 .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 position: relative;
 z-index: 1;
 width: min(800px, 100%);
 height: 100%;
 background: #fff;
 overflow-y: auto;
 -webkit-overflow-scrolling: touch;
 padding: 26px 26px 40px;
 display: flex;
 flex-direction: column;
 gap: 0;
 transform: translateX(28px);
 opacity: 0;
 transition: transform .38s cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1), opacity .38s cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1);
 box-shadow: -20px 0 48px rgba(0,0,0,.18);
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 transform: translateX(0);
 opacity: 1;
 }
 /* Mobile: bottom-sheet */
 @media (max-width: 767px) {
 .sie-dest-panel {
 align-items: flex-end;
 justify-content: stretch;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 width: 100%;
 height: 92vh;
 border-top-left-radius: 22px;
 border-top-right-radius: 22px;
 padding: 20px 16px 40px;
 transform: translateY(28px);
 box-shadow: 0 -16px 48px rgba(0,0,0,.18);
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 transform: translateY(0);
 }
 }
 /* ── Header ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__header {
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 justify-content: space-between;
 margin-bottom: 6px;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__titlewrap {
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 10px;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__globe {
 font-size: 22px;
 color: #1e66f5;
 line-height: 1;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__title {
 font-size: 1.5rem;
 font-weight: 800;
 color: #0b3770;
 margin: 0;
 line-height: 1.2;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__close {
 background: transparent;
 border: 0;
 font-size: 22px;
 color: #0b3770;
 cursor: pointer;
 padding: 6px 8px;
 border-radius: 8px;
 line-height: 1;
 opacity: .75;
 transition: opacity .15s, background .15s;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__close:hover {
 opacity: 1;
 background: #f0f4ff;
 }
 /* Subheading */
 .sie-dest-panel__sub {
 color: #466087;
 font-size: .94rem;
 margin: 0 0 20px;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 /* ── Country grid ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 display: grid;
 grid-template-columns: repeat(4, 1fr);
 gap: 14px;
 /* allow this to grow and scroll */
 flex: 1;
 align-content: start;
 }
 @media (max-width: 620px) {
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 grid-template-columns: repeat(2, 1fr);
 gap: 10px;
 }
 }
 @media (min-width: 621px) and (max-width: 860px) {
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);
 }
 }
 /* ── Country card ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__card {
 position: relative;
 display: block;
 aspect-ratio: 3 / 2;
 border-radius: 12px;
 overflow: hidden;
 text-decoration: none;
 background: #1d3557;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card--no-img .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 background: linear-gradient(135deg, #1d3557 0%, #1e66f5 100%);
 }
 /* Hero image layer — scales on hover */
 .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 transition: transform .4s ease;
 will-change: transform;
 }
 /* <img> fills the card exactly like background-size:cover did.
 loading="lazy" means the browser only fetches each image when the
 panel opens and the card enters the viewport — saving ~30 MB of
 upfront image requests on every page that includes this panel. */
 .sie-dest-panel__card-img {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 width: 100%;
 height: 100%;
 object-fit: cover;
 object-position: center;
 display: block;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card:hover .sie-dest-panel__card-bg,
 .sie-dest-panel__card:focus-visible .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 transform: scale(1.07);
 }
 /* Gradient overlay + text */
 .sie-dest-panel__card-body {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 display: flex;
 flex-direction: column;
 justify-content: flex-end;
 padding: 10px 12px 10px;
 background: linear-gradient(
 to top,
 rgba(0, 0, 0, .72) 0%,
 rgba(0, 0, 0, .30) 55%,
 transparent 100%
 );
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card-name {
 color: #fff;
 font-weight: 700;
 font-size: .92rem;
 line-height: 1.2;
 text-shadow: 0 1px 5px rgba(0,0,0,.55);
 display: block;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow {
 display: block;
 color: rgba(255,255,255,0);
 font-size: .75rem;
 margin-top: 2px;
 transition: color .2s ease, transform .2s ease;
 line-height: 1;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card:hover .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow,
 .sie-dest-panel__card:focus-visible .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow {
 color: rgba(255,255,255,.9);
 transform: translateX(4px);
 }
 /* ── Body-scroll lock ── */
 body.sie-dest-panel-open {
 overflow: hidden;
 }
 /* ── Country interest heart ── */
 .sie-country-heart {
 position: absolute;
 top: 8px;
 right: 8px;
 z-index: 10;
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);
 border: none;
 border-radius: 20px;
 padding: 4px 8px 4px 7px;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
 cursor: pointer;
 font-size: 13px;
 color: #94a3b8;
 box-shadow: 0 2px 8px rgba(0,0,0,.22);
 backdrop-filter: blur(6px);
 -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(6px);
 transition: color .18s, transform .18s, background .18s;
 line-height: 1;
 min-width: 28px;
 justify-content: center;
 }
 .sie-country-heart:hover {
 transform: scale(1.12);
 background: #fff;
 color: #ef4444;
 }
 .sie-country-heart.voted {
 color: #ef4444;
 background: #fff;
 }
 .sie-country-heart.voted i {
 animation: sie-heart-pop .35s cubic-bezier(.36,.07,.19,.97);
 }
 @keyframes sie-heart-pop {
 0%   { transform: scale(1); }
 40%  { transform: scale(1.45); }
 70%  { transform: scale(.88); }
 100% { transform: scale(1); }
 }
 .sie-country-heart__count {
 font-size: 11px;
 font-weight: 700;
 color: inherit;
 display: none;
 }
 .sie-country-heart.has-votes .sie-country-heart__count {
 display: inline;
 }
 /* ── Trigger button styles (for use in any menu) ── */
 /* Desktop globe icon */
 .se-dest-desktop-btn {
 font-size: 24px;
 color: #fff;
 text-decoration: none;
 cursor: pointer;
 transition: transform .2s, color .2s;
 position: relative;
 line-height: 1;
 background: transparent;
 border: 0;
 padding: 0;
 }
 .se-dest-desktop-btn:hover {
 transform: scale(1.15);
 color: #FFCC00;
 }
 /* Tooltip on desktop */
 @media (min-width: 1024px) {
 .se-dest-desktop-btn::after {
 content: "Study Destinations";
 position: absolute;
 bottom: -30px;
 left: 50%;
 transform: translateX(-50%);
 background: #007BFF;
 color: #fff;
 padding: 4px 8px;
 font-size: 12px;
 border-radius: 5px;
 opacity: 0;
 pointer-events: none;
 transition: opacity .2s;
 white-space: nowrap;
 }
 .se-dest-desktop-btn:hover::after {
 opacity: 1;
 }
 }
 /* Mobile pill button */
 .se-dest-btn {
 background: #0b3770 !important;
 color: #fff !important;
 }
 .se-dest-btn:hover {
 background: #1e66f5 !important;

<h1 class="title-h1 eac-page-title">Conference on the Future of Europe : the future is in your hands</h1>
<span><span>sandoel</span></span>
<span><time datetime="2021-12-07T08:55:30+01:00" title="Tuesday, December 7, 2021 - 08:55">Tue, 12/07/2021 - 08:55</time>
</span>
<div class="ecl"><h2><strong>What is the Conference?</strong></h2>

<p>The <strong>Conference on the Future of Europe </strong>is the first transnational discussion with Europeans on how to address Europe’s challenges together. This is an opportunity to think about what citizens and&nbsp; civil society want for the European Union.</p>

<p>&nbsp;</p>
</div>

  <div class="eac-body lc-stripe-wrapper-text"><h2><strong>How does the Conference work?</strong></h2>

<p>Europeans can share ideas via the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Multilingual Digital Platform</a>, and both national and&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/assemblies/citizens-panels" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">European Citizens' Panels</a>. These contributions feed into the&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/plenary" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference Plenaries</a>.</p>

<p>The Conference&nbsp;offers a new public forum for an open, inclusive, and transparent debate with citizens around a number of key priorities and challenges.</p>

<h2><strong>How can you participate?</strong></h2>

<ul>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]--><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/processes?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">share your own ideas or support others’ ideas</a> on the multilingual digital Conference platform</li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->organise your own events and promote it by adding them to the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference platform</a></li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->take a look at the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/meetings" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">events organised by people across the EU</a></li>
</ul>

<h2><strong>What will the outcome be?</strong></h2>

<p>All of the ideas gathered and reports on events are published on the platform openly and transparently. These reports will then directly influence the discussions in the European Citizens’ Panels as well as in the Plenaries, where citizens will enter into a dialogue with national and European decision makers.</p>

<p>By spring 2022, the Conference will provide guidance on the future of Europe to the European institutions</p>

<p><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/getinvolved" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Get involved and make your voice heard when it comes to education, culture, youth, sport, and more</a>.</p>

<p>Follow on Twitter at&nbsp;</p>

                        <div class="eche-officer-question-icon"><img class="eche-report-question-icon" src="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/profiles/custom/eac_profile/modules/eac_eche/images/ECHE__RECTORS_Q1.png" width="100%" height="100%" alt="Question Icon" title="Question Icon" loading="lazy">
</div>
                    </div>
                    <div class="eche-report-title-question-text-wrapper">
                        <div class="eche-officer-question">Your institution has a strategy and an overarching structure supporting internationalisation</div>
                        <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close"><i class="fa fa-plus-circle fa-3x"></i></div>
                    </div>
                </div>
                <div class="eche-officer-question-wrapper eche-report-question-wrapper-show">
                    <div class="eche-report-border"></div>
                    <div classs="eche-officer-must">
                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The internationalisation strategy is available and prominently displayed on your website</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Internationalisation is an important driver for institutional change, and has a great influence on the major activities of a higher education institution (HEI) i.e. education and research. The importance of internationalisation is recognised, and most institutions have a strategy for internationalisation. However, for a strategy to be efficient, and for it to drive the HEI's activities regarding internationalisation, there is a need for its acceptance from across the whole institution. In addition the strategy could also be accessible to external collaborative partners. It is highly important to have the institution's internationalisation and modernisation strategy published and easily accessible to all.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The institution has a clear plan to implement the strategy</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The strategy and policy should include explicit allocation of responsibilities for its efficient implementation to individuals at all levels of the institution, from senior management to the heads of departments, schools and faculties, to academic and administrative staff. This will ensure acceptance and accountability for the strategy. The internationalisation strategy and policy should outline a specific implementation plan that sets out explicitly the financial and human resources available.&nbsp; For example, it is recommended to set up an International Relations Office (IRO) to implement mobility and other international projects.</p><p>As with any other activity, the institutional implementation of the internationalisation strategy is dependent on the people behind the activities. It is highly important for an institution to have staff with the right set of skills and knowledge driving the internationalisation agenda and liaising with international students and staff members. Therefore understanding the development needs of the staff and supporting their professional development should be a high priority for the institution. Such development should focus on both staff engaged in international activities as well as the supporting staff, ensuring the most efficient implementation of international activities and cooperative projects across the institution. For example, trainings/webinars/projects could be organised on intercultural competences and communication, project management, enhancement of internationalisation at home/intercultural, or other activities suggested by the staff and supported by the hierarchy.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It promotes incoming and outgoing student and staff mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Mobility is important to the development of the institution as a whole as well as for the individual participants. Therefore the HEI should make mobility and international cooperation a central element in its institutional policies, and explicitly and consistently promote and support student and staff mobility. Non-discrimination policies and further emphasis on the promotion of mobility for under-represented groups should also form an integral part of the institutional support structures.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It promotes engagement in European and international cooperation projects</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The institution's internationalisation strategy and policy should explicitly and consistently promote the development of cooperation with partners in other EU and non-EU countries. The activities and co-operation projects agreed by the HEI should be based on identified needs.
